[{"q":"Compare sparse, dense, and hybrid retrieval. When does each win?","g":["hybrid search"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Sparse retrieval</strong> (BM25, TF-IDF, and learned-sparse models such as SPLADE) represents text as a very high-dimensional vector in which almost every entry is zero; each dimension corresponds to a term in the vocabulary. A document matches a query only when they share terms, and BM25 scores that overlap by weighting rare terms more heavily and normalising for document length. It wins whenever the exact token is the signal: error codes, SKUs, function and API names, legal citations, drug names, rare proper nouns, and any vocabulary the embedding model never saw during training. Classic BM25 needs no training at all, runs on an inverted index, and is fully interpretable because you can see exactly which terms produced the score. SPLADE is the exception worth naming: it is a trained model, but it still outputs a sparse vector that an inverted index can serve.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Dense retrieval</strong> uses a bi-encoder to map the query and every chunk into a low-dimensional continuous vector (commonly several hundred to a few thousand dimensions) and ranks by cosine similarity or dot product through an approximate nearest-neighbour index. It wins on meaning: paraphrases, synonyms, conceptual questions, and cross-lingual search, where the query and the answer share no words. Its weaknesses are the mirror image of BM25's strengths. It can blur exact strings (<code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">ERR_4021</code> and <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">ERR_4012</code> may embed almost identically), it degrades on specialised jargon unless the embedding model was trained or fine-tuned on similar text, and a similarity score is hard to explain when a result looks wrong.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Hybrid retrieval</strong> runs both retrievers over the same corpus and fuses the results. It wins in most real corpora because production queries are a mixture of intent and literal tokens. A query like <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">why is the checkout failing with ERR_4021</code> needs semantic understanding of failure and checkout plus an exact match on the error code. Neither retriever alone covers both halves, but their errors are largely uncorrelated, so combining them recovers documents that either one would miss. The common implementation is BM25 plus dense retrieval, merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion and followed by a cross-encoder re-ranker.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A simple selection rule to state in an interview: choose sparse when the corpus is small, highly technical, or identifier-heavy and you need a cheap baseline; choose dense when queries are natural language and vocabulary mismatch is the main failure; choose hybrid when you do not know the query mix in advance, which is the usual case. Hybrid does cost more: two indexes to build, store, and keep in sync, two queries per request, and a fusion step that needs its own evaluation.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Retrieval is the ceiling on answer quality: if the right chunk is not in the candidate set, no prompt or model can recover it. Sparse and dense retrieval fail on different queries, so the choice of retriever decides which class of user questions silently returns nothing useful. Hybrid search is usually the cheapest single change that removes both failure classes at once.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Practical example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">An internal support assistant indexes runbooks and incident write-ups. Engineers search by error code, service name, and symptom. Vector-only retrieval returns conceptually similar incidents but misses the runbook that contains the literal code; BM25-only retrieval finds the code but misses a write-up that describes the same failure in different words. Running both, fusing with RRF, and re-ranking the top 50 puts both documents in the final context. The team can confirm the gain by tagging queries as identifier-heavy or conceptual and comparing recall for each group.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Keep both indexes in one store where possible (Postgres with full-text search and pgvector, OpenSearch, Elasticsearch, Qdrant, and Weaviate all support hybrid queries), so one ingestion pipeline feeds both and they are less likely to drift apart. Fetch a generous candidate count from each retriever, for example 50 to 100, before fusion. Apply metadata filters and access control to both retrievers, not only one. Build an evaluation set that includes identifier queries and paraphrase queries, and report recall at k separately for each retriever and for the fused result, so you can show that hybrid helps on your data instead of assuming it.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Sparse wins on exact terms, dense wins on meaning, and hybrid wins on real traffic because queries contain both. For a document d, <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">RRF(d) = Σ over retrievers of 1 / (k + rank_i(d))</code>, where <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">rank_i(d)</code> is the document's rank in retriever i (starting at 1) and k is a smoothing constant, conventionally 60. A document that is missing from a list simply contributes nothing for that list. The fused ranking is the documents sorted by their summed score.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A worked example: a document ranked #1 by BM25 and #3 by the vector index scores <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">1/61 + 1/63</code>, about 0.0323. A document ranked #1 by BM25 only scores <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">1/61</code>, about 0.0164. The document that both retrievers like beats the one that only one likes, which is exactly the behaviour you want from fusion.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The alternative is <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">score normalisation</strong>: rescale each retriever's scores to a common range (min-max or z-score) and take a weighted sum. That approach is fragile because the scores are not comparable. BM25 scores are unbounded and depend on corpus statistics such as document frequency and average document length, so they shift when the corpus changes, and one query with a rare term can produce a very different range from the next. Cosine similarities sit in a narrow band that depends on the embedding model. Min-max normalisation over a top-k list is also distorted by a single outlier. Every weight you tune becomes a per-corpus, per-model assumption that can silently go stale.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">RRF avoids all of this. It needs no calibration, has essentially one parameter, works the same way for two retrievers or five, and is robust when one retriever returns pathological scores, because a bad score can only change a rank and cannot dominate a sum. The constant k controls how sharply top ranks are favoured: a small k makes rank 1 far more valuable than rank 5, while a larger k flattens the curve so agreement deeper in the lists counts for more. The trade-off to acknowledge is that RRF discards magnitude. A document that both retrievers scored overwhelmingly is treated the same as one they merely both ranked first, and plain RRF has no way to express that one retriever is more reliable for your queries, although weighted variants exist.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Fusion is where hybrid search either works or quietly fails. A brittle fusion step reintroduces the tuning problem that hybrid search was meant to avoid, and it tends to break exactly when the corpus or the embedding model changes. Rank-based fusion keeps the system stable under those changes.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Practical example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A hybrid search returns a BM25 top 50 and a vector top 50 for the query <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">refund window annual plan</code>. The Annual plan refund policy page is rank 2 in BM25 and rank 4 in vector search; a long billing FAQ is rank 1 in BM25 only. RRF gives the policy page <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">1/62 + 1/64</code>, about 0.0318, and the FAQ <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">1/61</code>, about 0.0164, so the policy page rises to the top without anyone tuning a weight.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Implement it as a small pure function over lists of document ids, deduplicating by a stable chunk id so the same chunk from two retrievers merges instead of appearing twice. Several engines, including Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, and some vector databases, ship RRF natively, so check before writing your own. Choose the rank depth per retriever deliberately, since deeper lists raise recall at the cost of latency. Treat k as a tunable hyperparameter with 60 as the starting point, and try weighted RRF only if evaluation shows that one retriever is consistently better. Always compare against a normalised-score baseline on your own queries, because the claim is that RRF is robust, not that it is always best.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">RRF fuses ranked lists by summing <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">1 / (k + rank)</code> per retriever, with k around 60. It is preferred over score normalisation because BM25 and cosine scores sit on incomparable, drifting scales while ranks are always comparable. The cost is that it ignores score magnitude.</p>\n</div>"},{"q":"Explain cross-encoder re-ranking. What does it cost and where does it fit?","g":["reranking"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">cross-encoder</strong> feeds the query and one candidate passage into a transformer together, as a single sequence such as <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">[CLS] query [SEP] passage [SEP]</code>, and outputs one relevance score. Because the query tokens and the passage tokens attend to each other in every layer, the model can judge whether the passage actually answers the question rather than merely sharing its topic. A bi-encoder, by contrast, embeds the query and the passage separately and compares two fixed vectors, so it cannot model fine-grained interactions such as negation, qualifiers, or which entity a number belongs to.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">That joint attention is why cross-encoders usually improve ranking quality over bi-encoder retrieval, often by a substantial margin on metrics such as nDCG. The size of the gain depends heavily on the dataset, the first-stage retriever, and the re-ranker model, so quote it as a range to verify, not as a promise.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The cost is that nothing can be precomputed. A bi-encoder embeds every passage once at ingest, but a cross-encoder must run a forward pass for each query-passage pair at query time, so scoring N candidates costs N passes. A compact open model such as bge-reranker-base can score tens of passages in tens to low hundreds of milliseconds on a GPU and noticeably more on CPU, depending on passage length, batch size, and hardware. Hosted re-ranking APIs trade that for network latency and per-request pricing.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">That cost dictates where it fits: strictly as <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">stage 2</strong> of a two-stage pipeline. Stage 1, usually hybrid search, retrieves a broad candidate set, typically 50 to 200 passages, with high recall and low latency. Stage 2 re-ranks only that set and keeps the top 3 to 5 for the prompt. Re-ranking the whole corpus is impossible, and re-ranking too few candidates wastes the model because the right passage may never be in the list.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">There are middle grounds worth knowing. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">ColBERT and other late-interaction models</strong> precompute per-token embeddings for passages and compute a cheap MaxSim between query tokens and passage tokens at query time, landing between bi-encoder speed and cross-encoder quality at the price of a larger index. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">LLM re-rankers</strong> ask a language model to order the passages; they can be the most accurate on hard queries and are also the slowest and most expensive.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Re-ranking is where precision is bought. First-stage retrieval is tuned for recall, so its top 5 is often noisy, while the prompt has room for only a few passages. Irrelevant context wastes tokens and can mislead the model, and a re-ranker concentrates the best evidence at the top of a small context window.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Practical example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A user asks <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">can contractors access the production database?</code>. Hybrid search returns 100 chunks, many of them about database access for employees, backups, or contractor onboarding. The cross-encoder scores each pair and promotes the one policy paragraph that explicitly addresses contractors and production access to rank 1, while demoting passages that only share keywords. The generation step then receives 4 chunks instead of 20 and answers from the correct paragraph.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Set the candidate count from a latency budget rather than a guess: measure re-ranker latency at 25, 50, 100, and 200 candidates on your hardware, then choose the largest that fits. Truncate long passages to the model's maximum input length, and remember that truncation can hide the answer. Batch the pairs in a single call, run the re-ranker on a GPU if traffic justifies it, and cache scores for repeated query-passage pairs. Evaluate recall at the candidate stage and nDCG or hit rate at the final top-k, since a re-ranker cannot fix a candidate set that lacks the answer. Check the model licence and multilingual coverage before production use.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A cross-encoder scores the query and passage jointly, which gives much better relevance judgements than a bi-encoder but needs one forward pass per candidate at query time. Instead of taking the top k by similarity to the query, it builds the result set greedily. At each step it chooses the candidate that maximises <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">MMR = λ * sim(q, d) - (1 - λ) * max sim(d, d_selected)</code>, where the first term is the similarity to the query and the second is the highest similarity to any document already chosen. A candidate that is relevant but nearly identical to something already selected is penalised, so a slightly less relevant but novel candidate can win.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The parameter λ controls the balance. At λ = 1 the formula reduces to ordinary relevance ranking. Lower values favour diversity, and values around 0.5 to 0.7 are a common starting range; the right value depends on how much duplication your corpus contains and how broad your queries are. The similarities are normally computed from embeddings, so MMR can run on top of any retriever whose candidate vectors are available or can be recomputed.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">You need it when the top-k is dominated by near-duplicates. That happens constantly: overlapping chunks from the same section, several versions of one document, boilerplate headers and footers, release notes repeating the same change, or an FAQ answer copied into ten pages. Without diversification, all five prompt slots go to one restated fact and the model never sees the second half of the answer. MMR helps most with broad, comparative, or multi-aspect questions such as <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">what are our options for X</code>, where coverage matters more than the single best passage.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">It is not free of downsides. A low λ can push marginally relevant text into the prompt, and the greedy procedure is sequential, so the cost grows with k times the candidate count. It also understands nothing beyond embedding similarity, so it will not notice that two passages that look different actually contradict each other. For narrow factual lookups where one passage holds the answer, it can only dilute the context, so it should be tuned or switched off for those query types.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Context slots are scarce, and every token costs money and attention. Duplicated evidence reduces the effective recall of the prompt even when retrieval recall looks high, and it can lead the model to overweight a point simply because it appears several times.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Practical example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A documentation assistant retrieves 20 chunks for <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">how do we handle API rate limits?</code>. Eight are overlapping chunks from the same Rate limits page, five come from three versions of an older guide, and only two cover retry headers and backoff, which live on a separate best-practices page. Plain top-5 selection puts four copies of the same limits table in the prompt. MMR at λ = 0.6 picks the best limits chunk, then the backoff guidance, then the header reference, so the answer covers limits, retries, and headers.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Deduplicate exact and near-exact duplicates at ingest first, because MMR is a poor substitute for clean data. Apply MMR after re-ranking, on the re-ranked top 20 to 50, so the diversity step works on high-quality candidates. Many frameworks implement it directly (LangChain retrievers expose an MMR search type, for example), but check whether the implementation uses the vector store's own embeddings or recomputes them. Tune λ and the candidate pool size against an evaluation set that includes both narrow and broad questions, and consider a per-query-type setting. Track a redundancy measure, such as the average pairwise similarity of the final context, alongside answer quality.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">MMR greedily selects passages that are relevant to the query and dissimilar to what is already chosen, controlled by λ. Use it when the top-k is full of near-duplicates or when questions are broad, and tune it down or skip it for narrow lookups.</p>\n</div>"},{"q":"What are query rewriting and query expansion, and why do they matter more than people expect?","g":["query transformation"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The user's raw question is often a poor retrieval key. People write conversationally, use pronouns, omit context, and choose words that differ from the corpus vocabulary. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Query rewriting</strong> turns the raw input into a self-contained, retrieval-friendly query. It resolves pronouns and ellipsis using the conversation history, so <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">and the second one?</code> becomes <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">what is the refund window for the annual plan?</code>. It also strips filler and can normalise terminology to match how the documents are written.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Query expansion</strong> adds terms instead of replacing the query: synonyms, acronym expansions (<code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">SSO</code> plus <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">single sign-on</code>), domain jargon, product names, or alternative phrasings. Expansion mainly helps lexical retrieval, which can only match words that actually appear, and it can help dense retrieval when the original query is very short. Both techniques are usually implemented with a small, fast LLM prompt that returns a structured result, such as a standalone question and an optional list of keywords.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">They matter disproportionately because retrieval quality is bounded by the query. Re-ranking can only reorder candidates that were retrieved, and no amount of downstream tuning recovers a chunk that never entered the candidate set. In multi-turn chat, rewriting is not optional: embedding a bare follow-up turn gives close to arbitrary results because the turn does not contain the topic. This is why a conversational RAG pipeline without rewriting looks fine in single-question demos and fails in real usage.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The risks are real. A rewrite can drift from the user's intent, drop a constraint such as a date or a customer name, or inject assumptions, and an expansion can add terms that pull in off-topic documents. The cost is one extra small-model call, roughly 100 to 300 ms depending on the model and prompt length, which can be partly hidden by running a first retrieval on the raw query concurrently and replacing or merging it when the rewrite arrives.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">In a production RAG system, many failures that look like generation problems are actually query problems. Fixing the query is cheaper than building a larger index or adding a bigger model, and the improvement carries through every downstream stage.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Practical example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A support chat has this exchange. Turn 1: <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">What is the refund policy on the annual plan?</code> Turn 2: <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">And for the monthly one?</code> The raw second turn retrieves generic billing content. The rewriter outputs <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">What is the refund policy for the monthly plan?</code>, and the keyword expansion adds <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">cancellation</code> and <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">pro-rated</code>. Retrieval now finds the monthly-plan refund section, and the answer matches what the user actually asked.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Give the rewriter only the last few turns and a strict output format, and instruct it to preserve every named entity, number, and date. Log the original and the rewritten query so you can audit drift, and evaluate on multi-turn test conversations, not only on single questions. Keep the original query as a fallback and consider retrieving with both. Use a small, fast model, set a timeout, and fall back to the raw query when the call fails. Apply expansion carefully to dense retrieval, where extra terms can dilute the embedding, and prefer it for the BM25 side of a hybrid system.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Rewriting makes the query self-contained and corpus-friendly; expansion adds vocabulary so retrieval has more to match. They matter because retrieval is bounded by the query, and multi-turn follow-ups cannot be embedded sensibly without rewriting. The cost is one small LLM call that concurrent retrieval can partly hide.</p>\n</div>"},{"q":"What is HyDE and when does it help?","g":["query transformation"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><strong style=\"font-weight:600\">HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings)</strong> asks an LLM to write a plausible answer to the question, embeds that hypothetical answer instead of the question, and searches the vector index with it. The generated text does not need to be correct, since it is never shown to the user; it only needs to look like the kind of passage that would contain the answer. The retrieved real documents then replace it as the evidence.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The rationale is an asymmetry problem. A question and the passage that answers it have different linguistic shapes: the question is short, interrogative, and lacks the specific terms, while the passage is declarative and detailed. A bi-encoder may place a question in a slightly different region of vector space than the passages that answer it. A hypothetical answer is written in the style and vocabulary of a document, so its embedding tends to land closer to real documents. The original HyDE work reported strong zero-shot gains with unsupervised retrievers, which is the setting where it makes the most sense.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">It helps most when you have no labelled data and no fine-tuned embedding model, when queries are short or vague, and when the LLM has enough general knowledge to guess the shape of an answer in the domain. It hurts when the model produces a confident but wrong answer that pulls retrieval towards the wrong topic, when the domain is private or very new so that the model has nothing to base its guess on, and for identifier-heavy queries where the exact token matters more than the style. It also adds a full generation call to the critical path, typically hundreds of milliseconds to seconds depending on the model and output length.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">In practice, a fine-tuned embedding model, hybrid search, or a good re-ranker often buys more quality for less latency, so HyDE is best treated as a targeted technique instead of a default. It combines naturally with other methods: embed both the original query and the hypothetical answer and fuse the results, which limits the damage when the hypothesis is wrong.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Interviewers use HyDE to test whether you understand the query-document mismatch and can weigh a clever trick against its latency and failure modes. Knowing when not to use it is the stronger signal.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Practical example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A research assistant over a corpus of materials-science papers receives the query <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">why do batteries degrade fast in cold weather</code>. The raw question embeds near generic battery explainers. HyDE has the LLM write a short paragraph mentioning electrolyte viscosity, lithium plating, and slowed ion transport, and embedding that paragraph retrieves papers that discuss those mechanisms. Had the LLM guessed an unrelated cause, the retrieved papers would be off-topic, which is why the team also searches with the raw query and fuses both lists.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Keep the hypothetical answer short, around 100 to 150 words, and prompt for a passage written in the corpus style instead of a chat reply. Measure it per query type on your evaluation set, enable it only for the categories where it improves recall, and watch latency percentiles and cost per query.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">HyDE embeds an LLM-written hypothetical answer instead of the question to bridge the question-document gap. It also handles compound questions naturally. <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">Compare our refund policy for EU and US customers</code> embeds as a blend that may match neither policy well, while two sub-questions, one about the EU and one about the US, each retrieve their own policy cleanly.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The costs are concrete and worth quoting. There is one extra LLM call to generate the variants. Retrieval load and embedding calls multiply by the number of variants. Tail latency rises, because the slowest of N searches sets the pace unless the searches are fanned out concurrently. The merged candidate set is also larger and noisier: variants can drift off-topic and pull in irrelevant context, so multi-query pairs naturally with a re-ranker that trims the pool afterwards.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Because of these costs it should be applied selectively. For a simple lookup such as <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">what is the SSO login URL?</code>, one good query suffices and extra variants only burn money. For complex analytical, comparative, or ambiguous questions where a single phrasing is unlikely to cover the evidence, it is often worth it. A simple router, such as a rule or a small classifier that detects compound or comparative questions, can decide when to enable it.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Single-query retrieval implicitly assumes that the user's wording is the best possible search key. Multi-query removes that assumption at a price you can control, and it is one of the most direct ways to improve recall on hard questions without retraining anything.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Practical example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A user asks <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">what are the security and cost implications of moving from Kafka to Kinesis?</code>. Each search returns different documents: a security review, a pricing comparison, and a migration case study. RRF merges them, the re-ranker keeps the top 6, and the answer covers both security and cost, which a single combined query would likely not.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Cap the number of variants and instruct the generator to cover distinct aspects instead of near-identical rewordings, since duplicates add cost without adding recall. Run the searches concurrently with a shared timeout. Deduplicate by chunk id before fusion, and apply the same metadata filters and access control to every variant. Always include the original query among the variants. Compare recall and latency with and without multi-query on a set of complex questions, and track cost per request, since retrieval cost scales with the number of variants.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Multi-query generates several paraphrases or sub-questions, retrieves for each, and fuses with RRF to raise recall and handle compound questions. You split documents into small chunks, for example about 200 tokens, and embed those. Each small chunk stores a pointer to its parent, which is a larger unit such as the full section, page, or document. At query time you search over the small chunks, then replace each hit with its parent before building the prompt.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">This resolves the central chunking tension. Small chunks embed cleanly because each covers a single idea, so the vector is focused and matches precise queries. But small chunks lack surrounding context, so a model that sees only the hit often cannot answer. The classic failure is a chunk containing <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">the limit is 500 requests per minute</code>: it retrieves perfectly for the query, but the model cannot tell which endpoint or plan the limit applies to. The parent section carries the heading and neighbouring text that make the chunk interpretable.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Two details separate a working implementation from a naive one. First, deduplicate parents. If five child chunks from the same section all match, they should expand to one parent, not five copies of it. Rank parents by the best child score, or by an aggregate such as the sum of child scores, and keep the order stable. Second, budget the context. Parents are large, so the number you can afford is small; if each parent is 1,500 tokens, a 6,000-token context budget holds four. This usually means retrieving more children than you need, collapsing them to a few parents, and re-ranking on the parent or the child text.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The pattern has trade-offs. Large parents can carry irrelevant text that distracts the model or wastes tokens, and parent size becomes another parameter to tune. Storage and ingestion become more complex because you maintain two levels of the document and a mapping between them. Where documents have no clear structure, the choice of parent boundary is arbitrary, and a multi-level hierarchy (sentence, paragraph, section) adds more tuning.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Retrieval precision and generation context need different chunk sizes. Parent-document retrieval lets you optimise each separately instead of compromising on one chunk size that is too big to match precisely and too small to answer from.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Practical example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">An API reference has a section titled Orders API with a table of limits and endpoint-specific notes. A child chunk containing <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">the limit is 500 requests per minute</code> is retrieved for the question <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">what is the rate limit for creating orders?</code>. Without expansion, the model sees only that sentence and may guess the endpoint. With parent expansion, it receives the whole Orders API rate-limit section, sees that 500 per minute applies to <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">POST /orders</code>, and answers correctly. Three other child hits from the same section collapse into the same parent, so the prompt contains it once.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Store parents in a document store keyed by parent id, and store the parent id as metadata on each child vector. Choose parent boundaries from document structure where you can (headings, sections, pages), and fall back to a fixed larger window when you cannot. Deduplicate parents before building the prompt, cap the number of parents, and truncate or window a parent when it exceeds the budget. Evaluate child size and parent size together on your queries, since changing one shifts the best value of the other. LangChain's ParentDocumentRetriever and LlamaIndex's hierarchical node parsers implement the pattern if you prefer not to build it yourself.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Index small chunks for precise embedding, retrieve on them, and return their larger parents to the model. It solves the trade-off between match precision and answer context. Dedupe parents and budget the context carefully, because parents are big.</p>\n</div>"},{"q":"What is sentence-window retrieval and how does it differ from parent-document retrieval?","g":["advanced chunking"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Sentence-window retrieval</strong> indexes individual sentences as the retrieval unit. Each sentence is embedded on its own, and its neighbouring sentences are stored as metadata or looked up by position when needed. On a hit, the system returns that sentence plus a fixed window around it, for example three sentences on either side, so the model reads the match in its immediate context. The embedding is precise because a single sentence expresses a single claim, and the generation context is still readable.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Parent-document retrieval</strong> solves the same problem differently. It returns a structural unit, such as the section or document the chunk belongs to. The difference is how the expansion boundary is chosen. Sentence-window uses a positional rule: always N sentences before and after. Parent-document uses document structure: expand to the heading-delimited section, the page, or the full document.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Each approach has characteristic strengths. Sentence-window is simple, works on unstructured prose such as transcripts, emails, or scraped text, and gives tight, uniform context sizes that are easy to budget. Its weakness is that the window knows nothing about meaning, so it can cross a heading or a topic boundary and pull in unrelated content, or cut off an explanation that continues beyond the window. Parent-document gives semantically coherent expansions that respect the author's structure, which usually means more complete context, but it requires the parser to have extracted that structure reliably, and parents can be much larger and less uniform.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Both belong to the same family of techniques, whose principle is to decouple the retrieval unit from the generation unit. The choice between them is practical: use sentence-window when the text has weak structure and you want small, predictable context, and use parent-document when the structure is clear and answers tend to span a whole section. They can also be combined, for instance by expanding to a window and then up to the parent when the budget allows.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Choosing the expansion strategy is a design decision that affects precision, token cost, and answer completeness. Being able to explain the difference shows that you treat chunking as a retrieval-versus-generation trade-off instead of a single chunk-size setting.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Practical example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A meeting-transcript assistant stores each utterance as a sentence-level unit. On its own, that sentence is meaningless; with a window of three sentences on either side, the model also sees the discussion of the trade-show conflict and who proposed the change. For the company handbook, by contrast, the team uses parent-document retrieval, because each policy sits under a clear heading and the whole section is the right answer unit.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Tune the window size on your own queries, beginning with 2 to 3 sentences on each side, and measure answer completeness as well as retrieval metrics, since a window that is too small truncates context and one that is too large adds noise. Use a reliable sentence splitter, because abbreviations, decimals, and code blocks break naive ones. Store sentence order and document id so neighbours can be fetched cheaply, and merge overlapping windows when several hits are adjacent so the same sentence is not sent twice. Guard against very short sentences becoming ambiguous by setting a minimum length or combining the approach with contextual techniques. LlamaIndex provides a SentenceWindowNodeParser for the pattern.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Sentence-window retrieval embeds sentences and returns a positional window of neighbours; parent-document retrieval returns the structural section. Both decouple what you search from what you generate from.</p>\n</div>"},{"q":"What is semantic chunking, and is it worth the cost over recursive splitting?","g":["advanced chunking"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Semantic chunking</strong> places chunk boundaries at genuine topic shifts instead of at arbitrary token counts. The usual algorithm splits a document into sentences, embeds each one, and computes the similarity between consecutive sentences, or between sliding groups of sentences. Wherever similarity drops below a threshold, or falls into a low percentile of the document's own similarity distribution, it starts a new chunk. Each resulting chunk is therefore a run of sentences about roughly the same thing.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">It produces measurably better chunks on flowing prose with weak structural markers, such as transcripts, long articles, interview notes, and meeting minutes, where a fixed-size splitter would cut mid-argument. Chunks that follow topics embed more cleanly, and the retrieved text is more self-contained.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">It is usually not worth the cost when documents already have strong structure. Markdown headings, HTML sections, legal clause numbering, API reference layouts, and code files give you boundaries for free, and a structure-aware recursive splitter, which tries paragraph, then sentence, then character boundaries within a size limit, yields the same cuts deterministically and at no embedding cost. Recursive splitting is also the standard baseline that you should beat before adopting anything more elaborate.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The costs are specific. Ingestion needs one embedding call per sentence, which is significant on a large corpus. Chunk sizes become non-deterministic, with some very small and some very large, which complicates context budgeting and may require minimum and maximum size limits. The similarity threshold or percentile needs tuning per document type, and noisy sentences such as short utterances or list items create spurious boundaries. Because the embeddings used to cut chunks are separate from the ones used for retrieval, you also have to decide whether to reuse them.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The honest summary is that the win is frequently smaller than the marketing suggests. Benchmark it against recursive splitting on your own evaluation set, measuring retrieval recall and end-to-end answer quality, and adopt it only for the document types where it clearly wins.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Chunking decides what the retriever can even find, and it is easy to over-engineer. Knowing when a cheap, deterministic splitter is enough is a sign of production judgement.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Practical example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A company records its weekly engineering all-hands and indexes the transcripts. A fixed 500-token splitter cuts sentences in the middle of a discussion about the migration and mixes the end of one topic with the start of the next. Semantic chunking detects the shift from migration status to hiring updates and cuts there, so a query about the migration retrieves one coherent chunk. The same team indexes its Markdown runbooks with a heading-aware recursive splitter, since the headings already mark the boundaries.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Start with a recursive splitter that respects document structure and treat it as the baseline. If you try semantic chunking, set minimum and maximum chunk sizes, use a percentile-based threshold, and reuse the sentence embeddings you compute where possible. Batch the embedding calls and cache them by content hash so that re-ingesting unchanged documents is free. Compare the two on a labelled set of queries, and include cost per thousand documents in the comparison. Re-evaluate when you change the embedding model, since the thresholds are tied to it.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Semantic chunking cuts where consecutive-sentence similarity drops, so boundaries follow topics. It helps on unstructured prose, but for structured documents a recursive splitter gives the same boundaries deterministically and cheaply, so benchmark before paying one embedding call per sentence.</p>\n</div>"},{"q":"What is late chunking and how does it differ from traditional chunking?","g":["advanced chunking"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Traditional chunking splits first and embeds second. Every chunk is embedded in isolation, so it has no knowledge of the document around it. A chunk that says <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">it costs $40 per seat</code> contains a pronoun with no referent, and the resulting vector represents an anonymous price, not the product the document is about. This is the context-loss problem that many advanced chunking techniques try to repair.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Late chunking</strong> inverts the order. You run the entire document, or a long span of it, through a long-context embedding model once, and take the token-level output embeddings, which have already attended to every other token in the document through the transformer layers. Only then do you split the token sequence at your chosen chunk boundaries and pool the token embeddings inside each span, usually with mean pooling, into one vector per chunk. Each chunk vector therefore carries document-level context even though the chunk text itself is short. The query side is unchanged, so query-time cost stays essentially the same.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">It materially helps on documents full of pronouns, abbreviations, and implicit references, such as contracts (<code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">the Company</code>, <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">the Services</code>), technical manuals, and articles that introduce an entity once and refer to it afterwards. The approach was popularised by Jina AI together with long-context embedding models that support it.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The requirements are the catch. You need an embedding model that exposes token-level outputs, not just a pooled vector, and that supports long inputs, commonly 8k tokens or more. That rules out most hosted embedding APIs that return only a final pooled embedding. Documents longer than the model context must be processed in overlapping long spans, so some chunks still lose far context. Ingestion is also heavier than embedding short chunks, because each forward pass handles a long sequence.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Contrast it with <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">contextual retrieval</strong>, which pursues the same goal by a different route: an LLM writes a short situating sentence for each chunk, and that sentence is prepended to the chunk text before embedding. Contextual retrieval is model-agnostic and works with any embedding API, and the added text can also feed BM25, but it costs an LLM call per chunk at ingest. Late chunking needs no LLM calls but needs a specific kind of embedding model, and its context lives implicitly in the vectors, so it is not visible text and does not help keyword search.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Context loss at chunk boundaries is one of the main reasons retrieval misses the right passage. Late chunking addresses it inside the embedding step instead of by adding text, which is why it is a recurring comparison point in discussions of advanced chunking.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Practical example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A 20-page master services agreement defines <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">the Supplier</code> on page 1 and states <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">the Supplier shall pay a penalty of 2 percent</code> on page 14. Chunk-then-embed produces a vector for that clause that knows nothing about which agreement or which obligation it belongs to. With late chunking, the token embeddings for the clause were computed while attending to the definitions and the surrounding sections, so a query such as <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">late delivery penalty in the supplier agreement</code> lands much closer to it.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Check model support before committing: you need token-level outputs, a long context window, and a licence that fits your use. Process each document in one pass where it fits, or in overlapping long spans where it does not, then pool by chunk spans using the tokenizer offsets. Align chunk boundaries to token indices carefully, since off-by-one errors silently degrade the vectors. Compare it against plain chunking and against contextual retrieval on your own queries, including ingestion time and cost. Keep BM25 on the raw chunk text, since late chunking changes only the vectors.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Late chunking embeds the whole document first and pools token embeddings into chunks afterwards, so each chunk vector is context-aware at no extra query-time cost. It needs a long-context model with token-level outputs; contextual retrieval reaches a similar goal by prepending LLM-written context at a higher ingest cost.</p>\n</div>"},{"q":"What is contextual retrieval (contextual embeddings) and what does it cost?","g":["advanced chunking","hybrid search"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Contextual retrieval</strong>, introduced by Anthropic, attacks the context-loss problem by making every chunk self-describing before it is indexed. For each chunk, a cheap LLM call receives the whole document (or enough of it) and the chunk, and is asked for a short situating summary of one or two sentences. For example: <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">This chunk is from the Q3 2026 earnings report, in the section on EMEA revenue, discussing the currency headwind.</code> That generated context is prepended to the chunk text, and the combined text is used both for the embedding (contextual embeddings) and for the BM25 index (contextual BM25).</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The effect is large because chunks stop being ambiguous. Without the prefix, a chunk saying <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter</code> does not say which company, region, or period it concerns, so the retriever cannot distinguish it from hundreds of similar sentences. The published evaluation reported retrieval failures falling by about 35% with contextual embeddings, about 49% when contextual BM25 was added, and about 67% when re-ranking was added on top. These are one vendor's benchmark numbers on its chosen datasets, so treat them as an indication of direction and order of magnitude, and measure on your own corpus.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The cost is real and worth quoting in an interview: one LLM call per chunk at ingest. On a corpus of a million chunks, that is a million calls, each of which includes the document as context. This is why <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">prompt caching</strong> of the document prefix is essential: the document is sent once as a cached prefix and each chunk's call reuses it, which can cut the cost by roughly an order of magnitude on long documents, depending on provider pricing. It is also why the cost is paid offline, once per document version, in a batch job, and not at query time, so query latency is unchanged.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">There are practical caveats. The generated context can be wrong, so the prompt should instruct the model to use only information from the document and to stay short. Very long documents may exceed the model context, in which case you pass a relevant window around the chunk instead. Re-ingestion is needed whenever the document changes, because the context sentence depends on it. And the technique complements hybrid search and re-ranking instead of replacing them: the largest reported gains came from combining all three.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Many retrieval-stage RAG failures are chunks that were correct but unfindable. Contextual retrieval is a direct, model-agnostic fix whose cost sits entirely at ingest, which makes it attractive for corpora that change rarely and are queried often.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Practical example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A finance team indexes hundreds of earnings reports. The chunk <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">Revenue increased 3% compared to the prior quarter</code> appears in dozens of reports. The contextual step prepends <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">From ACME Corp's Q3 2026 earnings report, EMEA segment discussion.</code> Now a query for <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">ACME EMEA revenue growth Q3 2026</code> matches both through embeddings and through the literal tokens in BM25, and the retriever returns the right chunk instead of a similar sentence from another company.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Write a tight prompt that outputs only the situating text, limited to one or two sentences, and tell the model not to add facts that are not in the document. Use prompt caching or batch APIs, process documents in parallel, and store the generated context next to the chunk so it can be inspected and reused. Index the contextualised text for both vector and BM25 search, but decide deliberately whether the model should see the prefix in the final prompt. Estimate cost before running: chunks multiplied by the cached and uncached tokens per call. Evaluate the gain with and without it, and re-run when the documents or the context prompt change.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Contextual retrieval prepends an LLM-generated, document-aware sentence to each chunk before embedding and BM25 indexing, so chunks become self-describing. Reported failure reductions are large, especially combined with hybrid search and re-ranking, but it costs one LLM call per chunk at ingest, which prompt caching and batching make manageable.</p>\n</div>"},{"q":"Which retrieval metrics do you track, and what does each tell you?","g":["rag evaluation"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Retrieval metrics tell you whether your system found the evidence needed to answer a question, whether that evidence appeared early enough to survive selection, and how much irrelevant material accompanied it. In a RAG application, they diagnose the evidence-delivery pipeline rather than certify the final answer. An application can retrieve excellent evidence and still generate a wrong response, or retrieve the wrong document and accidentally answer correctly from the model's prior knowledge. Evaluate retrieval and generation separately, then connect both to task success.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">I track metrics at distinct boundaries: candidate retrieval, reranking, and final context assembly. For each boundary, I record the evaluation population, relevance definition, cutoff, permission scope, and corpus version. A value such as Recall@10 is difficult to interpret without those details. Ten candidates before reranking and ten passages actually delivered to the model represent different opportunities for failure and different operational costs.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">First define relevance and the evaluation unit</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A relevant passage must contribute evidence toward the actual question, including its constraints. A passage about refunds is not necessarily relevant to a question about refunds for enterprise annual subscriptions in a particular jurisdiction. Topic overlap alone is insufficient. Labels should distinguish direct support, partial support, background context, and irrelevant material where that distinction matters to the application.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Choose whether the unit is a document, passage, source span, or required fact. If a document has twenty chunks and only one answers the question, document-level success can hide passage-level failure. Conversely, counting overlapping copies of the same passage as distinct relevant items can exaggerate coverage. Where multiple passages express equivalent evidence, use an equivalence group or source-span mapping instead of insisting on one arbitrary chunk identifier.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Recall@k measures evidence coverage</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For an answerable query, Recall@k equals the number of relevant evaluation units retrieved in the first k results divided by the total number of relevant units identified for that query. Suppose four passages are relevant and the top five contain three. Recall@5 is three divided by four, or 0.75. Retrieving the remaining passage at rank eight increases Recall@10 to one, assuming it survives later filtering.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Recall is especially useful early in a two-stage system because a reranker cannot promote evidence that never became a candidate. However, ordinary recall is not a literal universal ceiling on answer accuracy. The model may answer from prior knowledge, equivalent evidence may be unlabeled, and many relevant passages may be redundant. The more precise architectural statement is that missing indispensable evidence limits the system's ability to produce a verifiably supported answer.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Label completeness matters. For a large corpus, you rarely know every relevant passage. Pool candidates from several retrieval methods, review likely alternatives, and describe the metric as recall against the judged evidence set. Otherwise, a new retriever can be penalized for finding valid passages that the original labeling method never discovered. Treat unjudged documents deliberately rather than silently calling them irrelevant.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Hit Rate@k measures whether anything useful appeared</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Hit Rate@k is the fraction of eligible queries for which at least one relevant result appears within the cutoff. For each query the outcome is binary: hit or miss. If eighty of one hundred answerable questions have at least one relevant passage in the top five, Hit Rate@5 is 0.80. This is often easy to explain to product teams because it resembles the proportion of questions with some available evidence.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Hit rate and recall answer different questions. Imagine a query requiring a general policy and an exception. Retrieving only the general policy produces a hit, but the exception may determine the answer. Hit rate can therefore look excellent while multi-part answers remain unreliable. I supplement it with complete-evidence coverage: the fraction of questions for which every indispensable evidence group is present.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Unanswerable queries require separate handling. When no relevant evidence exists, recall has a zero denominator and a hit is not desirable. Do not manufacture a score of zero or one without documenting the convention. Report answerable-query retrieval metrics separately from unanswerable-query rejection, false-support rate, and abstention quality. Those populations represent different product obligations.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Precision@k measures useful results versus clutter</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Precision@k equals the number of relevant results among the first k divided by k, under the declared convention for result lists shorter than k. In the earlier example, three relevant passages among five results give Precision@5 of 0.60. This measures how much of a fixed result budget contains useful evidence. It is particularly important near the final prompt because irrelevant passages consume tokens and can introduce misleading alternatives.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Define the denominator carefully when filters return fewer results. Precision at the actual returned length and precision at the requested cutoff are different quantities. Both can be useful, but they should not share one unlabeled dashboard line. Also report empty-result rate so a system cannot appear clean simply by returning almost nothing.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Chunk precision does not fully describe cost. One irrelevant passage might contain fifty tokens, while another contains three thousand. Track relevant-token density or redundant-token share where practical. A final context with four useful short passages and one enormous irrelevant appendix can have good chunk precision yet poor efficiency. These additional measurements are application-defined diagnostics, not universally standardized metrics.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">MRR measures the position of the first relevant result</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For one query, reciprocal rank is one divided by the rank of the first relevant result. It is zero if no relevant result appears inside the evaluated cutoff. Mean Reciprocal Rank averages that value across queries. If three queries first find relevant evidence at ranks one, two, and nowhere within five, their reciprocal ranks are one, one-half, and zero. MRR@5 is therefore 0.50.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">MRR is useful for single-fact lookup and for detecting whether a reranker brings a useful answer-bearing passage toward the front. Moving the first useful result from rank ten to rank two changes reciprocal rank from 0.10 to 0.50. This improvement can matter because subsequent selection may keep only a small number of passages, and users reviewing search results often inspect early results first.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">MRR ignores every relevant result after the first. A ranking containing one useful passage followed by irrelevant content can receive the same reciprocal rank as a ranking containing all required evidence immediately after that first passage. Do not use MRR alone for comparison, synthesis, or questions requiring several documents. A high MRR establishes early access to something useful, not full answerability.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">nDCG@k measures graded ranking quality</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain supports relevance grades rather than only relevant or irrelevant labels. For example, assign grade three to a passage that directly answers the scoped question, two to substantial partial support, one to useful background, and zero to irrelevant content. Define those grades operationally so annotators do not assign them merely from topical familiarity.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">One common formulation gives each result a gain of two raised to its relevance grade minus one, then discounts that gain by the base-two logarithm of rank plus one. DCG sums those discounted gains through k. IDCG is the best achievable DCG from the same judged relevance set, ordered ideally. nDCG is DCG divided by IDCG. Other gain conventions exist, so record the chosen formula.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Consider grades three, two, and zero. With exponential gains, the ideal DCG@3 is seven plus three divided by log base two of three, approximately 8.893. A ranking with grades zero, two, three has DCG approximately 5.393: the second-ranked item contributes about 1.893 and the third contributes 3.5. Its nDCG is approximately 0.606. The calculation rewards placing strong evidence early without treating partial support as worthless.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">When every judged result has grade zero, the ideal denominator is zero. Your evaluation library may use a defined fallback, but the dashboard must explain it. More generally, nDCG is only as meaningful as its relevance grades and judged candidate pool. A precisely computed number does not repair inconsistent annotation.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Context precision needs an explicit definition</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">In informal discussion, context precision can mean the fraction of prompt passages judged useful. In evaluation frameworks, the same name can refer to an average-precision-like, rank-sensitive calculation. Token-level relevance density is another distinct concept. I never compare numbers called context precision until their units, reference inputs, and aggregation formulas are documented.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For example, a context ordered relevant, irrelevant, relevant has ordinary precision of two-thirds. An average-precision-style calculation averages precision at the relevant ranks: one at rank one and two-thirds at rank three, giving about 0.833 when divided by the two retrieved relevant items. These are both reasonable diagnostics, but they do not measure the same quantity. Naming the implementation prevents misleading comparisons.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Measure the complete retrieval funnel</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Suppose candidate retrieval returns fifty passages and contains all three required evidence groups. The reranker places two groups in the top five but pushes the third to rank twelve. The final prompt keeps five passages. Candidate coverage is high, but final-context coverage is incomplete. Calling this simply a retrieval success hides the stage that actually removed required evidence.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">I therefore store the candidate IDs, post-filter candidates, reranked order, selected context, and any compression output. At each transition I calculate evidence retention. If a policy exception appears before compression and disappears afterward, increasing the vector-search cutoff will not solve the problem. The fix belongs in context assembly or compression rules.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate ANN recall from semantic relevance recall</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">ANN Recall@k asks how many neighbors returned by an exact vector search also appear in the approximate result set. Its ground truth comes from exhaustive computation using the same vectors and distance metric. Semantic retrieval recall instead asks whether human-judged or otherwise validated answer-bearing evidence was found. These measurements use different definitions of correct results.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">An index can achieve excellent ANN recall while retrieving the wrong product manual because its embeddings poorly represent the query constraints. Conversely, an approximate search can omit an exact nearest neighbor but return another passage that answers equally well. I monitor both when tuning an ANN index, but I do not use one as a substitute for the other.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Aggregate without hiding important failures</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Macro averaging gives each query equal weight. Micro aggregation pools counts and can give evidence-rich queries more influence. Traffic weighting approximates expected production usage, but it can conceal rare failures with serious consequences. Report the method explicitly and retain slices for exact identifiers, paraphrases, languages, tenants, document formats, fresh content, and multi-evidence questions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use paired comparisons because retrieval configurations should be evaluated on the same queries and source snapshot. Report uncertainty with a suitable resampling procedure, and inspect per-query differences rather than only the mean. A two-point improvement from a tiny sample may be noise. A small aggregate gain accompanied by a large regression on critical policy exceptions may be unacceptable.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Connect retrieval quality to operating requirements</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Quality metrics belong beside p50 and p95 latency, empty-result rate, index freshness, permission failures, and tokens delivered to generation. A configuration that gains a small amount of recall but triples tail latency may not meet the service objective. Likewise, a fast retriever that serves stale policies has not met the real information need.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">My practical dashboard starts with candidate evidence recall and complete-evidence coverage, then shows final-context precision and nDCG, first-hit ranking where appropriate, and end-to-end grounded answer correctness. Each metric has a diagnostic role. No single score deserves to become the objective detached from the user's question, the authorized evidence, and the cost of delivering a reliable answer.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">A diagnostic example from a release comparison</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Consider two hypothetical retrievers evaluated on the same one hundred policy questions. Version A finds at least one useful passage for ninety questions, but retrieves every required fact for only sixty. Version B finds something useful for eighty-eight questions and complete evidence for seventy-eight. Looking only at hit rate would favor A, even though B may support more correct multi-part answers. Inspect which two questions became misses and whether those losses are acceptable before choosing either version.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Now suppose both versions retrieve complete evidence for the same seventy-eight queries, but B places the decisive exceptions earlier and sends fewer duplicated passages. The improvement should appear in ranking and final-context measurements, while candidate recall may remain unchanged. This is a useful optimization even when the headline recall graph looks flat. Conversely, if answer correctness remains unchanged, investigate whether the generator already handled the old ordering adequately or whether another bottleneck dominates. Metrics guide an experiment; they do not replace observing the task outcome. Record the hypothesis before changing the system so that each score has a clear interpretation after the experiment.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">One further safeguard is to separate relevance from permission compliance. A passage may be substantively relevant and still be prohibited for the current caller. In the expected retrieval set for that caller, it must not become a desired result. Test cross-tenant and revoked-access cases directly, because a high average ranking score can otherwise conceal a serious access failure. The search evaluator and the authorization evaluator should agree on the user's permitted information boundary.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Finally, assign ownership to metric changes. The retrieval team may own candidate evidence coverage, while the orchestration team owns context retention and the application team owns supported answer success. Shared dashboards help, but explicit boundaries make remediation faster. When the final prompt loses an exception because a token-budget rule favors short passages, the team that owns the vector index should not be tasked with solving an unrelated selection bug. This is why metric placement in the pipeline matters as much as the mathematical formula.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/evaluation-of-ranked-retrieval-results-1.html\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Ranked retrieval evaluation</a></p>\n</div>"},{"q":"What is RAGAS and what do its core metrics actually measure?","g":["ragas","rag evaluation"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Ragas is an evaluation framework that helps measure different aspects of retrieval-augmented applications, including evidence selection, response grounding, and whether the response addresses the user's question. Its value is decomposition: instead of assigning one vague quality score to an entire application, you can ask which stage appears to be failing. However, the framework is not an automatic source of truth. Each metric depends on particular inputs, assumptions, implementation details, and sometimes another language model acting as an evaluator.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The familiar description of Ragas as reference-free is only partly correct. Some metrics can operate without a human-written reference answer; others require a reference answer, reference contexts, or reference identifiers. Current and legacy APIs also expose different names and variants. Before using a score in a release decision, pin the package version, metric implementation, evaluator model, embedding model if applicable, and evaluator prompt. A metric name alone is not a reproducible experiment.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Start with the evaluation record</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For each evaluated request, preserve the user input, generated response, retrieved context passages in their actual order, and any reference information the chosen metrics require. Also record source versions and the final prompt context when it differs from raw retrieval. A metric applied to the initial candidate list cannot establish what the generator actually saw after filtering, compression, or token-budget selection.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Imagine a hypothetical refund assistant. The user asks whether an annual subscription purchased twenty days ago can be refunded. The reference answer states that a thirty-day window applies, enterprise plans are excluded, and prior subscription refunds affect eligibility. The retrieved context and generated answer become separate artifacts. We can now evaluate whether the context covers the reference facts and whether the answer stays within the context. Those are related but different questions.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Faithfulness measures support for generated claims</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Faithfulness examines the response's factual claims and asks whether the retrieved evidence supports them. Conceptually, identify atomic claims, judge support for each claim, and divide the number supported by the total number evaluated. A score of one means all evaluated claims were judged supported under that implementation.
