Preserve the failed arrangement as a regression case, and run it again when changing the model, prompt template, or context assembler. Position sensitivity is a property of the complete interaction, so a later upgrade can change both the problem and the effectiveness of the mitigation.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts</a></p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://github.com/nelson-liu/lost-in-the-middle\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Accompanying research materials</a></p>\n</div>"},{"q":"Explain the HNSW parameters M, efConstruction and efSearch, and how you would tune them.","g":["hnsw"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">HNSW, or Hierarchical Navigable Small World search, is an approximate nearest-neighbor method that organizes vectors into a navigable graph with multiple levels. Search uses sparse upper levels to approach a promising region, then explores the denser lower structure to identify nearby candidates. The parameters M, efConstruction, and efSearch control different parts of that process. Tuning them requires an explicit quality target, a realistic workload, and measurements of memory, build time, and query latency.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The first distinction is build-time versus query-time control. M influences graph connectivity and storage. efConstruction influences the effort spent choosing connections while building. efSearch influences exploration during a query. Raising query-time effort can sometimes compensate for a less effective graph, but it cannot guarantee that a poor graph will meet any recall target within an acceptable latency budget. Conversely, an expensive build may be wasted if the workload does not need its quality.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Understand what M controls</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">M is a connectivity parameter, commonly described as the number of neighbor links created or retained per element in the graph. Exact degree limits differ by implementation and graph level; the base layer may use a different limit from upper layers. Therefore, saying that M is a universal maximum number of bidirectional links at every layer is too simplistic. Read the chosen engine's definition and inspect its actual index behavior.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Greater connectivity can provide more routes toward the query's nearest neighbors and improve navigation on difficult datasets. It also increases graph storage and can increase construction work because more candidate connections must be considered. The best value depends on intrinsic data structure, target recall, and available memory, not simply the raw embedding dimension. A large vector dimension does not by itself reveal how difficult the neighbor structure is.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Budget vectors and graph storage separately</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A collection of N float32 vectors with dimension d requires approximately four times N times d bytes for raw vector values, before graph links, identifiers, metadata, allocator overhead, replicas, or database storage. For one million vectors of dimension 768, the raw values alone occupy about 3.072 billion bytes, roughly 2.86 GiB. The graph adds to that amount rather than replacing it.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A library may document a rough graph-memory estimate proportional to M, but pointer sizes, level distribution, alignment, and encoding change the constant. Do not present a formula such as M times a fixed number of bytes as a universal capacity guarantee. Measure resident memory and serialized index size in the actual deployment. Also include peak build memory and the temporary space needed for a replacement index during migration.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Understand efConstruction</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">efConstruction sets the exploration effort or candidate-list budget used while inserting elements and selecting graph connections. More build exploration can discover better neighbors and produce a graph that reaches a target recall with less query work. However, quality gains usually exhibit diminishing returns. Additional construction time does not guarantee a meaningful improvement once the graph is already adequate for the workload.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">This is mainly a build-time decision. Changing it usually requires constructing a new index or otherwise rebuilding affected graph structure, depending on the engine. It is therefore more expensive to experiment with than efSearch. Some implementations enforce relationships between construction effort and M internally. Use the documented behavior rather than assuming a value is honored exactly because the API accepted it.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Understand efSearch</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">efSearch, sometimes named ef, controls the search exploration budget, often through the size of a dynamic candidate list. Increasing it generally allows more thorough examination and tends to improve nearest-neighbor recall at the cost of additional computation and latency. In hnswlib, the documented search ef should not be lower than the requested number of neighbors k. Other engines may expose related controls with different semantics.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The trade-off is not a promise of strict monotonicity on every individual query or benchmark run. Measurement noise, caching, filters, implementation details, concurrency, and approximate navigation can produce irregular results. An increase from one value to another might add work without changing the returned neighbors. Plot the measured frontier and repeat trials rather than describing every increase as guaranteed improvement.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Define the recall target correctly</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For index tuning, ANN Recall@k compares approximate neighbors with the exact nearest neighbors under the same stored vectors and distance metric. Handle distance ties consistently because several equally valid neighbors can exist.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">This is not the same as RAG evidence recall. An exact vector neighbor may still be irrelevant to the question. First establish that the embeddings and metric retrieve useful evidence; then measure how much the approximate index loses relative to exact search. Adaptive tuning should not become an opaque mechanism that makes retrieval failures impossible to reproduce.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">A hypothetical tuning result</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Suppose a fixed graph yields ANN Recall@10 of 0.91, 0.96, and 0.98 at three increasing exploration settings. How do you choose between them?","g":["hnsw","vector database"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">HNSW, IVF-PQ, and DiskANN represent different ways to trade search quality, memory, computation, and storage access in approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval. Choosing among them is a workload and operations decision, not a rule based only on vector count. The same million-vector corpus can be easy on one machine and expensive on another depending on dimension, precision, replicas, filters, update rate, and latency targets. Begin by defining the required retrieval quality and the resources you can actually operate.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">It is also important to distinguish algorithms from product implementations. HNSW can be combined with quantized storage, IVF can use several encodings and coarse quantizers, and DiskANN has evolving implementations and integration patterns. A vector database may modify or compose these ideas. Compare the actual engine configuration you will deploy rather than assuming a familiar algorithm name guarantees a particular storage layout, deletion behavior, or performance envelope.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">HNSW uses graph navigation</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">HNSW builds a hierarchy of neighbor graphs. Upper levels help approach a useful region, while lower levels support more detailed exploration. It is often a strong option for low-latency search when the relevant working set fits comfortably in memory. Query exploration can be tuned to trade additional work for better approximate-neighbor recall. Construction settings influence the graph's quality and its storage requirements.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The cost is not just graph links. An uncompressed implementation also needs vector values, identifiers, and engine overhead, plus application metadata and replicas. A high-dimensional corpus can exhaust memory before the raw vector count looks large. Larger graphs may also create longer rebuild times and operational headroom requirements. Measure actual resident memory rather than relying solely on an estimate derived from link count.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Incremental inserts are supported in many HNSW implementations, but updates and deletions are implementation-specific. Some engines mark deleted nodes, some reuse capacity, and some impose restrictions or rebuild requirements. Do not describe soft deletion as an immutable property of every HNSW product. Verify what happens to recall, capacity, and latency after the update pattern your application will produce.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">IVF-PQ separates coarse search and compressed comparison</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">IVF, or inverted-file indexing, groups vectors around coarse centroids and stores vectors or codes in the associated lists. A query selects a subset of promising lists rather than scanning the entire corpus. Product quantization compresses vector information into learned subvector codes. Combined as IVF-PQ, these techniques can reduce memory and distance-computation costs substantially.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">There are two different approximation sources. Searching only selected lists can omit true neighbors in unsearched lists. Comparing compressed codes can misorder vectors even within searched lists. Increasing the number of probes addresses the first source, while better quantization, refinement, or full-precision rescoring can address the second. Treating all recall loss as one knob makes tuning unnecessarily confusing.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">IVF-PQ usually requires representative training data for the coarse partition and codebooks. Distribution changes can make that representation less suitable for new vectors. Training quality, list balance, code size, and query distribution all affect the outcome. A statement such as a fixed compression ratio causing a fixed percentage of recall loss is not a reliable deployment forecast. The relationship must be measured on the target data.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">DiskANN targets memory and storage efficiency</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">DiskANN is a family of graph-based vector-search techniques designed to support efficient retrieval when the complete search structure or vectors do not all reside in memory. Designs can combine compact in-memory representations with graph and vector access on SSD. Search must balance useful exploration with the cost and parallelism of storage reads.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The benefits depend strongly on hardware and implementation. SSD throughput, access latency, queueing, cache residency, and concurrent workloads influence tail latency. Do not promise that disk-based search adds only a small fixed number of milliseconds. Cold cache, storage contention, and restrictive filters can change behavior. Benchmark the complete storage path under realistic concurrency and with the operational update model you need.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A disk-oriented design may reduce RAM requirements but still need meaningful memory for compressed representations, navigation structures, caches, and serving buffers. It also introduces persistence, recovery, and I/O observability requirements. The engineering question is whether that resource mix provides a better cost-quality-latency frontier for your workload than a memory-heavy graph or a compressed inverted index.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">SPANN should not be collapsed into DiskANN</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">SPANN is also a memory-disk hybrid approach, but its published design follows an inverted-index methodology rather than simply being another name for DiskANN's graph architecture. It keeps a compact navigational representation associated with posting-list centroids in memory and larger posting lists on disk. That distinction matters when reasoning about query routing and storage access.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Both approaches address large-scale search under memory constraints, but shared goals do not imply identical internal mechanics. When comparing a product that uses SPANN or a related design, evaluate its actual filtering, update, and persistence features. Avoid grouping every SSD-backed index under one graph label. Accurate architectural distinctions lead to better expectations about tuning and failure modes.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Estimate the raw resource requirement first</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For N vectors with d float32 components, raw storage is approximately four times N times d bytes. Ten million vectors of dimension 768 need about 30.72 billion bytes for vector values alone, before graph structure, metadata, replication, and operational headroom. This simple calculation often explains why a seemingly moderate corpus creates a substantial memory bill.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Now include the real deployment: multiple replicas, tenant indexes, staging copies, caches, and a replacement index during rebuild. A solution that fits one static benchmark may not fit production safely. Conversely, a lower-dimensional or compressed corpus can make an in-memory design viable at a larger vector count. This is why fixed thresholds such as always use one algorithm below one million vectors are too crude.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Define the quality baseline with exact search</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use exhaustive search under the same vectors and metric to establish nearest-neighbor ground truth on a representative query set. Then measure the approximate index's neighbor recall. Keep this separate from human-judged evidence relevance in RAG. A configuration that faithfully reproduces exact vector neighbors can still fail on product identifiers or policy exceptions if the representation is inadequate.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For IVF-PQ, isolate coarse-list loss and quantization loss where possible. For a graph, explore different search budgets on a fixed build. For disk-oriented search, distinguish approximate navigation from rescoring and storage limits. These controlled comparisons show which resource increases could plausibly recover quality, rather than encouraging random changes across the entire system.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Compare at the same operating target</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A fair comparison asks what resources each design requires to meet a defined recall and latency objective. Comparing HNSW at high recall with IVF-PQ at lower recall and declaring the latter faster is incomplete. Likewise, a disk-backed test with warm caches may not represent the cold-start or failover condition of a memory-resident baseline.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Record quality, p50 and p95 latency, throughput at expected concurrency, build time, peak memory, steady-state memory, storage size, and update behavior. Include rescore costs if one design uses a second pass. Use the same eligible corpus and query set. Differences in filtering or metric normalization can otherwise dominate the result and be mistakenly attributed to the index family.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Filtering can change the preferred design</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A broad nearest-neighbor query and a highly selective tenant query are different workloads. A graph may navigate through many ineligible nodes, an inverted index may scan lists with few authorized matches, or an engine may switch to an exact scan for small eligible populations. The best choice depends on filter-aware execution, not just global vector count.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Benchmark common and worst-important filter selectivities, including combinations such as tenant, region, document version, and access group. Compute ground truth within the authorized subset. Verify that enough eligible results are returned and that post-filtering never exposes unauthorized candidates to the model. An index that wins unfiltered benchmarks may lose badly on the actual serving path.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Update frequency and lifecycle costs matter</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A mostly static archive can tolerate expensive offline training and rebuilding if online search is efficient. A rapidly changing support corpus needs predictable insert, delete, and permission-update behavior. Distribution drift can affect IVF training, while graph quality and deleted-node accumulation may require maintenance in particular implementations. Disk-oriented systems have their own compaction and recovery considerations.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Estimate the cost of rebuilding, validating, transferring, and swapping an index, not only the cost of querying it. Preserve versioned artifacts and a rollback path. A compressed design with excellent steady-state memory may still be unsuitable if retraining cannot keep pace with changes. The correct decision includes the whole data lifecycle.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Consider rescoring as part of the design</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A compressed first pass can retrieve a wider candidate set, then use higher-precision vectors to rescore those candidates. This often provides a useful trade-off between memory efficiency and final ranking fidelity. However, rescoring cannot recover a true neighbor that never became a candidate, and fetching full vectors can add random I/O and tail latency.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Keep the candidate count, rescore count, and final k separate in the benchmark. Include the storage footprint of retained originals. If full-precision vectors remain on disk, the system may reduce RAM substantially without reducing total stored bytes by the same factor. Report which resource is actually saved. This prevents a headline compression ratio from being mistaken for a complete infrastructure cost reduction.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use a workload-driven selection process</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">I would begin with the simplest available exact or approximate baseline that can plausibly meet the requirement. If memory and latency are comfortable, a familiar graph implementation may minimize operational complexity. If memory becomes the limiting resource, compare compression and IVF-PQ. If the corpus exceeds affordable memory and suitable SSD infrastructure is available, evaluate disk-oriented designs.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">These are starting hypotheses, not universal thresholds. A very large but low-query-volume archive may tolerate slower retrieval, while a smaller high-concurrency application may require aggressive optimization. The number of dimensions, filtering pattern, and update schedule can change the answer more than the vector count. Document the decisive measurements so future growth can trigger a justified reevaluation.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">A hypothetical decision example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Suppose an application has ten million vectors, restrictive tenant filters, and frequent policy updates. HNSW meets latency and recall goals but requires more replica memory than the budget allows. IVF-PQ fits memory, yet filtered recall falls below target until probes and rescoring increase latency. A disk-oriented implementation meets the combined target but introduces a storage service the team must operate. The choice depends on whether that operational burden is acceptable, not on an algorithm popularity ranking.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The interview answer should emphasize that HNSW favors graph navigation and often low-latency memory-resident search, IVF-PQ combines coarse partitions with compact codes, and DiskANN explores a graph-oriented memory-storage trade-off. I choose by benchmarking the actual engine at equal quality targets under realistic filters, load, updates, and lifecycle costs. Exact-neighbor ground truth and end-to-end evidence evaluation keep the comparison honest.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Plan the migration before committing to an index</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Changing index families can affect score distributions, update APIs, source identifiers, and retrieval latency. Build the replacement from the same verified corpus snapshot, compare against the current system, and route a bounded share of traffic or replay workload before full adoption. Preserve source metadata and permission semantics throughout the migration. An algorithmically strong index can still cause regressions if its adapter interprets a distance as a similarity or handles missing filters differently.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Choose rollback criteria before observing the results. For example, a candidate should not exceed the agreed tail-latency budget, reduce evidence coverage on critical tenant slices, or delay deletion propagation beyond the service target. These conditions are more useful than an informal impression that search feels faster. Also decide how inserts arriving during the build are replayed so the replacement does not begin serving an older corpus immediately after deployment.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Operational simplicity deserves an explicit cost entry. A database extension already operated by the team may be preferable to a new specialist system if both satisfy requirements with reasonable headroom. Conversely, forcing a poorly fitting index into existing infrastructure can create more operational work than adopting a suitable service. Make this comparison concrete: staffing, backup, recovery, observability, capacity planning, and vendor constraints all affect total cost.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Finally, keep the application-facing retrieval contract stable where possible. It should express the query, authorized scope, result count, provenance, and supported filtering behavior without exposing every engine-specific detail to callers. Preserve an escape hatch for engine tuning in controlled configuration. That separation makes later benchmarking and migration easier while preventing the rest of the RAG system from depending on undocumented assumptions about one index implementation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Also include failure recovery in the comparison. Measure how long an index takes to load after a restart, what happens when a replica is lost, and whether updates can be replayed without duplication or missing deletions. A design that meets steady-state targets but takes too long to recover may not meet the application's availability requirement. These measurements can favor a different configuration from the one that wins a single search benchmark. Index selection is a service-design decision because users experience retrieval during deployments, failures, and growth, not only during controlled warm-cache tests.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Faiss-indexes\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Faiss index families</a></p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://github.com/microsoft/DiskANN\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">DiskANN implementation</a></p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.08566\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">SPANN research paper</a></p>\n</div>"},{"q":"What is embedding quantisation (scalar, product, binary) and what does it cost you?","g":["vector database"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Embedding quantization compresses numerical vector representations so search can use less memory, storage bandwidth, or computation. The trade-off is information loss: compressed representations approximate the geometry used by the original embeddings. Whether that loss is acceptable depends on the embedding distribution, similarity metric, compression scheme, candidate search method, and the application's evidence requirements. Quantization is an engineering choice to validate, not an automatic optimization with a universal recall penalty.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Separate the resource being optimized. Compressing vectors in RAM can reduce resident memory while full-precision originals remain on disk for refinement. Network transfer may shrink even if total storage does not. Distance computation may become faster, but decoding, lookup tables, or extra rescoring can offset that benefit. A claim that vectors are four times smaller says little by itself about complete request latency, total database size, or infrastructure cost.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Establish the uncompressed baseline</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For N vectors of dimension d stored as float32, raw values require roughly four times N times d bytes. One million 768-dimensional vectors therefore require about 3.072 billion bytes before IDs, metadata, search structures, replication, and allocator overhead. This baseline makes potential savings concrete and prevents compression ratios from being applied to resources the scheme does not actually compress.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Measure exact-vector search quality and application evidence quality before quantizing. If the original embedding model already confuses product versions, compressing it is not the right first intervention. Keep the corpus, query set, filters, and distance semantics fixed when comparing precision formats. Otherwise, you cannot tell whether quality changes came from quantization or from another configuration change.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Scalar quantization compresses individual coordinates</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Scalar quantization maps each vector component into a smaller numerical representation, such as an eight-bit integer or another low-bit format. A quantizer uses a range and scaling rule to approximate each original value. The scale can be global, per dimension, per vector, or defined differently by the implementation. Those choices affect accuracy, metadata overhead, and how distances are computed.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Storing one byte instead of four bytes per component reduces the raw coordinate payload by about four times, excluding scales and other overhead. It does not guarantee a fourfold database reduction because graph links, metadata, and full-precision copies may remain unchanged. Nor does int8 guarantee less than one percent recall loss. Distribution, calibration, clipping, and task difficulty can produce very different outcomes.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">If a few extreme values stretch a shared range, many ordinary values may map to coarse bins. If future data moves outside the calibrated range, clipping or poor resolution can become significant. Use representative calibration data, inspect outliers, and evaluate new data over time. Normalization and metric choice also matter: a quantized vector's norm may differ from the original, affecting cosine or inner-product behavior if the engine does not account for it correctly.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Product quantization compresses groups of coordinates</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Product quantization divides a vector into several subvectors and represents each subvector by the identifier of a learned codeword. Instead of storing all original coordinates, the system stores a compact sequence of code identifiers. At query time, lookup tables or reconstructed approximations estimate distances. The codebooks encode structure learned from representative training vectors.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For a hypothetical 768-dimensional float32 vector, the raw payload is 3,072 bytes. If it is encoded into 96 subvector codes of eight bits each, the code payload is 96 bytes, giving a raw-vector-to-code ratio of 32 to one before codebooks, IDs, and index overhead. This is an arithmetic example, not a claim that every useful PQ configuration reaches that ratio with acceptable quality.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Code length, bits per code, subvector arrangement, training quality, and residual encoding affect fidelity. PQ is often combined with an inverted index, but it is a compression method rather than another name for IVF. Coarse-list selection and quantization introduce separate losses. A transformation such as an optimized rotation can improve how information is distributed across subvectors, but it adds training and deployment considerations of its own.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Binary quantization uses much more aggressive codes</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Binary approaches encode information into bits, often allowing very fast Hamming-distance comparisons using bit operations. A simple sign-based scheme records whether each component is positive or negative. Compared with float32 components, one bit per component reduces the raw coordinate payload by about 32 times. Again, that ratio excludes all other stored structures and any retained originals.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A sign code discards magnitude and fine differences within each side of zero. Whether it preserves useful neighbors depends strongly on how the embedding space was trained and transformed. Not every embedding model is equally compatible with binary search. Some methods use learned projections or different binary encoding strategies, so it is inaccurate to treat all binary quantization as one universal procedure with one predictable recall profile.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Hamming-nearest vectors need not be the same as cosine-nearest float vectors. That difference can be acceptable for a broad candidate stage if important evidence survives, but it must be measured. A very fast binary scan that misses a decisive exception cannot be rescued simply by asking the generator to reason harder. Compression changes the evidence delivery frontier and must be evaluated there.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Distinguish search loss from representation loss</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Approximate navigation can miss candidates even when distances are exact. Quantization can misorder candidates even when the compressed search itself is exhaustive. Combining ANN and quantization creates both effects. Compare exact full-precision search, exhaustive compressed search when feasible, and the deployed approximate compressed index to understand where loss enters.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use neighbor recall against exact full-precision results to quantify geometry preservation, and use human-judged evidence coverage to assess task impact. A different vector neighbor may contain equivalent evidence, while a small neighbor-recall change may hide a large loss on a rare critical category. Both levels of evaluation are necessary for a meaningful decision.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use two-pass retrieval when it helps</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A common design retrieves a wider candidate set with compressed vectors, then rescores those candidates with higher-precision representations. The second pass can correct some distance distortion among candidates. It cannot recover a relevant vector omitted from the candidate set, so oversampling and first-stage recall remain important.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Keep three values separate: compressed-search candidate count, refinement count, and final result count. Increasing all three at once makes the experiment difficult to interpret. Benchmark the candidate coverage before refinement and the ranking after refinement. If full-precision rescoring improves order but complete evidence is still missing, the first-stage candidate method or breadth is the next suspect.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Fetching original vectors can add random storage reads, especially under concurrent queries and restrictive filters. A warm-cache benchmark may understate that cost. Measure complete p95 latency and storage load as well as the compressed index's internal search time. Quantization can move the bottleneck from RAM capacity to I/O, which may still be a good trade but is not a free optimization.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Reduced dimension is a different operation</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Truncating dimensions reduces the number of coordinates; quantization reduces the precision used to represent them. These operations can be combined, but they lose information in different ways. Arbitrarily taking the first few coordinates of a standard embedding is not generally justified. The ordering of dimensions need not represent decreasing semantic importance.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Matryoshka-style embeddings are trained so selected prefixes remain useful representations at different dimensions. With a compatible model and supported sizes, a short prefix can support inexpensive candidate search while a longer representation supports refinement. Validate the exact model's documented behavior and renormalization requirements. The label does not guarantee that any prefix or any compression combination is equally accurate.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Calibrate and monitor the quantizer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Training or calibration data should reflect the vectors expected in service, including language, source type, product family, and recent content. A codebook trained on one narrow distribution may encode another poorly. Maintain configuration metadata so queries and stored codes are interpreted consistently. An incompatible codebook or scaling configuration can produce plausible-looking scores with invalid meaning.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Monitor new data and update patterns. If the corpus shifts from short prose to multilingual technical tables, both embeddings and quantization behavior can change. Re-evaluate quality on current samples, and plan how a new quantizer is trained, deployed, and rolled back. Re-encoding a large corpus is a lifecycle operation, not merely a runtime flag change.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Recalibrate thresholds after changing representation</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compression can alter score distributions and ordering. A similarity cutoff calibrated on full-precision cosine values may not transfer to integer or binary distances. Do not reuse the old threshold merely because the new search API returns a number in a familiar range. Validate evidence sufficiency using the new configuration and representative unanswerable questions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The same applies to hybrid fusion and reranker inputs. If downstream code assumes comparable raw scores, quantization can expose a hidden coupling. Rank-based fusion may reduce some score-scale problems, but it does not repair missing evidence. Keep score interpretation explicit and evaluate the complete retrieval path, including any final-context selection rules.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Decide with a quality-resource frontier</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Sweep a small number of precision formats, code sizes, and candidate counts while keeping the workload stable. Record resident memory, total storage, build and training cost, latency under load, neighbor recall, evidence coverage, and final answer correctness. Compare configurations that meet the same task requirements rather than celebrating compression alone.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For a hypothetical support assistant, int8 might reduce RAM enough to avoid a larger machine while preserving evaluated evidence coverage. Another corpus might require full-precision refinement to retain exact product distinctions. A binary first pass may be appropriate for one workload and unacceptable for another. These are empirical outcomes, not universal rankings of the quantization methods.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">What the architectural answer should emphasize</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Scalar quantization compresses coordinates, product quantization stores learned subvector codes, and binary methods use bit-level representations. They can save substantial resources, but their cost is potential distance distortion and missing or misranked evidence. I validate that cost with controlled baselines and application tests, then include refinement, storage access, and maintenance in the total comparison. No fixed recall-loss percentage should substitute for measuring the actual corpus.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">A worked capacity and quality experiment</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Assume a hypothetical system stores five million vectors with 768 float32 coordinates. The raw coordinate payload is about 15.36 billion bytes. Converting that payload to one byte per coordinate would reduce it to about 3.84 billion bytes, excluding scale metadata. If the graph, IDs, and other structures occupy another fixed amount, the total memory reduction will be less than fourfold. If a full-precision copy remains in RAM for refinement, the anticipated saving might largely disappear. Write down the actual storage plan before claiming the optimization achieved its goal.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Now define an experiment with three configurations: full precision, compressed search alone, and compressed search followed by original-vector refinement. Keep the corpus, eligible filters, exact ground truth, and final result count fixed. For each configuration, measure candidate evidence coverage, final ranking, complete request latency, and memory under expected concurrency. Include questions whose answers depend on nearly identical product codes or policy exceptions, because those may reveal losses that an average semantic-query score hides.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Suppose compressed search alone meets the memory target but misses several critical evidence groups. Refinement improves ranking for candidates that were found, yet the same groups remain absent. That result shows that increasing refinement precision alone cannot repair the omission. Increase first-stage breadth, change the code representation, or retain a different search route for those cases. If none meets the service budget, the more aggressive compression is not appropriate for the workload, even if its isolated distance calculations are extremely fast.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">After selecting a configuration, preserve the evaluation and monitor it after source growth. The compression decision was justified for a particular corpus and query distribution. New languages, document types, or embedding-model versions can invalidate that evidence. A migration to another embedding space generally requires rebuilding both the vector index and its trained compression artifacts. Keep old and new versions isolated during rollout rather than interpreting codes with an incompatible codebook.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">One final correction to the original framing is that compression should not almost always be enabled merely because the corpus is large. At some scales, operational simplicity and quality headroom may matter more than saving additional memory. At others, compression makes an otherwise impossible deployment feasible. The defensible position is conditional: choose the least costly representation that still satisfies the measured requirements, and retain enough observability to detect when those requirements stop being met.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For release acceptance, specify which regressions are disqualifying before inspecting the results. A small average improvement in latency should not automatically justify losing the only supporting passage for a critical policy category. Use paired queries and review the examples that changed, including cases where compressed search unexpectedly improves the result. Such improvements can happen because approximate ordering changes, but they do not prove the compressed representation is universally superior. Preserve the complete benchmark configuration so a later index, embedding, or quantizer upgrade can be compared on the same basis. This turns compression into a controlled capacity decision rather than a one-time optimistic assumption.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://www.sbert.net/examples/sentence_transformer/applications/embedding-quantization/README.html\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Sentence Transformers embedding quantization</a></p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Lower-memory-footprint\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Faiss memory reduction</a></p>\n</div>"},{"q":"How do you handle tables, images and complex PDFs in a RAG pipeline?","g":["multimodal rag"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Tables, images, and complex PDFs require a document-understanding pipeline rather than a plain text-extraction step. The objective is to preserve the information relationships needed to answer questions: reading order, headings, row and column labels, units, captions, footnotes, and links between visual elements and surrounding text. If those relationships are destroyed before indexing, a better retriever or larger language model may simply process a damaged representation more fluently.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">I separate source fidelity from retrieval convenience. Keep the original file or governed reference, a structured extracted representation, searchable derivatives, and provenance connecting them. A natural-language summary can help find a table, but the original table values should remain available for verification. A generated image caption can aid retrieval, but it must not become an unquestioned substitute for the image when the question depends on visual details.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Classify the source before choosing extraction</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A digitally generated PDF may contain a usable text layer, a scanned PDF may require OCR, and a mixed PDF may contain both. Multi-column reports, forms, slides, diagrams, and spreadsheets encode meaning differently. Detect these categories or route them using document metadata and layout inspection. Applying one parser blindly to every file creates predictable silent failures.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Preserve file version, page count, language, access scope, and ingestion status. Use bounded processing and explicit error reporting for malformed or unsupported documents. A successful file upload should not imply successful knowledge ingestion. The application should know whether extraction completed, whether important pages failed, and whether the resulting content is safe to serve as evidence.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Reconstruct layout and reading order</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Layout-aware parsing identifies blocks such as titles, paragraphs, lists, tables, captions, and page furniture. The goal is to reconstruct an order that follows the document's meaning rather than the order of text objects in the file. Repeating headers and footers should not be interleaved into every paragraph or treated as substantive policy text.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Tools such as Docling and document-AI services can provide structured representations, but their suitability depends on your document types and deployment constraints. Evaluate actual extraction outputs on representative files. A tool's ability to detect a table does not guarantee that it correctly handles merged cells, multi-page continuation, superscripts, or a footnote that changes one row's interpretation.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Preserve tables as relationships</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A table cell is meaningful because of its row label, column label, units, and surrounding qualifiers. Flattening cells into whitespace-separated text can turn 'Plan A, 20, 40' into an uninterpretable sequence. Markdown or HTML can preserve a simple rectangular table, while richer structures may require an explicit cell model with spans and header associations.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For a pricing table, store the plan name, billing period, currency, feature, and value together. A number without its unit is not reliable evidence. If a column means annual price but the user asks about monthly cost, the system needs an explicit transformation or a clarification. The extraction layer should not silently guess whether a value is a price, percentage, date, or count.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Chunk small and large tables differently</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A small table can remain one retrievable unit when it fits the evidence budget and preserves all relevant labels. Add its title and source location. A large table may need row groups, each repeating the necessary column headers and units. Keep a reference to the complete table so a retrieved fragment can be expanded when the question requires comparison across groups.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Do not split a merged header from the columns it governs. For multi-page tables, detect repeated headers and continuation relationships. If a footnote applies to selected rows, carry that relationship into the derived chunk. Naively repeating every footnote in every row can add confusion, while omitting it can produce a confident but materially incomplete answer.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use summaries for discovery, not numerical authority</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A table summary can describe what the table contains: annual revenue by region from one year to another, or feature availability by subscription plan. This gives semantic retrieval language that users are likely to ask. Keep the summary labeled as a generated derivative and connect it to the structured source table.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">When a question asks for an exact value, retrieve the relevant cells and their labels rather than trusting a prose summary to reproduce every number accurately. A summary may round values or omit a small category that later matters. If generation is used to create the summary, validate it and avoid silently promoting unsupported interpretations into the index.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Route computation to structured tools</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Questions about totals, maxima, trends, or filtered rows often benefit from SQL or a controlled dataframe operation once the table has been extracted reliably. The language model can help interpret the question and explain the result, while deterministic code performs arithmetic and filtering. Validate column names, types, units, and permissions before executing a query.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For example, 'Which region had the largest increase?' requires selecting comparable periods and computing differences. Retrieving the row with the largest final value would answer a different question. A structured execution path makes that distinction testable. Keep the calculation result and the source cells so the final answer can cite both the data and the operation performed.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Handle scans with OCR and quality controls</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">OCR introduces errors in characters, reading order, and structure. Confusing zero with the letter O can break an identifier; missing a minus sign can reverse a financial conclusion. Use language-appropriate recognition and preserve page coordinates where possible. Record confidence signals, but do not assume one universal threshold separates safe from unsafe pages.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Confidence is tool-specific and may be poorly calibrated for your corpus. Sample outputs for human review and measure field-level or task-level accuracy. Route uncertain or high-impact content for additional extraction, visual verification, or a clear limitation. Quarantining every low-scoring page without a recovery path can make essential evidence disappear silently, so track the resulting coverage gap.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Represent images and charts explicitly</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">An image can carry diagrams, screenshots, labels, or observations unavailable in nearby text. A vision model can produce a description for text search, while a compatible multimodal encoder can support image-related retrieval. Store the original image reference, page or region coordinates, caption, surrounding text, and permissions so the answer stage can inspect the actual evidence when needed.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Generated descriptions can hallucinate details, miss small labels, or oversimplify charts. Separate observed text from inferred interpretation. For a chart, capture axes, units, legend, time range, and plotted series before summarizing the trend. If exact values are not readable, say so rather than converting an approximate visual estimate into a precise fact.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Choose the retrieval representation for the task</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A text index over captions and descriptions helps with semantic questions about what a figure depicts. A multimodal index can help when queries or evidence depend on visual appearance. Structured table storage helps with exact numerical questions. These representations can coexist, but each adds cost, synchronization, and evaluation requirements.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Do not assume a CLIP-style embedding is ideal for small-text reading or precise chart arithmetic. Its representation objective may emphasize broad semantic or visual similarity. A screenshot with the right color scheme can be visually close while containing the wrong error code. Use exact text extraction and identifier search where the task requires it, and evaluate multimodal retrieval on realistic near misses.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Preserve provenance through every derivative</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Each chunk, table row group, image description, and generated summary should map to a source file version and a location such as page, section, bounding box, or cell range. This makes citations inspectable and supports reprocessing when extraction improves. Without this mapping, a plausible answer may be impossible to verify against the original artifact.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Version the parser and transformation configuration as well as the document. Re-running extraction can change reading order and chunk identifiers even when the file is unchanged. Stable source locations help migrate evaluation labels. When a derivative is superseded, delete or deactivate its old searchable forms so the system does not retrieve two conflicting interpretations of the same page.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Apply access control to originals and derivatives</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A caption, OCR transcript, or table summary can contain the same confidential information as the original file. Do not protect only the source URL while placing derivatives into a broadly shared index. Propagate tenant ownership, document permissions, deletion state, and retention rules to every representation and cache.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">When permissions change, update both search eligibility and source-view access. A citation should not grant access the caller did not already have. Also avoid leaking inaccessible titles or image previews through nearest-match suggestions. Multimodal processing adds more derived artifacts, so authorization and lifecycle handling become more important rather than less.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Evaluate extraction before evaluating answers</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Build a small document suite containing multi-column pages, scans, merged-cell tables, footnotes, charts, rotated pages, and repeated headers. Label critical fields and relationships. Measure reading-order correctness, cell association, OCR accuracy for important identifiers, and preservation of qualifications. A parser that performs well on prose may still fail the table category that dominates user questions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Then evaluate retrieval and answer generation against those extracted artifacts. If a wrong answer comes from a malformed table, fix extraction first. If the table is correct but the wrong row is retrieved, investigate search and query interpretation. If the correct row is present but arithmetic is wrong, investigate computation. Keeping these boundaries separate prevents expensive model changes from masking a data-quality defect.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Operate ingestion as a managed pipeline</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use idempotent processing, bounded retries, per-stage status, and a review queue for failures. Track extraction latency, cost per page, OCR usage, derivative sizes, and the fraction of documents requiring fallback. A vision-heavy pipeline may be unnecessarily expensive for ordinary digital text, while a cheap text-only path may be unacceptable for complex scans.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Choose fallbacks according to observed failure modes. A second OCR pass may help rotated text; a visual model may help a diagram; a different table extractor may help merged cells. Preserve the original and intermediate artifacts long enough to debug within your retention policy. The objective is reliable evidence, not simply maximizing the number of files marked processed.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">What a strong implementation delivers</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A reliable multimodal RAG pipeline keeps source fidelity, structured relationships, searchable representations, and provenance aligned. It uses layout-aware parsing, table-aware chunking, OCR where needed, and visual interpretation with appropriate verification. It routes exact calculations to structured tools and evaluates every transformation that can alter meaning. Better retrieval begins with evidence that still means what the original document meant.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">A worked table-processing scenario</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Suppose a hypothetical report lists subscription plans in rows and monthly price, annual price, and refund eligibility in columns. Enterprise eligibility is marked with an asterisk, and the footnote states that contract terms govern. A plain text extractor outputs the row values but drops the footnote and collapses the two price columns. The assistant later answers that every enterprise plan is refundable because it treats the asterisk as meaningless punctuation. This is not primarily an embedding problem; the source relationship disappeared during extraction.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A better representation preserves the table title, each column's billing period and currency, the plan name, and the asterisk-to-footnote relationship. A row-level chunk can repeat the necessary headers and include the applicable footnote. A table-level discovery summary can explain that the report compares pricing and eligibility, but should not replace the actual row for a precise answer. The final response should distinguish the standard table rule from contract-dependent enterprise terms.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Now imagine the user asks which plan has the largest percentage discount for annual billing. The system must compare twelve monthly payments with the annual price for each plan, accounting for any missing or negotiated values. A controlled calculation returns the eligible plans, formulas, and source cells. The model explains those results and excludes enterprise pricing if the report does not provide a comparable public value. Retrieving the cheapest annual plan would not answer the requested percentage comparison.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Add regression tests at each boundary. Extraction tests confirm the headers and footnote survive. Retrieval tests confirm that the enterprise row can be found with paraphrased queries. Calculation tests check the discount formula and missing-value handling. Answer tests check that the contract qualification appears and that the citations point to the correct report version. This layered approach makes a complex-PDF failure diagnosable and prevents a visually convincing answer from concealing an upstream loss of meaning.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For production acceptance, include a source-to-answer review rather than reviewing text alone. A reviewer should open the cited page or table region and confirm that the answer preserved labels, values, units, and exceptions. This catches errors that remain invisible when both retrieval and generation operate on the same flawed extraction. Sample especially from documents with low parser confidence, recent parser upgrades, and formats known to contain merged cells or diagrams. Keep these reviews targeted and measurable so they improve the pipeline rather than becoming an informal last-minute inspection that cannot identify where the representation failed.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://docling-project.github.io/docling/concepts/docling_document/\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Docling structured document representation</a></p>\n</div>"},{"q":"What is GraphRAG and when is the extra complexity justified?","g":["graph rag"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">GraphRAG is a broad architectural idea: use graph-structured information, alongside source content, to retrieve or organize evidence for generation. The graph may represent entities, relationships, document links, dependencies, or other domain structure. One prominent implementation is Microsoft's GraphRAG approach, which extracts graph information and produces community-level reports that can support local and global querying. That implementation is an important example, but it should not be treated as the only possible definition of graph-enhanced retrieval.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The motivation is that similarity search alone does not always expose the relationships or corpus-wide coverage a question requires. A passage can be semantically close to a query without containing the next connection in a dependency chain. A request for themes across hundreds of reports may need a broader view than a few nearest passages. Graph structure and summaries can help organize that evidence, provided the extracted relationships are accurate and source-traceable.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Distinguish local lookup from global synthesis</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Local questions focus on a particular entity and its nearby relationships: which services depend on this component, which contracts mention this supplier, or which incidents relate to this product. Graph traversal can identify linked entities and retrieve supporting passages. The graph supplies a navigational structure, while source text establishes the factual basis for the response.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Global questions ask for a broader picture: recurring themes across reports, patterns across incidents, or common dependency risks. A small nearest-neighbor list may overrepresent the most similarly worded documents and miss dispersed evidence. Community summaries or other corpus-level representations can support broader coverage. However, a broad summary is still a generated derivative and can omit minority findings or misstate prevalence.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Understand one common indexing approach</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">In a typical extraction-based design, ingestion identifies entities and relationships from source text, resolves references where possible, and records supporting provenance. A graph can then be clustered into communities, with reports summarizing their content. Query processing selects relevant entities, relationships, source passages, or community reports according to the task. The exact pipeline depends on the implementation and domain.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">This process can require substantial model inference and data management. Entity extraction, relationship extraction, descriptions, resolution, and summary generation can each introduce errors. You do not necessarily need a separate graph database; some implementations operate over stored graph artifacts or structured tables. Choose persistence based on query needs, update patterns, and scale rather than assuming the term graph requires a particular database product.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Explain the benefit with a dependency example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Imagine a hypothetical application inventory. A service depends on a library, the library depends on another component, and an internal advisory identifies a risk in that component. The user's question asks which customer-facing services may be affected. The answer requires following relationships and checking versions, not merely retrieving the passage most similar to the phrase customer-facing risk.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A graph can make the dependency path explicit, then retrieve the inventory and advisory passages supporting each edge. The response should explain the path and any uncertainty. If the graph omits version constraints or treats an optional development dependency as a production dependency, the conclusion can be wrong despite an apparently valid path. Graph connectivity is not equivalent to established operational impact.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Avoid claiming vector RAG cannot do multi-hop work</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A fixed, small top-k similarity lookup may struggle with multi-hop or global questions, but retrieval architectures can also use iterative search, query decomposition, structured tools, hierarchical summaries, and broad document processing. These are legitimate alternatives. GraphRAG is justified when its relational organization improves the measured workload enough to cover its extra complexity.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For the dependency example, a relational database query might already contain the authoritative edges and versions. Extracting a new graph from prose would add uncertainty rather than value. For a simple product FAQ, ordinary hybrid retrieval may be sufficient. The decision should compare realistic alternatives, not contrast GraphRAG with an intentionally weak baseline that lacks reranking, source expansion, or appropriate structured access.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Entity resolution is a central problem</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Different names can refer to the same entity, and identical names can refer to different entities. A company may appear under an abbreviation, historical name, or subsidiary name. A service identifier may be reused in separate environments. Incorrect merging creates false paths; failing to merge related references fragments the evidence and hides relevant connections.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use canonical identifiers when available, preserve aliases, and retain resolution confidence or review status where useful. Domain rules and deterministic matching can outperform a general model on well-defined identifiers. Ambiguous cases may require human review or explicit uncertainty rather than forced consolidation. Keep the original mentions and source locations so a mistaken resolution can be audited and corrected.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Relationship extraction needs scope and time</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">An edge such as supplier provides component is incomplete without context. Does it describe a current relationship or a historical one? Is the relationship asserted, proposed, denied, or conditional? Does it apply to one product version or an entire organization? A graph that strips these qualifiers can create misleading certainty and spurious multi-hop conclusions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Model relationships with the attributes needed for the domain, including time, direction, status, and provenance. Not every task needs a complex ontology, but the representation must preserve distinctions that change answers. Treat a statement that a partnership is being considered differently from evidence that the partnership exists. Generated extraction should not silently turn speculation into an authoritative edge.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Community summaries support navigation, not unquestioned truth</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Summaries can make broad collections easier to search and synthesize. A query about recurring themes may use reports from multiple communities rather than selecting isolated passages. This can improve access to distributed information. The final answer still needs to distinguish a theme inferred from sampled summaries from a quantified claim established across the full corpus.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">If the assistant says most reports mention a problem, it needs a valid counting basis. A summary repeating the problem several times does not establish prevalence. For numerical aggregation, use structured counts or verified document-level labels when possible. Preserve source coverage information and inspect contradictory or minority examples so broad synthesis does not erase important exceptions.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Design provenance as part of the graph</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Each extracted entity, relationship, and summary claim should connect to source evidence and a version. A path is more trustworthy when every edge can be inspected. Without provenance, a final response may cite a graph artifact that merely repeats an extraction error. The user needs a route back to the material that establishes the relationship.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For multi-hop answers, preserve the distinction between direct statements and inferred conclusions. If source A establishes one edge and source B establishes another, the combined implication should be labeled as reasoning from those facts. Do not present the inferred conclusion as a direct quotation from one document. This makes uncertainty and source limitations visible rather than hiding them in a fluent narrative.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Plan updates and deletions explicitly</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A source change can affect entities, edges, community assignments, and summaries. Deleting a document may invalidate an edge that was supported only by that document, while another edge remains valid because other sources support it. Track dependencies so updates remove unsupported derivatives without unnecessarily destroying valid shared information.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Global summary updates can be expensive, and incremental behavior depends on the implementation. Define freshness targets and expose update lag. A graph built last month can be less appropriate than a current text index for a rapidly changing policy question. Hybrid routing may use fresh passages for recent facts and graph summaries for stable relationships, with version information making that distinction explicit.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Authorization becomes more subtle across aggregation</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A graph can combine information from documents with different access permissions. A community summary may reveal a relationship inferred from restricted sources even if no restricted excerpt is quoted. Protecting only original files is therefore insufficient. Derived entities, edges, summaries, and cached answers need permission-aware handling.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Possible designs include separate graphs by security boundary, provenance-aware filtering, or generating summaries only within a permitted scope. Each has cost and complexity. Do not assume filtering source chunks after graph traversal prevents all leakage: the traversal result or summary itself may expose restricted information. Evaluate authorization at the derivative level and ensure the user's evidence universe governs the entire answer path.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Evaluate graph quality and task quality separately</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Graph-level checks include entity-resolution accuracy, relationship precision and recall on reviewed samples, temporal correctness, and provenance completeness. Retrieval checks measure whether the relevant path and source evidence were found. Generation checks measure whether the answer follows that evidence and communicates uncertainty. A wrong conclusion can originate at any of these stages.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Build cases with missing edges, ambiguous aliases, outdated relationships, false positive links, and contradictory sources. Include questions answerable by a single passage so the system is not rewarded only for graph-heavy tasks. A graph may improve some categories while increasing cost or error on others. Report those slices rather than declaring one overall winner from an unbalanced benchmark.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Compare total lifecycle cost</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Measure extraction and summary generation, storage, update processing, query latency, and review effort. A graph pipeline may spend much of its budget during ingestion, while a simpler system spends more during repeated retrieval. The right trade-off depends on how often documents change and how many queries reuse the derived structure.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Also include engineering costs: ontology design, resolution rules, provenance management, permission propagation, and failure diagnosis. A prototype can look impressive while hiding a large maintenance burden. Start with a narrow relationship problem and a verified source collection, then expand only if the graph improves real task success. A lightweight entity index or structured metadata filter may deliver much of the value with less operational complexity.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">When the added complexity is justified</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">GraphRAG is a strong candidate when important questions repeatedly require relationship traversal, corpus-level synthesis, or combining evidence scattered across many sources, and simpler alternatives fail measured requirements. It is less compelling when queries are mostly direct lookups or when authoritative structured relationships already exist elsewhere. In those cases, use the simpler retrieval or query path and retain graph methods for the categories that benefit.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The architectural answer is conditional: GraphRAG organizes evidence through relationships and potentially community summaries, but its value depends on accurate extraction, resolution, provenance, freshness, and permission-aware aggregation. The graph can improve navigation and synthesis; it does not create facts that the source collection never established. Demonstrate the benefit on representative tasks before accepting the additional lifecycle and governance work.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">A worked adoption decision</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Suppose an incident-analysis team asks which dependencies recur across several service outages. Its current hybrid retriever answers individual incident questions well, but broad comparisons require repeated manual searching. Before introducing GraphRAG, define reviewed examples that identify the services, dependencies, dates, and supporting incident passages. Include cases where similar service names refer to separate environments and cases where a dependency was mentioned but explicitly ruled out as a cause.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Build a narrow graph over those verified concepts rather than extracting every possible entity. Compare it with an iterative retrieval baseline that decomposes the question and a structured aggregation baseline where labels are available. Evaluate whether the graph improves path discovery, evidence coverage, and final explanation correctness. Also measure the extra ingestion work and how quickly a corrected incident report updates the derived relationships.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">If the graph discovers relevant connections but frequently merges separate environments, entity resolution is the limiting factor. Adding a larger answer generator will not reliably repair a false path already presented as evidence. If the graph is accurate but summaries overstate causation, distinguish observed co-occurrence from established cause in both the schema and response rules. A service appearing in two incident documents does not prove it caused both incidents.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The team might adopt the graph only for cross-incident analysis while keeping ordinary retrieval for direct runbook questions. That hybrid outcome is a successful design decision, not evidence that the graph must replace the entire search system. Record a routing rule, preserve source-based citations, and reevaluate as the corpus changes. The added structure should earn its cost on the questions that need it.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">This example also explains why claims of global insight need careful wording. A graph built from a selected subset of incidents supports conclusions about that subset, not automatically every outage the organization has experienced. Expose coverage limits and dates. If an answer extrapolates beyond them, label the inference or decline to quantify it. Graph-based organization can make the evidence easier to navigate, but it does not remove sampling bias or turn incomplete source material into a complete account of the world.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">One useful acceptance check is whether a reviewer can reconstruct the important answer paths without trusting generated descriptions. If the system identifies a dependency chain, the reviewer should be able to inspect the source for each edge, its time scope, and any qualification. If that reconstruction is impossible, a polished graph visualization does not establish evidence quality. Use the same check when updating or removing sources: unsupported paths should disappear, while paths with remaining valid support should persist.
