This makes provenance a working operational requirement rather than an optional citation feature added after the graph is built.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">GraphRAG research paper</a></p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://microsoft.github.io/graphrag/query/global_search/\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">GraphRAG global search</a></p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://microsoft.github.io/graphrag/query/local_search/\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">GraphRAG local search</a></p>\n</div>"},{"q":"What is CAG (cache-augmented generation) and when would you prefer it over RAG?","g":["rag pipeline"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Cache-augmented generation, or CAG, refers in this context to answering from a preloaded knowledge collection while reusing cached model computation associated with that knowledge. Instead of searching for a few passages for every question, the application places a bounded relevant corpus into the model's context and reuses a stable prefix where the serving system supports it. The model then generates an answer using that supplied knowledge. The term describes a useful design pattern, not one universally standardized product interface.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The central question is whether the right authorized knowledge can be supplied in a stable, manageable context without per-query retrieval. If it can, avoiding a retrieval stage may simplify the system and remove some evidence-selection failures. If it cannot, retrieval, structured queries, or a hybrid design remain necessary. CAG is not an unconditional replacement for RAG, and a corpus fitting within an advertised window does not establish that the model will use it accurately or economically.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Understand what is being cached</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Autoregressive model serving often separates prompt processing, or prefill, from subsequent token generation. During processing, attention-related key and value representations can be retained so they need not be recomputed for the same prefix. Prefix caching can reuse some of that computation across requests when the model, token sequence, configuration, and serving implementation are compatible.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">This is different from caching the final answer. An answer cache returns an earlier response for a matching request or semantic key. A knowledge-prefix cache reuses computation while still generating a response to the new question. It is also different from a retrieval cache that stores search results. These mechanisms can coexist, but they have different invalidation, correctness, and permission requirements.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Distinguish explicit KV reuse from managed prompt caching</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">In a self-hosted setup, the application may manage a reusable prefix or KV-cache representation through the serving engine. A managed API may offer prompt caching, cached content, or another abstraction, with rules about eligible prefixes, storage duration, billing, and request format. The user may still need to send or reference the full logical context for each request even when some computation is reused.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Do not assume every API allows uploading a cache artifact once and then sending only a question. Likewise, do not assume a cache hit makes cached input free or removes the model's need to attend to the knowledge during generation. Verify the exact serving contract. The architecture depends on its guarantees, not on the word cache appearing in a feature description.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Explain the benefit with a bounded manual</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Imagine a support application whose authorized knowledge consists of one maintained product manual and a small set of stable policies. If that collection fits comfortably within the usable context budget, every question can see the complete collection. There is no risk that a nearest-neighbor search excludes the one paragraph containing an exception, because no per-query passage selection is required.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The repeated manual prefix can be cached, reducing repeated processing work where supported. The model still needs to identify the relevant portions and generate a correct answer. The problem shifts from selecting passages outside the model to using a larger supplied context effectively. A retrieval miss disappears, but long-context interpretation errors, conflicting sources, and unsupported extrapolation remain possible.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Prefer CAG under specific conditions</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">CAG is attractive when the knowledge boundary is clear, the authorized corpus is small enough for effective use, updates are relatively infrequent, and many requests reuse the same prefix. The serving platform must support useful reuse, and the resulting latency and cost must meet the application target. Those conditions matter more than a universal token threshold.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A manual containing eighty thousand tokens may be workable for one model and workload but inefficient or unreliable for another. The same corpus may also expand after localization, version history, and tool definitions are included. Reserve space for instructions, conversation, the question, output, and any model-specific overhead. Evaluate effective use rather than filling every available token merely because capacity exists.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Retrieval remains useful for large or variable scopes</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">If the corpus is too large, user-specific, or rapidly changing, retrieval can select the evidence needed for each request. A large enterprise knowledge base may contain many irrelevant departments and access scopes. Loading all of it into one prompt is not simply expensive; it can create an incorrect authorization boundary and make decisive information harder to find.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Retrieval also provides an explicit evidence-selection artifact that can be inspected and evaluated. CAG removes one failure surface but does not automatically provide the same operational trace of which passages mattered. You can still require source citations and inspect model outputs, but you should test whether those citations accurately support claims within the larger context.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Citations are possible with cached knowledge</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">CAG does not inherently prevent source attribution. Label document sections, versions, and passage identifiers in the supplied corpus, instruct the model to cite those identifiers, and validate emitted references. The application can map valid IDs to authorized source views. The citation challenge is evidence support, not whether the prefix was cached.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A model may cite an existing section that does not establish its claim, or combine two documents without explaining their relationship. Validate citation existence separately from claim support. Preserve source versions so a later manual update does not silently change what an old citation means. These requirements are similar to RAG, even though the evidence-delivery mechanism differs.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Permission design is fundamental</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A cached corpus should contain only knowledge the request is allowed to use. It is unsafe to preload every tenant's documents and rely on a prompt telling the model to ignore unauthorized sections. The model has already received the restricted information. Authorization belongs in corpus construction, cache selection, and source-view access before generation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">You can create separate prefixes for tenants, roles, or other stable permission boundaries. This can make CAG feasible in a controlled application, but many distinct access combinations reduce reuse and increase memory or cache-management cost. When permissions change, invalidate or stop selecting affected cache entries. Shared cache infrastructure must preserve isolation according to the engine or provider's documented behavior.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Model cache memory can be substantial</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Cached model state is not simply the text file stored once. A rough KV-memory estimate depends on token count, number of layers, key/value heads, head dimension, and bytes per stored value. For a simplified architecture, per-token storage is approximately two times layers times key/value heads times head dimension times bytes, with additional implementation overhead and possible compression.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">As a hypothetical example, thirty-two layers, eight key/value heads, head dimension 128, and two-byte values produce about 131,072 bytes per token, or 128 KiB. At one hundred thousand tokens, that is roughly 12.2 GiB of KV values before overhead. Actual architectures and serving optimizations vary, and prefix sharing can change aggregate usage. The example shows why fitting text in context does not imply cheap cache residency.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Cache hits do not eliminate decoding work</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The new question must be processed, and the model must generate the answer. During decoding, attention can still depend on the long cached prefix. A cache can save repeated prefill while leaving meaningful memory-bandwidth and context-access costs. Under high concurrency, long prefixes can reduce throughput or compete for cache capacity.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Measure time to first token, generation rate, complete response latency, and throughput. Compare cold and warm requests, cache misses, evictions, and restarts. A design that appears fast immediately after preloading may behave differently after low traffic allows a managed cache to expire or after many permission-specific prefixes compete for residency.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Invalidation must follow source changes</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A cached prefix represents a particular source version and instruction configuration. When a policy changes, the application must ensure new requests use the updated content. Depending on where a token change occurs and how prefix reuse works, some unchanged prefix computation may remain reusable, while affected later states require recomputation. It is too simplistic to say every change universally destroys every cache.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Version cache keys with corpus identity, source versions, permission scope, model configuration, and relevant prompt structure. Coordinate answer-cache invalidation as well. Replacing the knowledge prefix does not automatically remove old generated answers from another cache. Treat each cache layer as a derived view with an explicit validity rule and a traceable relationship to source content.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Compare cost with a complete accounting model</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">RAG can pay for retrieval infrastructure, query embeddings, reranking, and a smaller generation context. CAG can pay for larger logical input, cached-prefix processing or storage, and long-context generation. Managed pricing varies, and self-hosting introduces capacity and operational costs. Neither architecture is inherently cheaper across all workloads.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For a high-reuse stable manual, cached prefill savings may be meaningful. For sporadic queries across many personalized corpora, cache hit rates may be poor and maintenance costs substantial. Estimate request volume, prefix reuse, update frequency, eviction behavior, output length, and infrastructure utilization. Compare cost per correctly completed task rather than per isolated model call.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Evaluate answer quality directly</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use the same representative questions and source snapshot to compare CAG with a well-configured RAG baseline. Include single-fact questions, exceptions, comparisons, ambiguous requests, and no-answer cases. Measure completeness, grounding, citation support, abstention, and permission behavior, as well as latency and cost. Do not assume full-corpus access must produce better answers.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Test position robustness by moving decisive evidence within the loaded collection where source meaning permits. Long-context models can still overlook middle passages or favor repeated general statements over a rare exception. CAG removes a retrieval bottleneck but can expose a context-use bottleneck. A fair evaluation recognizes both rather than counting the absence of a vector database as a quality result.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use a hybrid architecture when boundaries differ</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A practical design can cache stable, universally authorized core documentation and retrieve dynamic or specialized material per query. The model receives both, with clear source labels, versions, and precedence rules. Another design retrieves a bounded authorized document set, then reuses that set as a prefix across a multi-turn task. These approaches combine retrieval selection with cache efficiency.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Be explicit about authority when cached and retrieved content disagree. A current retrieved amendment may override a stable cached policy section, but the relationship must be established by source rules, not merely by prompt position. If the conflict cannot be resolved, the assistant should communicate uncertainty rather than silently blending the sources into a new rule.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Decide from the application boundary</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">I would prefer CAG when a stable, appropriately scoped corpus fits within an effective context budget and repeated-prefix reuse yields measured quality or operational benefits. I would prefer retrieval when the knowledge space is large, dynamic, permission-sensitive, or query-dependent. I would combine them when stable and changing knowledge have different characteristics. The decision follows evidence, not a universal claim that caching replaces search.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The interview framing is that CAG preloads a bounded knowledge context and reuses compatible model computation, while RAG selects external evidence at query time. CAG can simplify retrieval and avoid selection misses, but it retains long-context, freshness, cost, permission, and citation challenges. Cache mechanics and model capacity must be evaluated together because a reusable prefix is an optimization, not a guarantee of correct evidence use.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">A worked comparison for a support application</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Consider a hypothetical product team with one stable manual and a frequently changing incident bulletin. A pure CAG design loads both into a reusable prefix. It answers manual questions without passage-selection failures, but every bulletin update changes the knowledge state and may reduce reuse. A pure RAG design searches both sources for each question, offering freshness and smaller context at the cost of retrieval latency and possible omissions. The team should compare both on the same question set rather than assuming the simpler architecture is automatically superior.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A hybrid design caches the stable manual within the appropriate permission scope and retrieves the current bulletin when the question concerns a known incident. Source labels identify which text is stable documentation and which is a dated operational update. If the bulletin temporarily changes the recommended procedure, the response follows the documented override rule and cites the relevant version. It should not blend the old manual and new bulletin into an unsupported compromise.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The benchmark includes manual-only questions, bulletin-only questions, rule-plus-exception questions, unrelated requests, and permission changes. Measure warm and cold latency, cache hit rate, source-update propagation, complete evidence coverage, and supported answer correctness. A favorable result on warm manual questions is not enough if the system serves stale incident guidance or mishandles newly revoked access. Those cases are part of the architecture's real workload.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Finally, define what happens when the cache is unavailable or evicted. The application may rebuild it, fall back to ordinary prompting within a budget, or use retrieval until reuse is restored. Make the behavior explicit so a transient cache condition does not silently change the evidence boundary or bypass access checks. Caching should optimize a correct serving path, while cache misses remain correct and observable. That separation is the practical reason to evaluate CAG as part of a complete application rather than as a benchmark of prefix processing alone.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15605\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Cache-Augmented Generation research paper</a></p>\n</div>"},{"q":"What happens when retrieved documents contradict each other, and how do you handle it?","g":["rag evaluation"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">This is a <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">knowledge conflict</strong>, and the default LLM behaviour is poor. Given two passages that disagree, a model often silently picks one - frequently the one that appears first in the prompt or is phrased most confidently - and presents it as settled fact. The user never learns that a conflicting source existed, and the answer looks authoritative precisely when it is least reliable.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The first step is diagnosis, because not every contradiction is the same problem. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Temporal conflicts</strong> come from superseded versions of a policy or a price list. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Scope conflicts</strong> only look contradictory: the EU and US terms differ because they apply to different customers, and each passage is correct for its own scope. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Source-quality conflicts</strong> pit an official document against an informal wiki page, a forum answer, or an outdated email. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Genuine disagreements</strong> exist in the source material itself, such as two research papers with different findings. Three mechanisms do most of the work.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Immutable, deterministic chunk IDs</strong> derived from <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">doc_id</code> plus a content hash make ingestion idempotent. Re-running the pipeline on unchanged content produces the same IDs and does no work, a changed paragraph produces a new ID, and diffing two versions of a document becomes a set comparison of IDs. It also stops duplicate chunks from accumulating when a job is retried.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Blue/green indexes</strong> are the safe way to ship changes that affect every vector, such as a new embedding model, a new chunking strategy, or a new text analyzer. Build the new index alongside the live one, run the evaluation suite against it, then flip an alias atomically. Never mutate the serving index in place for a re-embedding or a chunking change, because during the rebuild the index holds a mixture of old and new vectors, which are not comparable with each other, and you cannot roll back cleanly. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Alias indirection</strong> in the vector store or in application config makes both the flip and the rollback a one-line change, and keeping the previous index for a retention period makes rollback real instead of theoretical.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For incremental content updates, upsert changed chunks and hard-delete removed ones. Hard deletion matters: a document withdrawn for legal or compliance reasons must disappear from retrieval, and a soft-deleted chunk that still ranks is a defect. It decides whether to retrieve at all, what to search for, and which index or tool to use, and it evaluates whether the results are sufficient. If they are not, it can retrieve again with a refined query before answering. The pipeline stops being a straight line and becomes a control flow with state, which is why frameworks such as LangGraph model it as a graph.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Common capabilities are <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">query decomposition</strong> for multi-hop questions (find the vendor, then find that vendor's contract terms), <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">routing</strong> across heterogeneous sources such as a vector index, a SQL database, and a web search tool, <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">self-correction</strong> when retrieved results look irrelevant or unsupported, and <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">tool use beyond retrieval</strong>, including SQL, calculators, and internal APIs. Patterns such as Self-RAG and Corrective RAG are variations on grading the retrieved evidence and acting on the grade.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">It is the <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">wrong</strong> solution when the query distribution is narrow and predictable. A support bot that answers FAQ-style questions gains nothing from planning and pays for it on every request. The costs are specific. Latency multiplies with each loop iteration, so a pipeline that answers in a couple of seconds in a single pass can take several times longer when it loops. Cost scales with the number of LLM calls. Behaviour becomes non-deterministic, so debugging and evaluation get much harder, because two runs of the same question can follow different paths. And you inherit agent failure modes: looping, premature termination, choosing the wrong tool, and compounding an early error through later steps.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The engineering rule is to <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">start single-pass</strong>, measure which queries fail, and add agentic behaviour only for the classes that structurally need it, such as multi-hop questions, questions that span several data sources, or questions whose answer needs computation. Then bound it: a maximum-iteration budget, a token or cost ceiling, a timeout, and a defined fallback answer for when the loop does not converge. A useful middle path is a router that sends simple queries down the fast pipeline and escalates only the hard ones to the agent loop.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Agentic RAG is currently fashionable, and a common interview trap is to propose it for everything. A single-pass pipeline retrieves a blend of both and answers poorly. An agent decomposes the question, queries the SQL tool, retrieves per vendor, checks that every vendor has a clause, and then writes the answer. The same agent applied to <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">how do I reset my password?</code> would only add seconds and cost.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Build the single-pass baseline first and keep it as the fast path. Log every step of the agent loop - decisions, tool calls, and retrieved evidence - so that runs are inspectable. Cap iterations (3 to 5 is a common starting point), set per-request cost and time budgets, and define a graceful fallback. Evaluate trajectories as well as final answers: tool-choice accuracy, number of steps, and success on a multi-hop set. Use a stronger model for planning and cheaper models for sub-steps where quality allows, and keep tool permissions narrow, since an agent with broad tool access widens the attack surface for prompt injection.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Agentic RAG puts the model in a loop that decides whether, what, and where to retrieve, and can retry with a refined query. A typical request spends time in query rewriting, embedding, ANN search, re-ranking, and generation, and generation usually dominates. A full transcript grows without limit, increases cost and latency on every turn, and degrades the model's attention to what matters. Summarise when the history crosses a token threshold. Keep <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">pinned facts</strong>, such as the user's account tier, the chosen product, or the region, in a small structured state object that is passed explicitly, instead of hoping they survive summarisation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Retrieved-document context.</strong> Decide whether previously retrieved chunks persist across turns. A good compromise is to keep the previous turn's chunks available as candidates, re-retrieve on every turn, and let ranking decide which evidence the new answer uses.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Also <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">detect topic changes</strong>. When the user genuinely switches subject, reset or down-weight the accumulated context, otherwise the assistant keeps dragging an old subject into new answers. A small classifier, or a check inside the rewrite step, can output whether the new turn continues the previous topic, and the rewriter can then ignore the history when it does not. Finally, keep the original user message for display and logging while using the rewritten query for retrieval, so that you can debug the difference.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Real users never ask isolated questions. After retrieval, an extractor keeps only the parts relevant to the query and discards the rest. The extractor can be a small LLM that is asked to copy the relevant sentences, an extractive model, or a cheaper embedding-similarity filter that scores each sentence against the query and keeps those above a threshold.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">It differs from lowering k in what it optimises. Lowering k reduces the number of documents, and risks dropping the one chunk that held the answer. Compression keeps document <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">coverage</strong> while cutting token <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">volume</strong>, so you can retrieve k = 10 for recall and still send the model roughly the token equivalent of k = 3. That is valuable when relevant chunks are long and mostly boilerplate, as in legal documents, log dumps, API references, and meeting transcripts, where the answer is a sentence or two inside a thousand-token chunk.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">It also differs from re-ranking. A re-ranker reorders whole passages and leaves their text intact, while compression edits the passages. The two combine well: re-rank to choose the best passages, then compress them to fit the context budget. Compression can also help the model directly, since long contexts full of irrelevant text can dilute attention and invite the model to latch onto distractors.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The costs are real. An extractor adds a model call on the critical path, so latency and cost rise, and an LLM-based extractor can paraphrase instead of copying, which breaks citation and verbatim quoting. There is a real risk of <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">over-compressing</strong>: a definition or a qualifier two sentences away from the matching sentence is dropped, and the answer becomes subtly wrong, for example by missing an exception clause. Compression can also remove the heading or identifier that tells the model which entity a sentence refers to.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Measure faithfulness and answer correctness before and after. If they drop, the compressor is too aggressive, and you should loosen the threshold, keep neighbouring sentences, or switch to a conservative extractive filter. If the gain is only token savings and quality is unchanged, check whether a smaller k plus a re-ranker would give the same saving more cheaply.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Context windows are limited, and context tokens cost money and attention. Compression is one of the few techniques that reduces prompt size without reducing recall at the retrieval stage, but it trades latency and risk for that benefit, so it needs to be justified with measurement.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Practical example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A contracts assistant retrieves 10 clauses of about 800 tokens each for the question <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">what is the notice period for termination without cause?</code>. Most of each clause is definitions and unrelated boilerplate. A sentence-level filter keeps the two sentences that state the notice period, plus the one that defines when it applies, and discards the rest, cutting the prompt from roughly 8,000 tokens to under 1,000. When the team tests it, one answer misses an exception for key accounts, so they add one neighbouring sentence on each side.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Start with a cheap sentence-level embedding filter and move to an LLM extractor only if quality demands it. Use extractive compression, which copies text verbatim, when citations must be exact. Keep neighbouring sentences and the chunk heading as protected context. Run compression after re-ranking, and apply it only when the context exceeds a token budget. LangChain's ContextualCompressionRetriever, with LLMChainExtractor and EmbeddingsFilter, implements these options. Compare answers with and without it on a golden set, tracking faithfulness, completeness, latency, and cost per request.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Contextual compression trims irrelevant text inside retrieved chunks, so you keep high recall but send fewer tokens, whereas lowering k throws away whole documents and risks losing the answer. It costs an extra step and can over-compress, so verify faithfulness before and after.</p>\n</div>"},{"q":"When would you fine-tune an embedding model, and how do you do it?","g":["embeddings"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Fine-tune when your <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">domain vocabulary diverges sharply</strong> from the embedding model's training distribution - medical coding, legal citation, internal product codenames, industrial part numbers - and your evaluation shows that semantically related domain pairs are not landing close together. The evidence should come from your own data: a labelled set where the correct passage ranks poorly under the off-the-shelf model, with failures concentrated in the jargon-heavy slice. Gains from domain adaptation are often several points of Recall@k, and sometimes more, which can exceed what any prompt change gives you, but the size depends entirely on how far your domain sits from the base model.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The method has four stages. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Build the training data</strong> as triplets of <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">(query, positive passage, negative passages)</code>. The best source is real query logs combined with click or feedback signals. Where those do not exist, synthesise queries for each chunk with an LLM, filter out the weak ones, and have humans review a sample. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Train</strong> with a contrastive objective. <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">MultipleNegativesRankingLoss</code> from sentence-transformers is the pragmatic default: it uses the other positives in the batch as in-batch negatives, so larger batches give more signal for free. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Mine hard negatives</strong>: passages that the current model retrieves as relevant but that are not the answer. Easy random negatives teach the model almost nothing, while hard negatives force it to learn the distinctions your domain cares about. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Evaluate</strong> on a held-out set of queries that the training data never touched.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Watch for false negatives in hard-negative mining. A passage the model ranks highly may really be a correct answer that your labels do not mark, and training against it pushes the model in the wrong direction. Review a sample of the mined negatives, or exclude candidates above a similarity ceiling relative to the positive. Also hold out by document and by time, not just by random row, so that you measure generalisation instead of memorisation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">State the costs plainly. You must <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">re-embed the entire corpus</strong> after training, since old and new vectors are not comparable. You now own a model artefact, with versioning, serving, and retraining concerns, and with a new failure mode where the model drifts away from general language ability. And you need a held-out evaluation to prove the gain. Try cheaper options first: hybrid search for identifiers, a re-ranker, better chunking, and query rewriting. A re-ranker is usually a bigger win for less operational burden, and fine-tuning the embedding model is justified when first-stage recall remains the bottleneck after those.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Retrieval recall caps the quality of the whole system, and an embedding model that does not understand your domain caps recall. Fine-tuning is the targeted fix, but it is also an operational commitment, so the interview signal is knowing both how to do it and when it is not yet worth it.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Practical example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A manufacturer's support assistant indexes manuals that use internal part codes and abbreviations, such as <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">HX-220 gasket</code>, that the base model barely knows. With illustrative figures, Recall at 10 on a labelled set of 400 real technician queries is only 0.62. The team mines query-passage pairs from resolved tickets, adds LLM-generated queries for uncovered manuals, mines hard negatives from similar part families, and fine-tunes with MultipleNegativesRankingLoss. Recall at 10 on a held-out set rises to 0.78, they re-embed the corpus into a new blue/green index, and they ship it after the evaluation gate passes.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Version the model and the training data together, and record which model version produced each vector. Keep a general-purpose evaluation alongside the domain one, to detect loss of general ability. Use a validation split that never appears in training, and tune the learning rate and the number of epochs conservatively, since small datasets overfit quickly. Plan the re-embedding as a blue/green index rebuild and budget compute for it. If your embedding provider offers hosted fine-tuning or adapters, compare that with self-hosting. Revisit the model when the corpus vocabulary shifts.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Fine-tune an embedding model when evaluation shows that domain vocabulary is hurting first-stage recall and cheaper fixes have not closed the gap. Train on query, positive, and hard-negative triplets with a contrastive loss, prove the gain on held-out queries, and accept the cost of re-embedding the corpus and owning a model.</p>\n</div>"},{"q":"How do you balance retrieval relevance against diversity for comprehensive answers?","g":["reranking"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Pure relevance ranking optimises for the single best passage, which is the wrong objective for questions like <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">what are the risks in this contract</code> or <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">summarise customer complaints about onboarding</code>. For those, <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">completeness</strong> matters more than the top hit, and the top five passages by similarity are often five variations on the same point.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">There are several levers. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">MMR</strong> penalises redundancy directly by choosing each next passage for its relevance to the query and its dissimilarity to those already selected. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Deduplication</strong> by content hash and by high pairwise cosine similarity removes copies before prompting. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Source diversity quotas</strong> cap how many chunks any one document may contribute, so that a single long document cannot monopolise the context. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Facet-aware retrieval</strong> decomposes the question into sub-aspects, such as pricing, security, and support for a vendor comparison, retrieves per aspect, and merges the results. <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Clustering</strong> the candidate set and taking a representative from each cluster guarantees that each theme in the candidates is represented.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Each lever has a cost. MMR needs tuning and can admit weaker passages. Quotas can exclude a document that really deserves more space. Facet decomposition needs an extra LLM call, and the facets themselves can be wrong. Clustering needs a method to choose the number of clusters and a way to choose a representative. In practice, teams combine a cheap lever, such as dedup plus a per-document cap, with one structural lever, such as facet-aware retrieval, for survey-type questions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The decision should be <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">query-dependent, not global</strong>. Classify intent as lookup versus survey, with a cheap classifier or as part of the query rewriter, and apply diversification only for survey-type queries. Forcing diversity on a precise factual lookup actively hurts it, because the second and third passages then dilute the one that holds the answer. Evaluate with coverage-oriented metrics, such as the fraction of known aspects that appear in the retrieved context, and not only with precision and recall of the single best passage.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Comprehensive answers are a common enterprise requirement, in audits, summaries, and comparisons, and a pipeline tuned for lookups quietly fails on them. Knowing that relevance and diversity are separate objectives, and how to switch between them, is a clear marker of experience.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Practical example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A product team asks, <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">what are customers complaining about during onboarding?</code> Retrieval returns 20 support tickets, 12 of which describe the same email-verification bug. With top-5 relevance, the answer talks only about verification. After deduplication, a cap of two chunks per ticket thread, and clustering into themes (verification, SSO setup, data import, pricing confusion), the context contains a representative from each theme and the answer covers the whole landscape. For the next query, <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">what is the SSO setup URL?</code>, the classifier marks it as a lookup and diversification is skipped.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Add an intent classification step to the query rewriter that outputs lookup, survey, or comparison. Apply MMR or clustering after re-ranking, on the top 30 to 50 candidates. Deduplicate at ingest as well as at query time. Build a survey-style evaluation set with a labelled list of aspects that a complete answer must mention, and measure aspect coverage. Track the effect on lookup queries separately, so that you can prove diversification is not hurting them. Keep the context budget in mind, since diversity pulls in more distinct passages and each one costs tokens.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Relevance finds the best passage; diversity finds the complete picture. Use MMR, deduplication, per-document caps, facet-aware retrieval, or clustering for survey-style questions, and keep pure relevance ranking for precise lookups, selecting between them with an intent classifier.</p>\n</div>"},{"q":"What is Matryoshka representation learning and why is it useful for RAG?","g":["embeddings"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><strong style=\"font-weight:600\">Matryoshka representation learning</strong> trains an embedding model so that the prefix of the vector is itself a usable embedding. The name comes from the nested Russian dolls: the first 256 dimensions of a 3072-dimension vector carry much of the signal, the first 768 carry more, and the full vector carries the most. Training achieves this by applying the loss at several truncation points at the same time, for example at 256, 512, 1024, and 3072 dimensions, which pushes the model to put the most important information into the earliest dimensions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Ordinary embeddings do not have this property. Their information is spread across all dimensions with no ordering of importance, so truncating them destroys quality. Matryoshka training is what makes truncation safe. How much quality survives at each size depends on the model, so you must measure it on your own data instead of trusting a headline figure.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The RAG payoff is a cheap <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">two-stage search</strong>. Store and search truncated vectors, for example 256 or 512 dimensions, for the first pass. For 3072-dimension vectors that cuts raw vector memory by about 12x and 6x respectively, and it speeds up distance computation roughly in proportion. Then <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">rescore</strong> the top candidates, such as the top 100, using the full-dimension vectors, which are kept on disk or in a cheaper tier. Recall stays close to the full-dimension baseline while memory and latency drop substantially, with the exact trade-off depending on the model and the corpus. Index overhead, such as HNSW graph links, does not shrink with dimension, so the total saving is smaller than the raw ratio.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">It also gives you a dial instead of a rewrite. You can trade quality for cost per index or per tenant without changing models or re-embedding, since the truncation happens at index time from the same stored vector. A free tier can use 256-dimension vectors while an enterprise tier uses the full size, all from one embedding pipeline. Several providers and open models expose this directly: OpenAI's text-embedding-3 models accept a dimensions parameter, and sentence-transformers supports training with a <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">MatryoshkaLoss</code>.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">There are details to respect. Truncated vectors usually need to be <strong style=\"font-weight:600\">re-normalised</strong> to unit length after truncation if you use cosine similarity or dot product. The prefix property only holds for models trained for it, so never truncate a standard model. And if the first stage uses a truncated vector, the recall of that first stage is what the rescoring step inherits, so the candidate count must be sized with that in mind.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why it matters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Vector storage and search cost grow with the number of vectors times their dimension. At millions or billions of chunks, memory is a primary cost driver, and Matryoshka embeddings are a model-level way to cut it without a second model or a separate compression pipeline.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Practical example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A SaaS platform stores 50 million chunk vectors of 3072 dimensions, which at 4 bytes per float is roughly 600 GB of raw vectors. Truncating to 512 dimensions for the main index reduces that to about 100 GB of raw vector data, which fits in memory on far fewer nodes. Search returns the top 200 candidates from the 512-dimension index, the system fetches their full vectors from a cheaper store, rescores them, and keeps the top 10. In this illustrative case, their evaluation shows Recall at 10 within a point or two of the full-dimension index, so they ship it.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Implementation considerations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Verify that the model is actually trained with a Matryoshka objective and note which truncation sizes it supports. Re-normalise after truncation. Choose the first-stage dimension and the candidate count by sweeping them against recall and latency on your golden set, and pick the knee. Store full vectors separately for rescoring, and budget for that second lookup. Combine with other compression, such as scalar or binary quantisation, if memory is still a constraint, and measure each step separately. Record the dimension in the index metadata so that queries are truncated identically.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interview-ready answer</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Matryoshka embeddings are trained so that vector prefixes are themselves good embeddings, which lets you search with truncated vectors and rescore with full ones. That cuts memory and latency at a small recall cost, and gives you a quality-versus-cost dial without re-embedding or switching models.</p>\n</div>"},{"q":"Which retrieval metrics do you track, and what does each tell you?","g":["rag evaluation"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Retrieval metrics tell you whether your system found the evidence needed to answer a question, whether that evidence appeared early enough to survive selection, and how much irrelevant material accompanied it. In a RAG application, they diagnose the evidence-delivery pipeline rather than certify the final answer. An application can retrieve excellent evidence and still generate a wrong response, or retrieve the wrong document and accidentally answer correctly from the model's prior knowledge. Evaluate retrieval and generation separately, then connect both to task success.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">I track metrics at distinct boundaries: candidate retrieval, reranking, and final context assembly. For each boundary, I record the evaluation population, relevance definition, cutoff, permission scope, and corpus version. A value such as Recall@10 is difficult to interpret without those details. Ten candidates before reranking and ten passages actually delivered to the model represent different opportunities for failure and different operational costs.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">First define relevance and the evaluation unit</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A relevant passage must contribute evidence toward the actual question, including its constraints. A passage about refunds is not necessarily relevant to a question about refunds for enterprise annual subscriptions in a particular jurisdiction. Topic overlap alone is insufficient. Labels should distinguish direct support, partial support, background context, and irrelevant material where that distinction matters to the application.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Choose whether the unit is a document, passage, source span, or required fact. If a document has twenty chunks and only one answers the question, document-level success can hide passage-level failure. Conversely, counting overlapping copies of the same passage as distinct relevant items can exaggerate coverage. Where multiple passages express equivalent evidence, use an equivalence group or source-span mapping instead of insisting on one arbitrary chunk identifier.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Recall@k measures evidence coverage</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For an answerable query, Recall@k equals the number of relevant evaluation units retrieved in the first k results divided by the total number of relevant units identified for that query. Suppose four passages are relevant and the top five contain three. Recall@5 is three divided by four, or 0.75. Retrieving the remaining passage at rank eight increases Recall@10 to one, assuming it survives later filtering.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Recall is especially useful early in a two-stage system because a reranker cannot promote evidence that never became a candidate. However, ordinary recall is not a literal universal ceiling on answer accuracy. The model may answer from prior knowledge, equivalent evidence may be unlabeled, and many relevant passages may be redundant. The more precise architectural statement is that missing indispensable evidence limits the system's ability to produce a verifiably supported answer.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Label completeness matters. For a large corpus, you rarely know every relevant passage. Pool candidates from several retrieval methods, review likely alternatives, and describe the metric as recall against the judged evidence set. Otherwise, a new retriever can be penalized for finding valid passages that the original labeling method never discovered. Treat unjudged documents deliberately rather than silently calling them irrelevant.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Hit Rate@k measures whether anything useful appeared</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Hit Rate@k is the fraction of eligible queries for which at least one relevant result appears within the cutoff. For each query the outcome is binary: hit or miss. If eighty of one hundred answerable questions have at least one relevant passage in the top five, Hit Rate@5 is 0.80. This is often easy to explain to product teams because it resembles the proportion of questions with some available evidence.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Hit rate and recall answer different questions. Imagine a query requiring a general policy and an exception. Retrieving only the general policy produces a hit, but the exception may determine the answer. Hit rate can therefore look excellent while multi-part answers remain unreliable. I supplement it with complete-evidence coverage: the fraction of questions for which every indispensable evidence group is present.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Unanswerable queries require separate handling. When no relevant evidence exists, recall has a zero denominator and a hit is not desirable. Do not manufacture a score of zero or one without documenting the convention. Report answerable-query retrieval metrics separately from unanswerable-query rejection, false-support rate, and abstention quality. Those populations represent different product obligations.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Precision@k measures useful results versus clutter</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Precision@k equals the number of relevant results among the first k divided by k, under the declared convention for result lists shorter than k. In the earlier example, three relevant passages among five results give Precision@5 of 0.60. This measures how much of a fixed result budget contains useful evidence. It is particularly important near the final prompt because irrelevant passages consume tokens and can introduce misleading alternatives.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Define the denominator carefully when filters return fewer results. Precision at the actual returned length and precision at the requested cutoff are different quantities. Both can be useful, but they should not share one unlabeled dashboard line. Also report empty-result rate so a system cannot appear clean simply by returning almost nothing.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Chunk precision does not fully describe cost. One irrelevant passage might contain fifty tokens, while another contains three thousand. Track relevant-token density or redundant-token share where practical. A final context with four useful short passages and one enormous irrelevant appendix can have good chunk precision yet poor efficiency. These additional measurements are application-defined diagnostics, not universally standardized metrics.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">MRR measures the position of the first relevant result</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For one query, reciprocal rank is one divided by the rank of the first relevant result. It is zero if no relevant result appears inside the evaluated cutoff. Mean Reciprocal Rank averages that value across queries. If three queries first find relevant evidence at ranks one, two, and nowhere within five, their reciprocal ranks are one, one-half, and zero. MRR@5 is therefore 0.50.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">MRR is useful for single-fact lookup and for detecting whether a reranker brings a useful answer-bearing passage toward the front. Moving the first useful result from rank ten to rank two changes reciprocal rank from 0.10 to 0.50. This improvement can matter because subsequent selection may keep only a small number of passages, and users reviewing search results often inspect early results first.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">MRR ignores every relevant result after the first. A ranking containing one useful passage followed by irrelevant content can receive the same reciprocal rank as a ranking containing all required evidence immediately after that first passage. Do not use MRR alone for comparison, synthesis, or questions requiring several documents. A high MRR establishes early access to something useful, not full answerability.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">nDCG@k measures graded ranking quality</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain supports relevance grades rather than only relevant or irrelevant labels. For example, assign grade three to a passage that directly answers the scoped question, two to substantial partial support, one to useful background, and zero to irrelevant content. Define those grades operationally so annotators do not assign them merely from topical familiarity.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">One common formulation gives each result a gain of two raised to its relevance grade minus one, then discounts that gain by the base-two logarithm of rank plus one. DCG sums those discounted gains through k. IDCG is the best achievable DCG from the same judged relevance set, ordered ideally. nDCG is DCG divided by IDCG. Other gain conventions exist, so record the chosen formula.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Consider grades three, two, and zero. With exponential gains, the ideal DCG@3 is seven plus three divided by log base two of three, approximately 8.893. A ranking with grades zero, two, three has DCG approximately 5.393: the second-ranked item contributes about 1.893 and the third contributes 3.5. Its nDCG is approximately 0.606. The calculation rewards placing strong evidence early without treating partial support as worthless.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">When every judged result has grade zero, the ideal denominator is zero. Your evaluation library may use a defined fallback, but the dashboard must explain it. More generally, nDCG is only as meaningful as its relevance grades and judged candidate pool. A precisely computed number does not repair inconsistent annotation.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Context precision needs an explicit definition</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">In informal discussion, context precision can mean the fraction of prompt passages judged useful. In evaluation frameworks, the same name can refer to an average-precision-like, rank-sensitive calculation. Token-level relevance density is another distinct concept. I never compare numbers called context precision until their units, reference inputs, and aggregation formulas are documented.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For example, a context ordered relevant, irrelevant, relevant has ordinary precision of two-thirds. An average-precision-style calculation averages precision at the relevant ranks: one at rank one and two-thirds at rank three, giving about 0.833 when divided by the two retrieved relevant items. These are both reasonable diagnostics, but they do not measure the same quantity. Naming the implementation prevents misleading comparisons.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Measure the complete retrieval funnel</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Suppose candidate retrieval returns fifty passages and contains all three required evidence groups. The reranker places two groups in the top five but pushes the third to rank twelve. The final prompt keeps five passages. Candidate coverage is high, but final-context coverage is incomplete. Calling this simply a retrieval success hides the stage that actually removed required evidence.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">I therefore store the candidate IDs, post-filter candidates, reranked order, selected context, and any compression output. At each transition I calculate evidence retention. If a policy exception appears before compression and disappears afterward, increasing the vector-search cutoff will not solve the problem. The fix belongs in context assembly or compression rules.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate ANN recall from semantic relevance recall</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">ANN Recall@k asks how many neighbors returned by an exact vector search also appear in the approximate result set. Its ground truth comes from exhaustive computation using the same vectors and distance metric. Semantic retrieval recall instead asks whether human-judged or otherwise validated answer-bearing evidence was found. These measurements use different definitions of correct results.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">An index can achieve excellent ANN recall while retrieving the wrong product manual because its embeddings poorly represent the query constraints. Conversely, an approximate search can omit an exact nearest neighbor but return another passage that answers equally well. I monitor both when tuning an ANN index, but I do not use one as a substitute for the other.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Aggregate without hiding important failures</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Macro averaging gives each query equal weight. Micro aggregation pools counts and can give evidence-rich queries more influence. Traffic weighting approximates expected production usage, but it can conceal rare failures with serious consequences. Report the method explicitly and retain slices for exact identifiers, paraphrases, languages, tenants, document formats, fresh content, and multi-evidence questions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use paired comparisons because retrieval configurations should be evaluated on the same queries and source snapshot. Report uncertainty with a suitable resampling procedure, and inspect per-query differences rather than only the mean. A two-point improvement from a tiny sample may be noise. A small aggregate gain accompanied by a large regression on critical policy exceptions may be unacceptable.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Connect retrieval quality to operating requirements</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Quality metrics belong beside p50 and p95 latency, empty-result rate, index freshness, permission failures, and tokens delivered to generation. A configuration that gains a small amount of recall but triples tail latency may not meet the service objective. Likewise, a fast retriever that serves stale policies has not met the real information need.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">My practical dashboard starts with candidate evidence recall and complete-evidence coverage, then shows final-context precision and nDCG, first-hit ranking where appropriate, and end-to-end grounded answer correctness. Each metric has a diagnostic role. No single score deserves to become the objective detached from the user's question, the authorized evidence, and the cost of delivering a reliable answer.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">A diagnostic example from a release comparison</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Consider two hypothetical retrievers evaluated on the same one hundred policy questions. Version A finds at least one useful passage for ninety questions, but retrieves every required fact for only sixty. Version B finds something useful for eighty-eight questions and complete evidence for seventy-eight. Looking only at hit rate would favor A, even though B may support more correct multi-part answers. Inspect which two questions became misses and whether those losses are acceptable before choosing either version.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Now suppose both versions retrieve complete evidence for the same seventy-eight queries, but B places the decisive exceptions earlier and sends fewer duplicated passages. The improvement should appear in ranking and final-context measurements, while candidate recall may remain unchanged. This is a useful optimization even when the headline recall graph looks flat. Conversely, if answer correctness remains unchanged, investigate whether the generator already handled the old ordering adequately or whether another bottleneck dominates. Metrics guide an experiment; they do not replace observing the task outcome. Record the hypothesis before changing the system so that each score has a clear interpretation after the experiment.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">One further safeguard is to separate relevance from permission compliance. A passage may be substantively relevant and still be prohibited for the current caller. In the expected retrieval set for that caller, it must not become a desired result. Test cross-tenant and revoked-access cases directly, because a high average ranking score can otherwise conceal a serious access failure. The search evaluator and the authorization evaluator should agree on the user's permitted information boundary.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Finally, assign ownership to metric changes. The retrieval team may own candidate evidence coverage, while the orchestration team owns context retention and the application team owns supported answer success. Shared dashboards help, but explicit boundaries make remediation faster. When the final prompt loses an exception because a token-budget rule favors short passages, the team that owns the vector index should not be tasked with solving an unrelated selection bug. This is why metric placement in the pipeline matters as much as the mathematical formula.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/evaluation-of-ranked-retrieval-results-1.html\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Ranked retrieval evaluation</a></p>\n</div>"},{"q":"What is RAGAS and what do its core metrics actually measure?","g":["ragas","rag evaluation"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Ragas is an evaluation framework that helps measure different aspects of retrieval-augmented applications, including evidence selection, response grounding, and whether the response addresses the user's question. Its value is decomposition: instead of assigning one vague quality score to an entire application, you can ask which stage appears to be failing. However, the framework is not an automatic source of truth. Each metric depends on particular inputs, assumptions, implementation details, and sometimes another language model acting as an evaluator.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The familiar description of Ragas as reference-free is only partly correct. Some metrics can operate without a human-written reference answer; others require a reference answer, reference contexts, or reference identifiers. Current and legacy APIs also expose different names and variants. Before using a score in a release decision, pin the package version, metric implementation, evaluator model, embedding model if applicable, and evaluator prompt. A metric name alone is not a reproducible experiment.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Start with the evaluation record</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For each evaluated request, preserve the user input, generated response, retrieved context passages in their actual order, and any reference information the chosen metrics require. Also record source versions and the final prompt context when it differs from raw retrieval. A metric applied to the initial candidate list cannot establish what the generator actually saw after filtering, compression, or token-budget selection.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Imagine a hypothetical refund assistant. The user asks whether an annual subscription purchased twenty days ago can be refunded. The reference answer states that a thirty-day window applies, enterprise plans are excluded, and prior subscription refunds affect eligibility. The retrieved context and generated answer become separate artifacts. We can now evaluate whether the context covers the reference facts and whether the answer stays within the context. Those are related but different questions.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Faithfulness measures support for generated claims</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Faithfulness examines the response's factual claims and asks whether the retrieved evidence supports them. Conceptually, identify atomic claims, judge support for each claim, and divide the number supported by the total number evaluated. A score of one means all evaluated claims were judged supported under that implementation. It does not mean every important fact was included, the source was authoritative, or the answer was useful.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Suppose the assistant responds with three claims: annual subscriptions have a thirty-day window, enterprise plans are excluded, and refunds always arrive within two hours. If the first two are supported but no passage establishes the third, a simple claim-count interpretation produces two-thirds faithfulness. This is a diagnostic signal for unsupported generation. The numerical value depends on how the evaluator decomposes sentences and interprets entailment, so inspect the claim-level verdicts.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A faithful answer can still be wrong in the real world. If an obsolete policy says sixty days and the answer repeats sixty days accurately, the answer may score well against that context while violating the current policy. Source freshness, authority, and scope need separate checks. Similarly, a faithful response can omit an essential exception. Faithfulness is primarily about the support for what was said, not the completeness of what should have been said.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Response relevancy measures whether the answer addresses the question</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The commonly documented response-relevancy approach generates possible questions from the answer and compares their embeddings with the original question. If the answer contains the requested information, its reconstructed questions should resemble the actual information need. The score is therefore a proxy for alignment between question and response, not a direct factual-correctness calculation. The naming may appear as response relevancy or answer relevancy depending on the API and version.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For example, the user asks about refund eligibility, but the assistant provides a history of the subscription product. That history could be perfectly supported by retrieved documents, producing strong faithfulness, while reconstructed questions focus on product history. Response relevancy should identify that mismatch. Conversely, an answer that directly states an invented refund policy could appear highly relevant while remaining false or unsupported.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Embedding similarity creates limitations. A question about enterprise refunds and one about personal-plan refunds can be semantically close while requiring different answers. Reconstructed questions might also overlook a critical qualifier such as region, purchase date, or subscription type. Test the metric on your domain's near-miss examples, and do not interpret a high value as proof that every constraint was addressed. Cosine-based scores are not calibrated probabilities of usefulness.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Context precision measures usefulness and ordering</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Context precision asks whether retrieved passages are useful for answering the question and whether useful passages occur early. In Ragas variants, usefulness may be judged against a reference answer or against available response information. Those variants do not have identical dependencies or failure modes. Reference-free evaluation can be convenient, but a mistaken response may distort judgments if it becomes the basis for deciding which evidence was useful.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The rank-sensitive formulation is closer to average precision over judged context relevance than to ordinary relevant-count divided by total-count. Consider three passages ordered irrelevant, relevant, relevant. Ordinary precision is two-thirds. A formulation averaging precision at relevant ranks gives one-half at rank two and two-thirds at rank three, averaged to approximately 0.583. This penalizes delaying useful evidence behind a distractor. Reverse the ordering to relevant, relevant, irrelevant and that rank-sensitive value becomes one.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">This example also illustrates a limitation: some precision formulations can be perfect even when an important reference fact is entirely absent. They judge ordering among the useful contexts that were retrieved rather than the total evidence that should have been retrieved. Always read the exact denominator and complement precision with a recall or coverage measure. Do not compare these values directly with a dashboard that reports plain Precision@k.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Context recall measures missing reference information</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The LLM-based context-recall approach uses a reference answer as a proxy for the information retrieval should support. It decomposes the reference into claims and checks whether each claim can be attributed to the retrieved contexts. If the reference has three required facts and the context supports two, the conceptual score is two-thirds. This tells you something about evidence coverage before generation, assuming the reference is correct and sufficiently complete.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">In the refund example, retrieving the thirty-day rule but missing the enterprise exclusion and prior-refund condition produces poor reference-claim coverage. Changing the generation prompt cannot reliably recover those missing policy facts. The next investigation is whether they were absent from ingestion, excluded by permissions or version filters, ranked below the cutoff, or dropped during context assembly. The score identifies a symptom; the request trace identifies the mechanism.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Other context-recall variants can compare reference contexts or context identifiers rather than reference-answer claims. These are useful when you possess reliable evidence annotations, but they measure different units. Identifier-based recall is sensitive to chunk versioning, while claim-based recall depends on the quality of claim extraction and entailment judgments. Record which representation is authoritative when documents are rechunked or evaluation data is migrated.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interpret combinations as hypotheses, not verdicts</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Low context recall with low answer quality suggests missing evidence, but it does not prove the vector index is responsible. The reference may be wrong, the expected document may be inaccessible to this user, or a later transformation may have removed relevant text. Begin with source and trace inspection rather than immediately adjusting an ANN parameter.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">High context recall combined with low faithfulness suggests that sufficient evidence was available but the generated response added unsupported claims or misread it. Possible causes include conflicting instructions, misleading distractors, poor context formatting, and model capability. However, evaluator disagreement can also create that pattern. Review representative examples before changing the model. A judge can incorrectly infer reference support or incorrectly reject a valid paraphrase.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">High faithfulness with low response relevancy often indicates grounded but off-target output. High relevance with low faithfulness suggests an answer that addresses the question but invents details. Strong scores on all these dimensions still do not establish source freshness, authorization correctness, numerical accuracy, or successful business action. Add explicit checks for those requirements rather than expecting a general metric to infer them.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Build a small, interpretable evaluation experiment</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Create a versioned sample containing straightforward questions, paraphrases, exact identifiers, multi-document cases, and questions with no authorized answer. Include deliberately flawed responses: correct and concise, unsupported but confident, faithful but irrelevant, and incomplete despite available evidence. These controlled cases test whether your evaluator distinguishes the failures you care about before you apply it to thousands of unknown cases.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Store the intermediate evaluator artifacts when permitted: extracted claims, per-claim support judgments, reconstructed questions, passage relevance decisions, and error states. A single scalar hides important information. If the score changes after upgrading the evaluator model, inspect whether the application improved or the measurement instrument changed. Re-score a stable calibration set to estimate the effect of that evaluator upgrade.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Handle unanswerable and empty-response cases explicitly</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">An answerable-query reference metric can behave awkwardly when no answer should be given. A legitimate abstention may receive low response relevance under a reconstruction-based approach even though it is the correct product behavior. An empty response may avoid unsupported claims without being useful.
