Distinguish parameter storage, compute dtype, gradient flow, and optimizer ownership.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Inspect learning curves and representative outputs together. Lower training loss can coexist with overfitting, forgetting, spurious correlations, or reward exploitation. Validation should cover the target task and capabilities that must remain intact. Dataset size alone does not determine the number of useful epochs, and one learning-rate recipe does not transfer unchanged across every model, adapter, and objective.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Record effective batch size, token masking, sequence packing, loss normalization, optimizer settings, and checkpoint selection. These details can change results substantially even when a method name is unchanged. Use a reproducible baseline and a bounded search over justified configurations. The architectural question is which update process provides the required behavior at acceptable cost and regression risk, not which training acronym is currently most popular.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Treat data quality and coverage as explicit design variables</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Training and evaluation depend on what the data represents, how it was collected, and what errors it contains. High-quality examples should match the intended task and include the constraints that change answers. A polished synthetic explanation can still be wrong, and a large corpus can underrepresent important languages, edge cases, or user groups.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Track provenance, source permissions, transformation steps, and applicable use restrictions. Separate examples used for tuning from held-out assessment, and group near duplicates or related task families appropriately when splitting. Otherwise, the evaluation can reward memorization or template recognition rather than the capability the product needs.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Balance filtering with coverage. Removing obvious corruption and duplicates can help, but a narrow quality classifier can discard dialects, technical formats, or rare but legitimate material. Inspect what is rejected and evaluate category-level effects. Repeated text can be boilerplate, meaningful code, or deliberate emphasis; deduplication needs a unit and policy appropriate to the dataset rather than indiscriminate deletion.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use human review and objective checks where they are valuable, while acknowledging their limits. A passing test may not cover all requirements, and a preference label can reflect style rather than factual quality. Preserve disagreement and uncertainty when the evidence does not support one definitive label. Data curation is a measurable information-management process, not a claim that smaller or larger datasets always win.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate prefill, decoding, and training behavior</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A decoder-based language model has different execution regimes. Training commonly processes known sequences in parallel while computing gradients. Prefill processes the available prompt and establishes state for generation. Autoregressive decoding then produces successive tokens conditioned on previous ones. These regimes share model components but differ in shapes, parallelism, and resource pressure.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">An optimization that helps prefill may do little for long-output decoding. Reusing a prompt prefix can reduce repeated prompt processing while each new output token still attends to a growing context. A faster attention kernel may have a different benefit at one query position than at thousands. Conversely, an approach that improves low-batch decoding can reduce throughput when the device is already well utilized.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Record time to first token, output-token latency, total completion time, throughput, and tail latency under realistic concurrency. Include input and output length distributions. A benchmark using a tiny prompt and huge answer is not interchangeable with document analysis using a long prompt and a short answer. User-visible responsiveness and completed-task cost can favor different configurations.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Training measurements need their own accounting: examples or tokens processed, optimizer steps, activation strategy, gradient accumulation, and communication. A technique that reduces trainable parameters may still require backpropagation through much of the network. Keep these distinctions explicit so an inference optimization is not mistakenly presented as a universal training acceleration, or a storage saving as a complete reduction in computation.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Benchmark the hardware-software combination actually deployed</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Accelerator specifications do not guarantee that a model uses their fastest path. Datatype support, matrix shapes, kernel availability, memory layout, compiler behavior, and library versions determine realized performance. A compressed checkpoint can occupy less storage yet run slowly if the backend repeatedly converts it or lacks an efficient kernel for that representation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare the same workload at the same quality target. Warm-up, synchronization, batch size, concurrency, device placement, and cache state must be controlled or reported. Include end-to-end service overhead where it affects users, while preserving separate kernel measurements for diagnosis. A speedup measured in one operator is not automatically the same speedup for the whole request.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Distributed execution adds communication and scheduling effects. Tensor parallelism, expert routing, sharding, and offloading can move the bottleneck away from arithmetic. Network topology and interconnect bandwidth matter, as do uneven work distribution and synchronization waits. A theoretically sparse computation may become communication-heavy in the actual deployment.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use profiling to identify whether the limiting resource is compute, bandwidth, memory capacity, I/O, or coordination. Then choose an optimization that addresses that limit. Avoid universal claims that modern kernels are always memory-bound or that a certain numeric format always makes decoding faster. Performance conclusions should name the model, workload, hardware, and software conditions under which they were observed.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Evaluate the task contract, not just a proxy score</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Perplexity, numerical reconstruction error, benchmark accuracy, and human preference measure different properties. A model can preserve average language-model loss while regressing on exact identifiers, rare languages, long-range reasoning, or structured extraction. Select metrics that establish the actual capability being promised rather than assuming one aggregate proxy captures every important effect.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Build representative cases with ordinary requests, difficult constraints, ambiguous inputs, missing evidence, and appropriate no-answer behavior. Use objective checks where available, and calibrate model-based or human review against explicit criteria where exact matching is inadequate. A passing schema checks shape; a passing test checks its specified behavior; neither automatically establishes complete correctness.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare candidate and baseline on the same cases and source snapshot. Inspect per-category differences and severe failures before accepting an average improvement. Report uncertainty and repeated-run behavior when sampling is relevant. A small gain from a tiny sample can be noise, while a rare but important regression can be hidden by many easy successes.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Keep held-out assessment separate from iterative tuning. Version the model, tokenizer, prompts, decoding, data, and relevant serving settings with each result. This makes it possible to tell whether an observed change comes from the technique being tested or from another part of the stack. The useful conclusion is that a configuration meets a defined task requirement under measured conditions, not that it is universally near-lossless or best.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use controlled comparisons and meaningful ablations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Before changing a model or serving configuration, write the hypothesis and the expected measurable effect. If the proposed change is meant to reduce cache memory, measure cache memory separately from weights. If it is meant to improve evidence use, hold the evidence constant while testing the model behavior. A successful output after several simultaneous changes does not reveal which intervention mattered.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Vary one important factor at a time where practical, then evaluate interactions deliberately. Rank, scaling, learning rate, target modules, precision, and batch size can affect one another. A fair comparison may require either equal training compute, equal parameter budget, equal memory, or equal quality; state which resource is held fixed. Different choices answer different engineering questions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use a simple reference and include negative controls. For example, a mask test should fail when the future-token restriction is deliberately removed, and an evaluator should notice an intentionally unsupported claim. Such checks establish that the experiment is sensitive to the property it claims to measure. They are often more informative than increasing the benchmark size without inspecting examples.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Preserve configurations and intermediate artifacts needed to interpret results. Record failed runs and resource limits rather than reporting only the best seed. Once required checks pass, broaden experiments only to resolve a new uncertainty or justify a deployment decision. The aim is enough evidence for a reliable choice, not an endless collection of attractive but incomparable numbers.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Include artifact compatibility and lifecycle in the design</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A model is deployed with a tokenizer, configuration, numeric representations, runtime kernels, and often adapters or auxiliary models. These components must agree. A weight file that loads successfully can still be interpreted with the wrong token IDs, positional settings, chat template, or quantization metadata. Validate the effective deployed configuration rather than only the training checkpoint.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Version the complete artifact set and keep dependencies explicit. An adapter usually depends on a particular base checkpoint; a prefix cache depends on compatible model computation; a compressed representation depends on its scales and format. Changes to one component can invalidate another. Plan conversion and merging steps with enough temporary memory and quality checks instead of assuming deployment is a file copy.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Measure startup, steady-state behavior, concurrency, failure recovery, and rollback. A configuration that fits after warm-up may exceed memory during loading or produce poor latency after cache eviction. A model update can affect long-running sessions and stored outputs. Decide how active work migrates or remains on an earlier version, and how permissions and source freshness continue to apply.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Avoid attaching guarantees to brand names or broad formats. Supported kernels, licences, APIs, and hardware paths change over time. Use the current documented capabilities for the chosen versions and verify the behavior that matters to your workload. Deployment quality includes maintainability and recoverability as well as the best latency achieved in a notebook.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models</a></p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Compute-optimal training and Chinchilla</a></p>\n</div>"},{"q":"Explain LoRA. What are rank and alpha, and how do you choose them?","g":["lora"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">LoRA, or Low-Rank Adaptation, freezes a pretrained weight matrix and learns a factorized update to it. For a matrix W with output dimension d_out and input dimension d_in, a common form is <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">W' = W + (alpha/r)BA</code>, where A has shape <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">r × d_in</code> and B has shape <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">d_out × r</code>. The rank r restricts the update's factorization size; alpha controls an explicit multiplier under that convention.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Explain the parameter saving</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The original matrix has <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">d_out × d_in</code> entries, while the two factors have <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">r(d_in + d_out)</code> entries. For a square 4,096-dimensional matrix and rank 16, that is 131,072 trainable factor entries instead of 16,777,216 full-matrix entries, or about 0.78 percent for that matrix. Whole-model savings depend on which matrices are targeted and which other parameters remain trainable.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The useful hypothesis is that many adaptation updates can be represented effectively within a restricted low-rank family. This is empirical and task-dependent, not a theorem that every new skill has low intrinsic rank. A low-rank update can change behavior substantially, and a task may require more capacity, different target modules, or another training approach.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Initialization and gradient behavior</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A common initialization makes one factor random and the other zero, so the initial update is zero and the adapter starts from the base model's behavior. This convention also affects the initial gradient flow: one factor can receive zero gradient before the other moves. Frameworks support alternative initializations, so do not assume every LoRA implementation starts identically.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The base weights remain frozen, but training can still require forward and backward computation through the network to obtain adapter gradients. The largest savings are not automatically proportional reductions in total FLOPs. Optimizer and gradient storage shrink for frozen parameters, while activations and base-weight memory remain important.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Choose rank and scaling together</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Higher rank increases the update family's capacity and adapter size, but does not guarantee better generalization. Small data can overfit, and a low rank can be sufficient for some behaviors. Familiar rank ranges are starting experiments, not rules that style always needs one value and domain adaptation another.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Under the standard scaling convention, rank 16 with alpha 32 gives an explicit multiplier of two. Setting alpha proportional to rank can keep that multiplier constant across a rank sweep, but it does not keep optimization dynamics identical. Initialization, gradients, learning rate, and rank all interact. Some variants use a different scaling rule, such as square-root normalization, so report the actual implementation.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Target modules are part of the capacity choice</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Attention projections, output projections, and feed-forward matrices are possible targets depending on the model. Applying adapters broadly can improve some workloads but also changes the parameter budget and compute. It is too strong to promise that all-linear targeting always beats attention-only targeting at the same budget. Compare fair configurations and inspect target-task and retained capabilities.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Deploy adapters deliberately</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Separate adapters can be small relative to the base and can support task-specific serving where the runtime provides compatible loading and batching. Their actual size depends on rank, targets, layers, and storage dtype; it is not universally tens of megabytes. Multi-adapter serving adds scheduling, authorization, cache-compatibility, and operational requirements.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For compatible linear layers, the update can be merged into base weights, removing separate adapter computation at inference. Merging has numeric, memory, and artifact consequences and may need special handling for quantized bases. Validate the merged result and preserve the original artifacts. LoRA is useful when its restricted update meets the measured task requirement with lower training and storage burden, not because one rank-alpha recipe is universally correct.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Track tensor shapes and invariants explicitly</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A useful explanation should identify the batch axis, sequence axes, feature dimensions, and the meaning of every transformation. Many model bugs are not failures of the underlying mathematics but mistakes in broadcasting, head layout, masks, or normalization. Write a small reference implementation with obvious shapes before replacing it with a fused kernel or distributed operation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For attention, distinguish the number of query positions from the number of key positions. They can differ in cross-attention and cached decoding. A square matrix is a common self-attention case, not a universal requirement. Confirm which axis softmax normalizes and whether a boolean mask means permitted or blocked entries in the chosen library. Identical tensor dimensions do not imply identical semantics.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Test invariants that follow from the operation. Attention weights should normalize over eligible keys when a row has valid entries; masked future positions must not influence an earlier causal output. A low-rank update must have the same input-output dimensions as the weight it modifies. A cache must associate each stored vector with the correct position and request. These checks provide stronger diagnostic evidence than a large end-to-end output that merely looks plausible.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use tiny deterministic examples and compare intermediate values. Include padding, unequal lengths, empty or fully masked cases where supported, and different batch sizes. Then test gradients if training is involved. Passing a forward-only example does not establish correct differentiation. Clear dimensional contracts make both the conceptual explanation and the production implementation easier to inspect.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Connect the training objective to the behavior being changed</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A training method specifies an objective, data distribution, trainable parameters, and optimization process. Those choices determine what signal the model receives; they do not guarantee the desired application behavior. Next-token prediction, supervised demonstrations, contrastive similarity, preference comparisons, and verifier rewards teach related but different properties.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">State which parameters change and which remain frozen. A small number of trainable parameters can reduce gradient and optimizer storage while still requiring substantial forward and backward computation. Conversely, a frozen quantized base can participate in differentiable computation without receiving weight updates. Distinguish parameter storage, compute dtype, gradient flow, and optimizer ownership.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Inspect learning curves and representative outputs together. Lower training loss can coexist with overfitting, forgetting, spurious correlations, or reward exploitation. Validation should cover the target task and capabilities that must remain intact. Dataset size alone does not determine the number of useful epochs, and one learning-rate recipe does not transfer unchanged across every model, adapter, and objective.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Record effective batch size, token masking, sequence packing, loss normalization, optimizer settings, and checkpoint selection. These details can change results substantially even when a method name is unchanged. Use a reproducible baseline and a bounded search over justified configurations. The architectural question is which update process provides the required behavior at acceptable cost and regression risk, not which training acronym is currently most popular.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Choose adaptation according to the measured failure</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Separate missing knowledge, inconsistent formatting, domain terminology, task capability, and deployment constraints. Retrieval can supply current evidence; prompting and structured output can clarify a contract; fine-tuning can alter learned behavior. These interventions can be combined, but they solve different problems. Training should not be the automatic response whenever the base model produces a poor answer.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Establish a prompt-only or retrieval-assisted baseline before a costly adaptation run when those are plausible alternatives. If the correct evidence is absent, a weight update may merely teach plausible answers rather than solve freshness and attribution. If the evidence is present but the model repeatedly fails a specialized operation, a targeted training comparison becomes more informative.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Parameter-efficient methods restrict the update family but can still change behavior substantially. Full updates offer more freedom but require more resources and regression control. Neither method guarantees better generalization or preservation of unrelated capabilities. Evaluate the actual target modules, data, optimization, and serving integration rather than treating trainable-parameter percentage as a direct quality predictor.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Keep adaptation artifacts tied to the exact base model and tokenizer configuration. Test how adapters are loaded, selected, merged, and removed, and preserve a rollback path. For multiple tenants or tasks, separate storage does not automatically provide privacy or authorization. The application must still control which data trains an adapter and which requests may use it. A successful adaptation is one that improves the intended contract without unacceptable regressions or operational burden.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Account for the complete memory footprint</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Model capacity planning requires more than multiplying parameter count by an advertised storage precision. Weights may need scales, zero points, alignment, and selected higher-precision tensors. Training adds gradients, optimizer states, activations, and temporary buffers. Serving adds cache blocks, request metadata, workspaces, and memory needed for batching or speculative branches.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Write a component budget in bytes and distinguish decimal gigabytes from binary gibibytes. For float32, one parameter value occupies four bytes; for packed low-bit values, metadata and incomplete packing alter the effective average. A nominal reduction in one component is not the same ratio for the entire process. If weights are compressed while caches dominate, total concurrency may improve much less than expected.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Peak memory can decide feasibility. Loading, adapter merging, checkpoint saving, attention computation, and optimizer steps can create temporary allocations beyond the steady state. Distributed sharding and offloading change where memory resides, but introduce communication and transfer costs. Do not call a configuration impossible or guaranteed to fit without stating the hardware and execution assumptions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Measure allocated and reserved memory with the actual framework, representative lengths, batch sizes, and active features. Include worst-important cases, not only a short warm-up prompt. Leave operational headroom for concurrent requests and maintenance. This makes memory estimates useful for choosing a design while avoiding false precision from a formula that omits half the serving stack.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate mathematical equivalence from floating-point behavior</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Equations describe ideal arithmetic, while implementations use finite representations, approximations, reduction orders, and hardware-specific kernels. Two implementations can compute the same mathematical operation without producing bit-identical results. Small differences are often harmless, but they can matter near a decision boundary or grow across a long generated sequence. State which equivalence claim is being made.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use stable normalization and inspect the quantities that can overflow or underflow. Softmax is commonly evaluated after subtracting the row maximum, which preserves its mathematical value while reducing numerical risk. This does not solve every issue: fully masked rows, invalid inputs, extreme scales, or low-precision accumulation still need defined behavior. Scaling and normalization should follow the model and kernel contract rather than an improvised rule.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Precision choices affect weights, activations, gradients, optimizer state, and caches differently. A model described as four-bit may keep several of these in higher precision. Quantization scales and metadata also consume memory. Report the actual representations instead of assuming one advertised bit width describes the entire training or serving system.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare against a suitable higher-precision reference with explicit tolerances and task checks. A tiny tensor error does not automatically establish a negligible application effect, and a changed generated token does not automatically establish a meaningful quality regression. Inspect both numerical behavior and downstream requirements. The core idea is to store pretrained weights compactly while training adapter parameters through computations involving those weights. The original work used four-bit base-weight storage and higher-precision computation and adapters, together with additional memory techniques. It is a training-memory strategy, not simply a different name for ordinary inference quantization.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Distinguish storage from computation</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The quantized base stays frozen. Relevant weight values are dequantized or handled through supported kernels for forward and backward computation, while gradients update the adapter rather than the original base weights. Higher-precision activations, gradients, optimizer state, and selected tensors still exist. A four-bit base therefore does not make the complete training process four-bit.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For a hypothetical 65-billion-parameter base, ideal four-bit payload alone is about 32.5 billion bytes before scale metadata and other allocations. Training also needs adapters, optimizer state, activations, and workspaces. The original demonstration of a 65B model on one 48 GB GPU reflects a particular method and configuration; it is not a guarantee that any sequence length, batch, or implementation fits that hardware.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Explain NF4 with its assumptions</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">NormalFloat4 uses a four-bit codebook designed around an assumed normal-like weight distribution. Allocating levels according to that distribution can preserve information better than a naive uniform integer grid under relevant conditions. Per-block scaling and the actual weight distribution affect the result.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Calling it information-theoretically optimal requires the stated assumptions. Neural weight tensors are not all exactly normal, and different architectures or outliers can behave differently. The important practical question is reconstruction and task behavior for the actual quantized tensors, not whether a datatype name guarantees superior fidelity in every model.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Double quantization targets metadata</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Blockwise weight quantization requires scale or related constants. Quantizing those constants reduces metadata overhead, in addition to compressing the weights themselves. The paper reports a particular average bit saving under its configuration; the exact amount depends on block sizes, formats, and implementation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">This distinction matters in capacity estimates. Multiplying parameter count by exactly half a byte ignores metadata, while counting every scale in full precision can overstate memory when the method compresses them too. Use effective stored bytes from the actual artifact and runtime.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Paged optimizers address optimizer-memory pressure</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The original technique uses paging mechanisms to manage optimizer-related memory pressure and avoid certain peak-memory failures. Paging can move data between memory tiers and introduces transfer behavior. It does not make activation memory disappear or guarantee that every out-of-memory case is solved. Gradient checkpointing and sequence length remain separate considerations.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Profile peak usage across the optimizer step, forward/backward pass, and checkpoint saving. A setup that fits an initialization test may fail on a longer batch or at a later allocation boundary. Offloading can make training feasible while changing step time substantially.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Compare with ordinary LoRA fairly</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">QLoRA is especially attractive when base-weight memory limits the experiment. Plain LoRA may be simpler when a suitable higher-precision base already fits. Relative speed is not universally slower or faster: dequantization overhead, bandwidth savings, kernels, and hardware all contribute. Compare equal task quality and complete training cost.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Preserve the serving interpretation</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">An adapter trained against a quantized base approximates behavior in that training context. Loading it with a higher-precision original base or merging it into another representation can change outputs. Such export is possible in supported workflows but should be evaluated rather than assumed identical. Keep base identity, quantization configuration, adapter settings, and validation results together. The benefit of QLoRA is a better feasible training frontier under memory constraints, paid for through numeric and systems complexity that must remain visible.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate mathematical equivalence from floating-point behavior</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Equations describe ideal arithmetic, while implementations use finite representations, approximations, reduction orders, and hardware-specific kernels. Two implementations can compute the same mathematical operation without producing bit-identical results. Small differences are often harmless, but they can matter near a decision boundary or grow across a long generated sequence. State which equivalence claim is being made.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use stable normalization and inspect the quantities that can overflow or underflow. Softmax is commonly evaluated after subtracting the row maximum, which preserves its mathematical value while reducing numerical risk. This does not solve every issue: fully masked rows, invalid inputs, extreme scales, or low-precision accumulation still need defined behavior. Scaling and normalization should follow the model and kernel contract rather than an improvised rule.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Precision choices affect weights, activations, gradients, optimizer state, and caches differently. A model described as four-bit may keep several of these in higher precision. Quantization scales and metadata also consume memory. Report the actual representations instead of assuming one advertised bit width describes the entire training or serving system.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare against a suitable higher-precision reference with explicit tolerances and task checks. A tiny tensor error does not automatically establish a negligible application effect, and a changed generated token does not automatically establish a meaningful quality regression. Inspect both numerical behavior and downstream requirements. This distinction prevents claims such as exact attention means identical bits or lower precision always preserves quality.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Account for the complete memory footprint</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Model capacity planning requires more than multiplying parameter count by an advertised storage precision. Weights may need scales, zero points, alignment, and selected higher-precision tensors. Training adds gradients, optimizer states, activations, and temporary buffers. Serving adds cache blocks, request metadata, workspaces, and memory needed for batching or speculative branches.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Write a component budget in bytes and distinguish decimal gigabytes from binary gibibytes. For float32, one parameter value occupies four bytes; for packed low-bit values, metadata and incomplete packing alter the effective average. A nominal reduction in one component is not the same ratio for the entire process. If weights are compressed while caches dominate, total concurrency may improve much less than expected.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Peak memory can decide feasibility. Loading, adapter merging, checkpoint saving, attention computation, and optimizer steps can create temporary allocations beyond the steady state. Distributed sharding and offloading change where memory resides, but introduce communication and transfer costs. Do not call a configuration impossible or guaranteed to fit without stating the hardware and execution assumptions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Measure allocated and reserved memory with the actual framework, representative lengths, batch sizes, and active features. Include worst-important cases, not only a short warm-up prompt. Leave operational headroom for concurrent requests and maintenance. This makes memory estimates useful for choosing a design while avoiding false precision from a formula that omits half the serving stack.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Connect the training objective to the behavior being changed</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A training method specifies an objective, data distribution, trainable parameters, and optimization process. Those choices determine what signal the model receives; they do not guarantee the desired application behavior. Next-token prediction, supervised demonstrations, contrastive similarity, preference comparisons, and verifier rewards teach related but different properties.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">State which parameters change and which remain frozen. A small number of trainable parameters can reduce gradient and optimizer storage while still requiring substantial forward and backward computation. Conversely, a frozen quantized base can participate in differentiable computation without receiving weight updates. Distinguish parameter storage, compute dtype, gradient flow, and optimizer ownership.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Inspect learning curves and representative outputs together. Lower training loss can coexist with overfitting, forgetting, spurious correlations, or reward exploitation. Validation should cover the target task and capabilities that must remain intact. Dataset size alone does not determine the number of useful epochs, and one learning-rate recipe does not transfer unchanged across every model, adapter, and objective.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Record effective batch size, token masking, sequence packing, loss normalization, optimizer settings, and checkpoint selection. These details can change results substantially even when a method name is unchanged. Use a reproducible baseline and a bounded search over justified configurations. The architectural question is which update process provides the required behavior at acceptable cost and regression risk, not which training acronym is currently most popular.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Choose adaptation according to the measured failure</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Separate missing knowledge, inconsistent formatting, domain terminology, task capability, and deployment constraints. Retrieval can supply current evidence; prompting and structured output can clarify a contract; fine-tuning can alter learned behavior. These interventions can be combined, but they solve different problems. Training should not be the automatic response whenever the base model produces a poor answer.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Establish a prompt-only or retrieval-assisted baseline before a costly adaptation run when those are plausible alternatives. If the correct evidence is absent, a weight update may merely teach plausible answers rather than solve freshness and attribution. If the evidence is present but the model repeatedly fails a specialized operation, a targeted training comparison becomes more informative.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Parameter-efficient methods restrict the update family but can still change behavior substantially. Full updates offer more freedom but require more resources and regression control. Neither method guarantees better generalization or preservation of unrelated capabilities. Evaluate the actual target modules, data, optimization, and serving integration rather than treating trainable-parameter percentage as a direct quality predictor.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Keep adaptation artifacts tied to the exact base model and tokenizer configuration. Test how adapters are loaded, selected, merged, and removed, and preserve a rollback path. For multiple tenants or tasks, separate storage does not automatically provide privacy or authorization. The application must still control which data trains an adapter and which requests may use it. A successful adaptation is one that improves the intended contract without unacceptable regressions or operational burden.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Benchmark the hardware-software combination actually deployed</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Accelerator specifications do not guarantee that a model uses their fastest path. Datatype support, matrix shapes, kernel availability, memory layout, compiler behavior, and library versions determine realized performance. A compressed checkpoint can occupy less storage yet run slowly if the backend repeatedly converts it or lacks an efficient kernel for that representation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare the same workload at the same quality target. Warm-up, synchronization, batch size, concurrency, device placement, and cache state must be controlled or reported. Include end-to-end service overhead where it affects users, while preserving separate kernel measurements for diagnosis. A speedup measured in one operator is not automatically the same speedup for the whole request.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Distributed execution adds communication and scheduling effects. Tensor parallelism, expert routing, sharding, and offloading can move the bottleneck away from arithmetic. Network topology and interconnect bandwidth matter, as do uneven work distribution and synchronization waits. A theoretically sparse computation may become communication-heavy in the actual deployment.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use profiling to identify whether the limiting resource is compute, bandwidth, memory capacity, I/O, or coordination. Then choose an optimization that addresses that limit. Avoid universal claims that modern kernels are always memory-bound or that a certain numeric format always makes decoding faster. Performance conclusions should name the model, workload, hardware, and software conditions under which they were observed.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Include artifact compatibility and lifecycle in the design</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A model is deployed with a tokenizer, configuration, numeric representations, runtime kernels, and often adapters or auxiliary models. These components must agree. A weight file that loads successfully can still be interpreted with the wrong token IDs, positional settings, chat template, or quantization metadata. Validate the effective deployed configuration rather than only the training checkpoint.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Version the complete artifact set and keep dependencies explicit. An adapter usually depends on a particular base checkpoint; a prefix cache depends on compatible model computation; a compressed representation depends on its scales and format. Changes to one component can invalidate another. Plan conversion and merging steps with enough temporary memory and quality checks instead of assuming deployment is a file copy.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Measure startup, steady-state behavior, concurrency, failure recovery, and rollback. A configuration that fits after warm-up may exceed memory during loading or produce poor latency after cache eviction. A model update can affect long-running sessions and stored outputs. Decide how active work migrates or remains on an earlier version, and how permissions and source freshness continue to apply.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Avoid attaching guarantees to brand names or broad formats. Supported kernels, licences, APIs, and hardware paths change over time. Use the current documented capabilities for the chosen versions and verify the behavior that matters to your workload. Deployment quality includes maintainability and recoverability as well as the best latency achieved in a notebook.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Evaluate the task contract, not just a proxy score</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Perplexity, numerical reconstruction error, benchmark accuracy, and human preference measure different properties. A model can preserve average language-model loss while regressing on exact identifiers, rare languages, long-range reasoning, or structured extraction. Select metrics that establish the actual capability being promised rather than assuming one aggregate proxy captures every important effect.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Build representative cases with ordinary requests, difficult constraints, ambiguous inputs, missing evidence, and appropriate no-answer behavior. Use objective checks where available, and calibrate model-based or human review against explicit criteria where exact matching is inadequate. A passing schema checks shape; a passing test checks its specified behavior; neither automatically establishes complete correctness.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare candidate and baseline on the same cases and source snapshot. Inspect per-category differences and severe failures before accepting an average improvement. Report uncertainty and repeated-run behavior when sampling is relevant. A small gain from a tiny sample can be noise, while a rare but important regression can be hidden by many easy successes.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Keep held-out assessment separate from iterative tuning. Version the model, tokenizer, prompts, decoding, data, and relevant serving settings with each result. This makes it possible to tell whether an observed change comes from the technique being tested or from another part of the stack. The useful conclusion is that a configuration meets a defined task requirement under measured conditions, not that it is universally near-lossless or best.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use controlled comparisons and meaningful ablations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Before changing a model or serving configuration, write the hypothesis and the expected measurable effect. If the proposed change is meant to reduce cache memory, measure cache memory separately from weights. If it is meant to improve evidence use, hold the evidence constant while testing the model behavior. A successful output after several simultaneous changes does not reveal which intervention mattered.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Vary one important factor at a time where practical, then evaluate interactions deliberately. Rank, scaling, learning rate, target modules, precision, and batch size can affect one another. A fair comparison may require either equal training compute, equal parameter budget, equal memory, or equal quality; state which resource is held fixed. Different choices answer different engineering questions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use a simple reference and include negative controls. For example, a mask test should fail when the future-token restriction is deliberately removed, and an evaluator should notice an intentionally unsupported claim. Such checks establish that the experiment is sensitive to the property it claims to measure. They are often more informative than increasing the benchmark size without inspecting examples.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Preserve configurations and intermediate artifacts needed to interpret results. Record failed runs and resource limits rather than reporting only the best seed. Once required checks pass, broaden experiments only to resolve a new uncertainty or justify a deployment decision. The aim is enough evidence for a reliable choice, not an endless collection of attractive but incomparable numbers.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">QLoRA paper</a></p>\n</div>"},{"q":"Compare full fine-tuning, LoRA, adapters, prefix tuning and prompt tuning.","g":["lora"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Full fine-tuning, LoRA, bottleneck adapters, prefix tuning, and prompt tuning adapt a pretrained model by changing different parameter subsets or adding different trainable structures. Their trade-offs involve update capacity, training memory, artifact size, inference behavior, and compatibility. There is no universal rule that one method is the only way to learn genuinely new behavior or that another always matches full fine-tuning.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Full fine-tuning changes the original parameters</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Updating all model weights provides a large adaptation space. It can be useful when sufficient data, compute, and regression controls justify that flexibility. It also requires gradient and optimizer storage for the updated parameters, plus activations and any master-weight copies used by the training system.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The exact multiplier over model size depends on optimizer, dtypes, sharding, and offloading. A fixed two-to-four-times estimate is not a complete memory budget. It can offer strong quality with relatively small training artifacts. Compatible updates can be merged for serving, or kept separate for supported task-specific loading. Rank, scaling, targets, and data jointly determine its behavior.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A percentage such as one percent is configuration-dependent. Data curation is a measurable information-management process, not a claim that smaller or larger datasets always win.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Evaluate the task contract, not just a proxy score</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Perplexity, numerical reconstruction error, benchmark accuracy, and human preference measure different properties. They are often discussed together, but PPO and GRPO are policy-optimization approaches while DPO directly fits a preference objective from comparisons. RLHF describes a broader process involving human feedback, not a synonym for PPO. Verifier-based reinforcement learning may use related optimizers without human preference labels for every sample.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">PPO-based alignment</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A common pipeline first trains an instruction-following policy, collects response preferences, trains a reward model, and optimizes policy samples with a PPO-style objective and a reference-policy regularization mechanism. A value estimator can help compute advantages, and clipping limits certain policy-ratio changes under the optimization design.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Policy, reference, reward, and value are conceptual roles, not necessarily four independent full model copies resident on one GPU. Implementations can share components, precompute some quantities, shard, or offload. Resource requirements and stability depend on the exact system. PPO can use learned rewards or other reward signals; it is not restricted to one preference-labeling recipe.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Direct Preference Optimization</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">DPO uses chosen and rejected responses to optimize a policy relative to a reference. Under the method's derivation, a relationship between reward and policy allows a direct preference loss rather than a separate reward-model-plus-online-RL loop. A familiar form compares the policy-versus-reference log-probability ratios for the chosen and rejected answers inside a logistic loss.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The reference can sometimes be precomputed for a fixed dataset, changing the memory picture. DPO is operationally attractive for offline comparisons, but its performance depends on pair quality, coverage, regularization settings, and optimization. It is not guaranteed more stable or better than PPO in every task, nor does an offline dataset prevent every iterative or refreshed-data variant.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Group Relative Policy Optimization</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">GRPO estimates a relative learning signal from a group of responses sampled for a prompt, avoiding a separately trained value network in its standard formulation. Rewards can be compared with a group baseline and normalized under the chosen implementation. This can be effective when responses can be evaluated with a reliable automatic signal, such as a checked mathematical answer.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Removing a critic does not remove rollout cost, reward evaluation, reference handling, or all stability issues. If every response has the same reward, the group provides little relative information and the implementation needs defined handling. Reward normalization, response length, clipping, and data selection can change behavior substantially.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Compare feedback, exploration, and cost</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A fixed preference set is convenient when desired behavior can be represented through comparisons. A reward can favor verbosity, formatting, or an exploit rather than the intended skill; preference labels can reflect style or evaluator bias.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For a hypothetical code-task trainer, use tests only with understood coverage and inspect whether the policy learns to satisfy the real requirement rather than exploit weak checks. The meaningful answer separates objectives and data from optimizer names and rejects fixed claims about model-copy counts, universal defaults, or guaranteed quality.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Distinguish preference fitting from reward-based exploration</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Preference data, model-estimated rewards, and verifiable task rewards provide different learning signals. A preferred answer may be more polite without being more correct, while a test result may establish a narrow behavior without measuring usefulness. State what the optimization signal actually represents before calling a method aligned or a reasoning improvement.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Offline preference fitting learns from a fixed set of comparisons. Online policy optimization generates new samples and evaluates them under a reward process. These approaches differ in exploration, data cost, stability, and implementation. Reference models, reward models, value estimates, and group statistics can be stored, shared, precomputed, or offloaded differently, so counting conceptual roles does not always equal counting full independent copies in accelerator memory.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Inspect reward and task quality together. The reward function and data coverage can matter more than the optimizer's name.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Maintain held-out tasks and capabilities that should remain unchanged. Evaluate length, refusal behavior, factual support, and category-level performance where relevant. Choose the simplest optimization process that provides the desired improvement under the available feedback. Neither a fixed preference dataset nor an automatic verifier guarantees broad alignment, and no universal method choice replaces validation of the actual training signal.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Connect the training objective to the behavior being changed</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A training method specifies an objective, data distribution, trainable parameters, and optimization process. Those choices determine what signal the model receives; they do not guarantee the desired application behavior. Next-token prediction, supervised demonstrations, contrastive similarity, preference comparisons, and verifier rewards teach related but different properties.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">State which parameters change and which remain frozen. It can appear as reduced general instruction following, weaker performance on another language or task, changed refusal behavior, or loss of a capability the deployment still needs. The severity depends on the data, update method, optimization, and evaluation. It is not inevitable that every narrow fine-tune destroys all general skills.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Distinguish forgetting from related regressions</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A task may appear worse because the output style changed, the tokenizer or template is incompatible, the benchmark differs, or serving precision changed. Preserve the base model and compare the same prompts, decoding, and evaluation conditions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A target-domain improvement can coexist with a regression elsewhere. Keeping the base unchanged also allows disabling the adapter. However, the adapted model can still forget or suppress behavior while the adapter is active. A small update does not guarantee a small functional change, and PEFT does not automatically solve most forgetting problems.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Separate adapters or task routing can preserve specialized variants without combining every update into one checkpoint. This adds selection and serving complexity, and the wrong adapter can still harm the current task. Evaluate the actual active configuration.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Mix data according to measured retention needs</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Replay or data mixing can expose the model to general instructions and retained tasks during adaptation. Data curation is a measurable information-management process, not a claim that smaller or larger datasets always win.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Evaluate the task contract, not just a proxy score</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Perplexity, numerical reconstruction error, benchmark accuracy, and human preference measure different properties. A model can preserve average language-model loss while regressing on exact identifiers, rare languages, long-range reasoning, or structured extraction. Select metrics that establish the actual capability being promised rather than assuming one aggregate proxy captures every important effect.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Build representative cases with ordinary requests, difficult constraints, ambiguous inputs, missing evidence, and appropriate no-answer behavior. Use objective checks where available, and calibrate model-based or human review against explicit criteria where exact matching is inadequate. A passing schema checks shape; a passing test checks its specified behavior; neither automatically establishes complete correctness.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare candidate and baseline on the same cases and source snapshot. Inspect per-category differences and severe failures before accepting an average improvement. Report uncertainty and repeated-run behavior when sampling is relevant. A small gain from a tiny sample can be noise, while a rare but important regression can be hidden by many easy successes.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Keep held-out assessment separate from iterative tuning. Version the model, tokenizer, prompts, decoding, data, and relevant serving settings with each result. This makes it possible to tell whether an observed change comes from the technique being tested or from another part of the stack. The useful conclusion is that a configuration meets a defined task requirement under measured conditions, not that it is universally near-lossless or best.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use controlled comparisons and meaningful ablations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Before changing a model or serving configuration, write the hypothesis and the expected measurable effect. If the proposed change is meant to reduce cache memory, measure cache memory separately from weights. If it is meant to improve evidence use, hold the evidence constant while testing the model behavior. A successful output after several simultaneous changes does not reveal which intervention mattered.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Vary one important factor at a time where practical, then evaluate interactions deliberately. Rank, scaling, learning rate, target modules, precision, and batch size can affect one another. A fair comparison may require either equal training compute, equal parameter budget, equal memory, or equal quality; state which resource is held fixed. Different choices answer different engineering questions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use a simple reference and include negative controls. For example, a mask test should fail when the future-token restriction is deliberately removed, and an evaluator should notice an intentionally unsupported claim. Such checks establish that the experiment is sensitive to the property it claims to measure. They are often more informative than increasing the benchmark size without inspecting examples.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Preserve configurations and intermediate artifacts needed to interpret results. Record failed runs and resource limits rather than reporting only the best seed. Once required checks pass, broaden experiments only to resolve a new uncertainty or justify a deployment decision. The aim is enough evidence for a reliable choice, not an endless collection of attractive but incomparable numbers.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Include artifact compatibility and lifecycle in the design</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A model is deployed with a tokenizer, configuration, numeric representations, runtime kernels, and often adapters or auxiliary models. These components must agree. A weight file that loads successfully can still be interpreted with the wrong token IDs, positional settings, chat template, or quantization metadata. Validate the effective deployed configuration rather than only the training checkpoint.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Version the complete artifact set and keep dependencies explicit. An adapter usually depends on a particular base checkpoint; a prefix cache depends on compatible model computation; a compressed representation depends on its scales and format. Changes to one component can invalidate another. Plan conversion and merging steps with enough temporary memory and quality checks instead of assuming deployment is a file copy.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Measure startup, steady-state behavior, concurrency, failure recovery, and rollback. A configuration that fits after warm-up may exceed memory during loading or produce poor latency after cache eviction. A model update can affect long-running sessions and stored outputs. Decide how active work migrates or remains on an earlier version, and how permissions and source freshness continue to apply.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Avoid attaching guarantees to brand names or broad formats. Supported kernels, licences, APIs, and hardware paths change over time. Use the current documented capabilities for the chosen versions and verify the behavior that matters to your workload. Deployment quality includes maintainability and recoverability as well as the best latency achieved in a notebook.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Record enough information to reconstruct the experiment</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Model behavior depends on more than a checkpoint name. Preserve the tokenizer, prompt template, data version, preprocessing, numeric settings, decoding configuration, seeds where meaningful, and hardware-software environment. A moving model alias or a library upgrade can change results without any apparent change to application code.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Deterministic mathematics does not guarantee identical operational output. Floating-point reductions, parallel scheduling, kernel choices, and provider changes can introduce differences. Low sampling randomness may reduce one source of variation but cannot make an incorrect method correct or establish perfect repeatability across every platform.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use small reference cases to localize divergence, then test representative workloads. Compare intermediate tensors for numerical changes and task outcomes for behavioral changes. Record failures and unsupported configurations rather than silently excluding them. A successful run under one environment does not prove compatibility under another.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For applications with external evidence, preserve the relevant source snapshot or governed artifact references. A rerun against updated documents is not a clean reproduction of the original result. Hashes can verify identity, but they cannot recover missing inputs. Decide what must remain accessible under the retention policy. The goal is a result that another qualified engineer can interpret and test, even when exact bitwise replay is not feasible.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use the strongest available check for each requirement</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Verification should match the property being claimed. Arithmetic can be checked with calculation, code behavior with relevant tests, schema shape with a validator, and source support with evidence review. A model-generated explanation of why it is correct is not an independent guarantee. Equally, a narrow objective check does not establish every aspect of a broad task.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For reasoning tasks, distinguish a correct final answer from a valid method and from a robust process. Several sampled solutions can agree on the same wrong assumption. A verifier may catch some errors, but can itself be incomplete, exploitable, or dependent on an incorrect reference. Test verifier failure modes rather than assuming that an executable signal makes training or inference automatically safe.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For numerical and performance methods, verify the claimed resource saving separately from task quality. Smaller tensors do not establish faster serving, and close output logits do not establish unchanged user outcomes. Check the full configuration under the conditions where the claim will be used.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">When no adequate deterministic check exists, use explicit rubrics, calibrated model judgment, or human review. Preserve uncertainty instead of inventing a false binary certainty. Associate verification with the exact artifact or model version evaluated. A later revision, merge, precision conversion, or decoding change may need reassessment. Verification is useful when it limits what can legitimately be concluded, not when it becomes a ceremonial pass label.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.00796\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Catastrophic forgetting and EWC</a></p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">LoRA adaptation</a></p>\n</div>"},{"q":"Explain quantization: PTQ vs QAT, and the differences between GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF and FP8.","g":["quantization"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Quantization represents selected model quantities with lower numeric precision or compact codes to reduce storage, bandwidth, or computation. PTQ and QAT describe when and how the model adapts to quantization. GPTQ and AWQ are quantization methods. GGUF is an artifact format supporting several representations. FP8 is a family of floating-point encodings used with appropriate scaling and hardware. These terms belong to different categories and should not be treated as interchangeable algorithms.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">PTQ versus QAT</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Post-training quantization starts from an already trained model. It may use calibration data to choose scales or optimize reconstruction, though some schemes require little or no calibration. It can be substantially cheaper than a new training run, but time and quality depend on the model and method rather than a fixed minutes-to-hours guarantee.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Quantization-aware training incorporates quantization effects during training or adaptation, often through simulated quantization and suitable gradient approximations. The model can adjust to the representation, which can help at aggressive precision levels. QAT still needs data, optimization, supported export, and evaluation; it is not automatically better under every budget.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">GPTQ optimizes a post-training approximation</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">GPTQ uses layerwise or blockwise approximation techniques informed by second-order information to reduce quantization-induced output error. Calibration activations and implementation choices affect the approximation. A weight reconstruction objective is useful, but it does not directly guarantee preserved reasoning, multilingual behavior, or structured extraction.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The original method and modern serving variants can differ in supported groups, kernels, and storage. Evaluate the actual exported artifact with the intended runtime. A checkpoint labeled GPTQ is not sufficient evidence that every GPU has an efficient compatible execution path.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">AWQ uses activation-aware information</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">AWQ identifies important weight structure using activation statistics and applies scaling to improve low-bit weight quantization. The goal is to preserve influential behavior without treating all channels identically. It is not simply retaining an arbitrary fixed fraction of full-precision weights in every implementation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Relative quality and conversion speed versus GPTQ depend on the model, calibration, and backend. Do not promise one always wins. Compare the same task suite and actual serving configuration, including conversion overhead and whether the runtime uses the expected low-bit kernel.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">GGUF packages models and metadata</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">GGUF is a binary format associated with GGML-based inference ecosystems. It can store model tensors and configuration metadata, including different quantized tensor types. Labels such as particular Q4 or Q5 variants identify representations within that ecosystem; GGUF itself is not one quantization objective or one bit width.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">It can support CPU, GPU, or mixed execution depending on the engine and backend. The format does not guarantee a particular speed or deployment location. Verify architecture, tokenizer, quantization type, and runtime compatibility rather than equating file extension with performance.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">FP8 requires more than eight stored bits</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Common FP8 encodings include E4M3 and E5M2, which trade precision and exponent range differently. Scaling and accumulation rules matter, as do outliers and kernel support. FP8 can be useful for weights, activations, or training quantities under suitable recipes, but it is not inherently calibration-free or universally near-lossless.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Hardware capability varies across products and software versions. Check the exact supported path rather than assuming every accelerator in a broad family executes every FP8 operation efficiently. Lower storage precision does not automatically produce a proportional latency gain.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Choose by task and system evidence</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Eight-bit formats can preserve quality well in many settings, and lower bits can be valuable, but no fixed quality ladder applies to all models and tasks. Measure target correctness, rare-category behavior, memory, throughput, and tail latency. Retain a higher-precision baseline and inspect whether changes come from weights, activations, caches, or another conversion step. Quantization is successful when it improves the relevant resource frontier while still meeting the application contract.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate mathematical equivalence from floating-point behavior</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Equations describe ideal arithmetic, while implementations use finite representations, approximations, reduction orders, and hardware-specific kernels. Two implementations can compute the same mathematical operation without producing bit-identical results. Small differences are often harmless, but they can matter near a decision boundary or grow across a long generated sequence. State which equivalence claim is being made.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use stable normalization and inspect the quantities that can overflow or underflow. Softmax is commonly evaluated after subtracting the row maximum, which preserves its mathematical value while reducing numerical risk. This does not solve every issue: fully masked rows, invalid inputs, extreme scales, or low-precision accumulation still need defined behavior. Scaling and normalization should follow the model and kernel contract rather than an improvised rule.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Precision choices affect weights, activations, gradients, optimizer state, and caches differently. A model described as four-bit may keep several of these in higher precision. Quantization scales and metadata also consume memory. Report the actual representations instead of assuming one advertised bit width describes the entire training or serving system.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare against a suitable higher-precision reference with explicit tolerances and task checks. A tiny tensor error does not automatically establish a negligible application effect, and a changed generated token does not automatically establish a meaningful quality regression. Inspect both numerical behavior and downstream requirements. This distinction prevents claims such as exact attention means identical bits or lower precision always preserves quality.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Account for the complete memory footprint</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Model capacity planning requires more than multiplying parameter count by an advertised storage precision. Weights may need scales, zero points, alignment, and selected higher-precision tensors. Training adds gradients, optimizer states, activations, and temporary buffers. Serving adds cache blocks, request metadata, workspaces, and memory needed for batching or speculative branches.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Write a component budget in bytes and distinguish decimal gigabytes from binary gibibytes. For float32, one parameter value occupies four bytes; for packed low-bit values, metadata and incomplete packing alter the effective average. A nominal reduction in one component is not the same ratio for the entire process. If weights are compressed while caches dominate, total concurrency may improve much less than expected.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Peak memory can decide feasibility. Loading, adapter merging, checkpoint saving, attention computation, and optimizer steps can create temporary allocations beyond the steady state. Distributed sharding and offloading change where memory resides, but introduce communication and transfer costs. Do not call a configuration impossible or guaranteed to fit without stating the hardware and execution assumptions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Measure allocated and reserved memory with the actual framework, representative lengths, batch sizes, and active features. Include worst-important cases, not only a short warm-up prompt. Leave operational headroom for concurrent requests and maintenance. This makes memory estimates useful for choosing a design while avoiding false precision from a formula that omits half the serving stack.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Benchmark the hardware-software combination actually deployed</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Accelerator specifications do not guarantee that a model uses their fastest path. A compressed checkpoint can occupy less storage yet run slowly if the backend repeatedly converts it or lacks an efficient kernel for that representation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare the same workload at the same quality target. Warm-up, synchronization, batch size, concurrency, device placement, and cache state must be controlled or reported. Include end-to-end service overhead where it affects users, while preserving separate kernel measurements for diagnosis. A speedup measured in one operator is not automatically the same speedup for the whole request.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Distributed execution adds communication and scheduling effects. Network topology and interconnect bandwidth matter, as do uneven work distribution and synchronization waits. A theoretically sparse computation may become communication-heavy in the actual deployment.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use profiling to identify whether the limiting resource is compute, bandwidth, memory capacity, I/O, or coordination.
