Performance conclusions should name the model, workload, hardware, and software conditions under which they were observed.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Connect the training objective to the behavior being changed</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A training method specifies an objective, data distribution, trainable parameters, and optimization process. Those choices determine what signal the model receives; they do not guarantee the desired application behavior. Next-token prediction, supervised demonstrations, contrastive similarity, preference comparisons, and verifier rewards teach related but different properties.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">State which parameters change and which remain frozen. A small number of trainable parameters can reduce gradient and optimizer storage while still requiring substantial forward and backward computation. Conversely, a frozen quantized base can participate in differentiable computation without receiving weight updates. Distinguish parameter storage, compute dtype, gradient flow, and optimizer ownership.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Inspect learning curves and representative outputs together. Lower training loss can coexist with overfitting, forgetting, spurious correlations, or reward exploitation. Validation should cover the target task and capabilities that must remain intact. Dataset size alone does not determine the number of useful epochs, and one learning-rate recipe does not transfer unchanged across every model, adapter, and objective.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Record effective batch size, token masking, sequence packing, loss normalization, optimizer settings, and checkpoint selection. These details can change results substantially even when a method name is unchanged. Use a reproducible baseline and a bounded search over justified configurations. The architectural question is which update process provides the required behavior at acceptable cost and regression risk, not which training acronym is currently most popular.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Include artifact compatibility and lifecycle in the design</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A model is deployed with a tokenizer, configuration, numeric representations, runtime kernels, and often adapters or auxiliary models. It reorganizes computation around blocks and numerically stable online normalization. The key distinction is exact attention versus approximate attention: the algorithm targets the same mathematical dense attention operation while changing data movement and intermediate storage.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Identify what ordinary materialization costs</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A straightforward implementation computes all query-key scores, stores the large matrix, normalizes it, and multiplies by values. At long sequence length, moving those intermediates between memory levels can be expensive. The pairwise matrix grows quadratically, even though many applications only need the final weighted outputs rather than the matrix itself.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">FlashAttention tiles the relevant computation so blocks can be processed using faster on-chip storage and carefully scheduled transfers. It avoids writing the full matrix out as an intermediate. This is a systems-algorithm improvement, not a claim that the attention pattern becomes sparse or that every pairwise interaction disappears.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Explain online softmax</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For a query row, maintain a running maximum, a running exponential sum, and a running weighted-value accumulator. When a new block contains a larger score maximum, rescale the old accumulators into the new reference scale before adding the new block's contributions. Normalize the final value accumulator by the final exponential sum.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">This preserves the global softmax calculation rather than averaging independently normalized block outputs. Simply computing a local softmax for each block and averaging those results would generally be wrong because the blocks can have very different total exponential mass. The rescaling step is what makes streamed normalization mathematically consistent.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate memory savings from arithmetic</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Dense attention still has quadratic pairwise work in sequence length. The avoided quadratic intermediate can make much longer sequences feasible, but it does not turn dense attention into a linear-time algorithm. Inputs, outputs, statistics, activations elsewhere in the model, weights, and KV caches still consume memory.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">During training, optimized recomputation and backward scheduling also matter. Whole-model peak memory depends on more than the attention kernel. During one-token decoding, the shapes and bottlenecks differ from full-sequence prefill, so a kernel's training or prefill speedup is not automatically the same serving speedup.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Interpret exactness correctly</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Exact means the mathematical attention operation is preserved under the algorithm's intended formulation, not that every output bit matches every other implementation. Floating-point precision, reduction order, approximations in low-level operations, and selected kernels can introduce small numeric differences. Such differences can occasionally alter a generated token without implying the algorithm approximates the attention pattern.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare numerics with appropriate tolerances and evaluate application behavior. Masks, dropout, head dimensions, and supported dtypes must match. A fallback path or unsupported shape can change performance or semantics, so confirm which kernel actually ran.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Understand versions and hardware dependence</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Later FlashAttention work improves parallelism, work partitioning, and hardware utilization. Some variants target specific accelerator features and precision paths. These advances are valuable but do not establish one universal two-to-four-times speedup. Sequence length, head shape, batch, hardware, software, and surrounding operations determine the measured benefit.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For a hypothetical long-document workload, benchmark peak attention memory, prefill latency, complete answer latency, and throughput under realistic concurrency. If feed-forward computation or service overhead dominates, a large kernel speedup may yield a smaller end-to-end improvement. The strategic lesson is to optimize data movement where it is a measured bottleneck while preserving the mathematical contract, not to assume every slow operator is memory-bound.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Track tensor shapes and invariants explicitly</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A useful explanation should identify the batch axis, sequence axes, feature dimensions, and the meaning of every transformation. Many model bugs are not failures of the underlying mathematics but mistakes in broadcasting, head layout, masks, or normalization. Write a small reference implementation with obvious shapes before replacing it with a fused kernel or distributed operation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For attention, distinguish the number of query positions from the number of key positions. They can differ in cross-attention and cached decoding. A square matrix is a common self-attention case, not a universal requirement. Confirm which axis softmax normalizes and whether a boolean mask means permitted or blocked entries in the chosen library. Identical tensor dimensions do not imply identical semantics.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Test invariants that follow from the operation. Attention weights should normalize over eligible keys when a row has valid entries; masked future positions must not influence an earlier causal output. A low-rank update must have the same input-output dimensions as the weight it modifies. A cache must associate each stored vector with the correct position and request. These checks provide stronger diagnostic evidence than a large end-to-end output that merely looks plausible.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use tiny deterministic examples and compare intermediate values. Include padding, unequal lengths, empty or fully masked cases where supported, and different batch sizes. Then test gradients if training is involved. Passing a forward-only example does not establish correct differentiation. Clear dimensional contracts make both the conceptual explanation and the production implementation easier to inspect.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate mathematical equivalence from floating-point behavior</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Equations describe ideal arithmetic, while implementations use finite representations, approximations, reduction orders, and hardware-specific kernels. Two implementations can compute the same mathematical operation without producing bit-identical results. Small differences are often harmless, but they can matter near a decision boundary or grow across a long generated sequence. State which equivalence claim is being made.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use stable normalization and inspect the quantities that can overflow or underflow. Softmax is commonly evaluated after subtracting the row maximum, which preserves its mathematical value while reducing numerical risk. This does not solve every issue: fully masked rows, invalid inputs, extreme scales, or low-precision accumulation still need defined behavior. Scaling and normalization should follow the model and kernel contract rather than an improvised rule.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Precision choices affect weights, activations, gradients, optimizer state, and caches differently. A model described as four-bit may keep several of these in higher precision. Quantization scales and metadata also consume memory. Report the actual representations instead of assuming one advertised bit width describes the entire training or serving system.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare against a suitable higher-precision reference with explicit tolerances and task checks. A tiny tensor error does not automatically establish a negligible application effect, and a changed generated token does not automatically establish a meaningful quality regression. Inspect both numerical behavior and downstream requirements. This distinction prevents claims such as exact attention means identical bits or lower precision always preserves quality.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Distinguish asymptotic cost from the actual bottleneck</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Complexity describes how work grows with variables such as sequence length, dimension, batch size, or parameter count. It does not by itself predict wall-clock time. A kernel can perform fewer operations and still run slower because of memory movement, synchronization, poor occupancy, or conversion overhead. Explain which term is being analyzed and which parts of the model are excluded.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For dense attention, pairwise query-key and attention-value work grows quadratically with sequence length during a full sequence pass. Projection and feed-forward work have different dependence on width and length. During cached single-token decoding, the new query attends over the existing prefix, changing the per-step shape. Total generation cost and one decoding step are therefore different measurements.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Memory complexity also needs a scope. Temporary attention scores, persistent model weights, saved training activations, optimizer state, and the growing KV cache are distinct allocations. Removing a quadratic intermediate does not make every resource in the model linear or eliminate persistent storage. Include peak usage as well as steady-state requirements when deciding whether a configuration fits.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use a profiling hypothesis derived from the equation, then measure it under the intended workload. Vary one dimension at a time and check whether the observed scaling matches expectations. If it does not, investigate the implementation or another dominating term before declaring the theory wrong. This approach connects the mathematical explanation to an actionable performance diagnosis.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Account for the complete memory footprint</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Model capacity planning requires more than multiplying parameter count by an advertised storage precision. Weights may need scales, zero points, alignment, and selected higher-precision tensors. Training adds gradients, optimizer states, activations, and temporary buffers. Serving adds cache blocks, request metadata, workspaces, and memory needed for batching or speculative branches.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Write a component budget in bytes and distinguish decimal gigabytes from binary gibibytes. For float32, one parameter value occupies four bytes; for packed low-bit values, metadata and incomplete packing alter the effective average. A nominal reduction in one component is not the same ratio for the entire process. If weights are compressed while caches dominate, total concurrency may improve much less than expected.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Peak memory can decide feasibility. Loading, adapter merging, checkpoint saving, attention computation, and optimizer steps can create temporary allocations beyond the steady state. Distributed sharding and offloading change where memory resides, but introduce communication and transfer costs. Do not call a configuration impossible or guaranteed to fit without stating the hardware and execution assumptions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Measure allocated and reserved memory with the actual framework, representative lengths, batch sizes, and active features. Include worst-important cases, not only a short warm-up prompt. Leave operational headroom for concurrent requests and maintenance. This makes memory estimates useful for choosing a design while avoiding false precision from a formula that omits half the serving stack.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate prefill, decoding, and training behavior</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A decoder-based language model has different execution regimes. Training commonly processes known sequences in parallel while computing gradients. Prefill processes the available prompt and establishes state for generation. Autoregressive decoding then produces successive tokens conditioned on previous ones. These regimes share model components but differ in shapes, parallelism, and resource pressure.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">An optimization that helps prefill may do little for long-output decoding. Reusing a prompt prefix can reduce repeated prompt processing while each new output token still attends to a growing context. A faster attention kernel may have a different benefit at one query position than at thousands. Conversely, an approach that improves low-batch decoding can reduce throughput when the device is already well utilized.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Record time to first token, output-token latency, total completion time, throughput, and tail latency under realistic concurrency. Include input and output length distributions. A benchmark using a tiny prompt and huge answer is not interchangeable with document analysis using a long prompt and a short answer. User-visible responsiveness and completed-task cost can favor different configurations.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Training measurements need their own accounting: examples or tokens processed, optimizer steps, activation strategy, gradient accumulation, and communication. A technique that reduces trainable parameters may still require backpropagation through much of the network. Keep these distinctions explicit so an inference optimization is not mistakenly presented as a universal training acceleration, or a storage saving as a complete reduction in computation.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Benchmark the hardware-software combination actually deployed</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Accelerator specifications do not guarantee that a model uses their fastest path. Datatype support, matrix shapes, kernel availability, memory layout, compiler behavior, and library versions determine realized performance. A compressed checkpoint can occupy less storage yet run slowly if the backend repeatedly converts it or lacks an efficient kernel for that representation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare the same workload at the same quality target. Warm-up, synchronization, batch size, concurrency, device placement, and cache state must be controlled or reported. Include end-to-end service overhead where it affects users, while preserving separate kernel measurements for diagnosis. A speedup measured in one operator is not automatically the same speedup for the whole request.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Distributed execution adds communication and scheduling effects. Tensor parallelism, expert routing, sharding, and offloading can move the bottleneck away from arithmetic. Network topology and interconnect bandwidth matter, as do uneven work distribution and synchronization waits. A theoretically sparse computation may become communication-heavy in the actual deployment.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use profiling to identify whether the limiting resource is compute, bandwidth, memory capacity, I/O, or coordination. Then choose an optimization that addresses that limit. Avoid universal claims that modern kernels are always memory-bound or that a certain numeric format always makes decoding faster. Performance conclusions should name the model, workload, hardware, and software conditions under which they were observed.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use the strongest available check for each requirement</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Verification should match the property being claimed. Arithmetic can be checked with calculation, code behavior with relevant tests, schema shape with a validator, and source support with evidence review. A model-generated explanation of why it is correct is not an independent guarantee. Equally, a narrow objective check does not establish every aspect of a broad task.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For reasoning tasks, distinguish a correct final answer from a valid method and from a robust process. Several sampled solutions can agree on the same wrong assumption. A verifier may catch some errors, but can itself be incomplete, exploitable, or dependent on an incorrect reference. Test verifier failure modes rather than assuming that an executable signal makes training or inference automatically safe.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For numerical and performance methods, verify the claimed resource saving separately from task quality. Smaller tensors do not establish faster serving, and close output logits do not establish unchanged user outcomes. Check the full configuration under the conditions where the claim will be used.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">When no adequate deterministic check exists, use explicit rubrics, calibrated model judgment, or human review. Preserve uncertainty instead of inventing a false binary certainty. Associate verification with the exact artifact or model version evaluated. A later revision, merge, precision conversion, or decoding change may need reassessment. Verification is useful when it limits what can legitimately be concluded, not when it becomes a ceremonial pass label.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use controlled comparisons and meaningful ablations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Before changing a model or serving configuration, write the hypothesis and the expected measurable effect. If the proposed change is meant to reduce cache memory, measure cache memory separately from weights. If it is meant to improve evidence use, hold the evidence constant while testing the model behavior. A successful output after several simultaneous changes does not reveal which intervention mattered.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Vary one important factor at a time where practical, then evaluate interactions deliberately. Rank, scaling, learning rate, target modules, precision, and batch size can affect one another. A fair comparison may require either equal training compute, equal parameter budget, equal memory, or equal quality; state which resource is held fixed. Different choices answer different engineering questions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use a simple reference and include negative controls. For example, a mask test should fail when the future-token restriction is deliberately removed, and an evaluator should notice an intentionally unsupported claim. Such checks establish that the experiment is sensitive to the property it claims to measure. They are often more informative than increasing the benchmark size without inspecting examples.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Preserve configurations and intermediate artifacts needed to interpret results. Record failed runs and resource limits rather than reporting only the best seed. Once required checks pass, broaden experiments only to resolve a new uncertainty or justify a deployment decision. The aim is enough evidence for a reliable choice, not an endless collection of attractive but incomparable numbers.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">FlashAttention</a></p>\n</div>"},{"q":"What is speculative decoding and when does it pay off?","g":["kv cache"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by proposing several future tokens cheaply and verifying them with a more expensive target model. In the classic setting, a draft model generates a candidate continuation, the target evaluates the relevant conditional probabilities in a batched pass, and an acceptance-and-correction procedure produces samples from the target distribution. The distributional guarantee belongs to the specified algorithm and assumptions, not to every system labeled speculative.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Explain proposal and verification</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The draft proposes a short sequence autoregressively. Because the proposed tokens are known, the target can evaluate their prefix-conditioned probabilities using parallel sequence processing with appropriate causal masking. Verification still performs real work; checking several positions is not universally the same cost as one token. The potential benefit comes from better hardware utilization and fewer sequential target invocations.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">At the first rejection, the algorithm corrects the sample distribution rather than simply choosing the target's favorite token. Accepted draft tokens can be committed, and the remaining speculative state must be handled consistently. EOS, stopping rules, and cache rollback are part of the serving implementation.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Describe the correction rule</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For a proposed token with draft probability q and target probability p at the relevant prefix, the classic acceptance probability is the smaller of one and <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">p/q</code>, with suitable handling of the proposal support. If rejected, sample from a normalized positive residual based on <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">max(p-q,0)</code>. This correction is what preserves the target distribution in the standard construction.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">As a small example, let target probabilities be <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">[0.6,0.3,0.1]</code> and draft probabilities <code style=\"font-size:0.9em; padding:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\" data-box=\"1\">[0.5,0.4,0.1]</code>. The middle candidate is accepted with probability 0.75, while the other two are accepted fully. A rejection correction allocates residual mass to the first candidate. A naive accept-or-target-argmax replacement would not generally preserve the same distribution.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Predict benefit from acceptance and overhead</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">High draft-target agreement makes more proposals useful. A longer proposal horizon can increase tokens accepted per target call, but also spends more draft work and can waste effort after an early rejection. Under a simplified constant independent acceptance approximation, the expected accepted-plus-bonus pattern can be described by a geometric sum; real workloads vary by position and task.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Draft latency, target verification cost, cache handling, batching, and scheduling determine the actual speedup. Low-to-moderate batch interactive workloads can have useful spare parallel capacity, while highly utilized serving may see less benefit or reduced throughput. Benchmark both latency and throughput instead of promising a fixed two-to-three-times gain.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Treat compatibility and variants carefully</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The basic same-token-space construction assumes compatible tokenization and probabilities. Different-tokenizer variants exist, but need additional alignment machinery and their own guarantees. A draft from the same family can be convenient, but family membership is not a mathematical requirement for useful proposals.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Auxiliary heads, feature-level drafting, prompt lookup, and self-drafting approaches can reduce separate-model overhead. They are not all architecturally identical or automatically distribution-preserving under every acceptance rule. State whether the deployed system is exact sampling, greedy-equivalent, or an approximate quality-speed trade-off.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Evaluate the complete serving path</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use realistic input/output lengths, request concurrency, domains, and stopping behavior. Speculative decoding pays off when proposal quality and hardware utilization overcome its added work while preserving the required output behavior; it is not a guarantee that adding a smaller model makes any target faster.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate sequence likelihood, task utility, and output constraints</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Decoding selects an output sequence from a model's conditional distribution. The highest-probability next token, the highest-probability complete sequence, and the most useful answer are different objectives. A decoding method can optimize one while failing another. Explain the objective before labeling a strategy better or worse.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Greedy selection follows one locally maximal path. The teacher can provide probability distributions, responses, intermediate representations, or permitted task explanations. Distillation transfers a training signal; it does not automatically copy every capability, guarantee privacy, or impose a universal ceiling on student performance.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Classical soft-target distillation</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A teacher's output distribution contains information beyond one hard label. Temperature can soften distributions, and a distillation loss can compare teacher and student probabilities alongside other objectives.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For autoregressive models, token-level comparisons must respect the conditioning prefix and compatible output representations. This can work with a teacher accessible only through a generation interface, subject to permissions and terms. The student learns from the provided outputs rather than receiving the full probability distribution.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The data must represent the intended workload. Compare actual outcomes rather than asserting that the student must always match or always remain below the teacher.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Choose distillation for a measured deployment goal</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For a hypothetical support extractor, define the required fields, uncertain cases, and source-grounding rules. Preserve provenance and applicable data-use permissions. Distillation is justified when the student meets the task contract with a better lifecycle cost, not merely because its parameter count is smaller.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Connect the training objective to the behavior being changed</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A training method specifies an objective, data distribution, trainable parameters, and optimization process. Those choices determine what signal the model receives; they do not guarantee the desired application behavior. Next-token prediction, supervised demonstrations, contrastive similarity, preference comparisons, and verifier rewards teach related but different properties.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">State which parameters change and which remain frozen. A small number of trainable parameters can reduce gradient and optimizer storage while still requiring substantial forward and backward computation. Conversely, a frozen quantized base can participate in differentiable computation without receiving weight updates. It is inaccurate to assume every model was pretrained at four or eight thousand tokens and later extended. Some models are trained directly with long or varied sequence lengths. For an existing short-context checkpoint, however, extension methods must address unfamiliar positional and dependency patterns rather than simply increasing an input-length setting.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Position interpolation</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For a RoPE-based model, position interpolation compresses a longer sequence's position indices into a range more similar to that encountered during training. If the desired span is eight times larger, a simple mapping can scale positions by one eighth. The model avoids some out-of-range positional behavior, but the compressed representation also changes how local distances appear.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">This is not a free extension. Nearby positions become less separated under the transformed coordinate system, and training may be needed to adapt. The useful extension factor and retained short-context quality depend on the checkpoint and procedure. A method being defined for a large position does not establish accurate reasoning at that distance.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Frequency-aware RoPE modifications</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Other approaches adjust rotary frequencies or scales nonuniformly so local and long-range behavior are affected differently. Names such as NTK-aware scaling refer to particular ideas and implementations, not one universally interchangeable recipe. Keep the actual frequency transformation and model configuration explicit.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">YaRN combines a frequency-aware extension approach with an attention-scaling adjustment and a training procedure. Its reported efficiency gains are results under particular experimental conditions, not a promise that every extension needs exactly one tenth the data. Validate the procedure on the target model and compare both original-range and extended-range behavior.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Architecture and training matter beyond RoPE</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Sliding-window attention can limit local attention span in compatible architectures. Global layers or tokens can add longer communication paths. Recurrence, state-space components, sparse patterns, and hierarchical processing provide other trade-offs. Attention sinks and streaming techniques can support certain ongoing processing patterns, but retaining selected states is not equivalent to full faithful recall of every earlier token.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Changing the attention pattern of an existing checkpoint can alter learned behavior. A sparse or bounded-memory architecture must be trained or adapted appropriately. Do not present one serving trick as a universal replacement for dense long-range attention.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate addressability from useful capability</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A model may accept a long prompt while missing a middle exception, confusing repeated entities, or failing to combine distant facts. A single-needle test checks a limited retrieval property. Add multi-fact coverage, comparisons, temporal changes, conflicting sources, structured data, and evidence-supported answers at varied positions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Inspect whether failure comes from omitted input, positional use, tokenization, or reasoning. A larger maximum does not fix every issue, and a short retrieved context is not always sufficient for a genuinely corpus-wide task. Choose the evidence strategy according to what the question requires.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Include serving economics and memory</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Longer sequences increase cache and attention work under the relevant architecture. FlashAttention and allocation techniques can reduce specific costs without removing every scaling term. A million-token input may be justified in some applications and uneconomic in others; there is no universal verdict from length alone.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Benchmark real distributions and compare direct long-context processing, selective retrieval, and hierarchical designs. Preserve compatibility among position configuration, cache reuse, tokenizer, and model weights. Long context is achieved by making representation, training, and systems support a larger useful span, then demonstrating that the model can actually use it at an acceptable resource cost.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Preserve the evidence needed for the next decision</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Context length is a capacity limit, not a guarantee that every supplied fact will be used correctly. Select information according to the task, maintain important constraints and source relationships, and remove redundant material deliberately. A smaller prompt can still be incomplete or misleading, while a larger prompt can sometimes be justified for broad synthesis.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Distinguish absence from ineffective use. If a passage was never included, the issue is selection or assembly. If complete evidence is present but the answer ignores it, investigate position, interference, instructions, and model capability with controlled comparisons. Moving the same evidence while holding other factors fixed can reveal position sensitivity without assuming every model has the same pattern.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compression and summarization create additional transformation boundaries. Preserve exceptions, units, dates, negations, and provenance. A summary that erases a condition may make the final generator appear faithful while the complete system remains wrong. This distinction applies equally to long-context models, retrieval systems, and cached prefixes.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Track tensor shapes and invariants explicitly</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A useful explanation should identify the batch axis, sequence axes, feature dimensions, and the meaning of every transformation. Many model bugs are not failures of the underlying mathematics but mistakes in broadcasting, head layout, masks, or normalization. Write a small reference implementation with obvious shapes before replacing it with a fused kernel or distributed operation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For attention, distinguish the number of query positions from the number of key positions. They can differ in cross-attention and cached decoding. A square matrix is a common self-attention case, not a universal requirement. Identical tensor dimensions do not imply identical semantics.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Test invariants that follow from the operation. Attention weights should normalize over eligible keys when a row has valid entries; masked future positions must not influence an earlier causal output. Clear dimensional contracts make both the conceptual explanation and the production implementation easier to inspect.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Define what a cache reuses and when it remains valid</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Model weights, prompt-prefix state, retrieval results, tool observations, and final answers are different cached objects. Reusing one does not establish validity of the others. A prefix cache can save repeated computation while the model still generates a new answer; an answer cache returns prior content and must account for source freshness and current user scope.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compatibility can depend on token sequence, model weights, adapters, positional configuration, cache layout, and runtime settings. A text change near the beginning may prevent reuse after the divergence, while an unchanged earlier prefix can sometimes remain reusable. Do not assume all cache implementations operate on raw byte identity or expose the same persistence guarantees.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Measure hit rate, cold behavior, eviction, memory consumption, and the resource actually saved. Faster prefill does not eliminate decoding or long-context attention. A cached prefix can occupy substantial memory, and many permission-specific variants can reduce reuse. Managed-provider pricing and retention are service-specific rather than universal percentages or durations.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Treat caches as derived state with explicit invalidation and isolation. A revoked permission or updated policy may require immediate exclusion rather than waiting for a TTL. It does not by itself predict wall-clock time. A kernel can perform fewer operations and still run slower because of memory movement, synchronization, poor occupancy, or conversion overhead. Explain which term is being analyzed and which parts of the model are excluded.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For dense attention, pairwise query-key and attention-value work grows quadratically with sequence length during a full sequence pass. Projection and feed-forward work have different dependence on width and length. During cached single-token decoding, the new query attends over the existing prefix, changing the per-step shape. Total generation cost and one decoding step are therefore different measurements.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Memory complexity also needs a scope. Temporary attention scores, persistent model weights, saved training activations, optimizer state, and the growing KV cache are distinct allocations. Removing a quadratic intermediate does not make every resource in the model linear or eliminate persistent storage. Include peak usage as well as steady-state requirements when deciding whether a configuration fits.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use a profiling hypothesis derived from the equation, then measure it under the intended workload. Vary one dimension at a time and check whether the observed scaling matches expectations. If it does not, investigate the implementation or another dominating term before declaring the theory wrong. This approach connects the mathematical explanation to an actionable performance diagnosis.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Account for the complete memory footprint</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Model capacity planning requires more than multiplying parameter count by an advertised storage precision. Weights may need scales, zero points, alignment, and selected higher-precision tensors. Training adds gradients, optimizer states, activations, and temporary buffers. Serving adds cache blocks, request metadata, workspaces, and memory needed for batching or speculative branches.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Write a component budget in bytes and distinguish decimal gigabytes from binary gibibytes. For float32, one parameter value occupies four bytes; for packed low-bit values, metadata and incomplete packing alter the effective average. A nominal reduction in one component is not the same ratio for the entire process. If weights are compressed while caches dominate, total concurrency may improve much less than expected.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Peak memory can decide feasibility. Loading, adapter merging, checkpoint saving, attention computation, and optimizer steps can create temporary allocations beyond the steady state. Distributed sharding and offloading change where memory resides, but introduce communication and transfer costs. Do not call a configuration impossible or guaranteed to fit without stating the hardware and execution assumptions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Measure allocated and reserved memory with the actual framework, representative lengths, batch sizes, and active features. Include worst-important cases, not only a short warm-up prompt. Leave operational headroom for concurrent requests and maintenance. This makes memory estimates useful for choosing a design while avoiding false precision from a formula that omits half the serving stack.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Connect the training objective to the behavior being changed</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A training method specifies an objective, data distribution, trainable parameters, and optimization process.
