Next-token prediction, supervised demonstrations, contrastive similarity, preference comparisons, and verifier rewards teach related but different properties.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">State which parameters change and which remain frozen. A small number of trainable parameters can reduce gradient and optimizer storage while still requiring substantial forward and backward computation. Conversely, a frozen quantized base can participate in differentiable computation without receiving weight updates. Distinguish parameter storage, compute dtype, gradient flow, and optimizer ownership.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Inspect learning curves and representative outputs together. Lower training loss can coexist with overfitting, forgetting, spurious correlations, or reward exploitation. Validation should cover the target task and capabilities that must remain intact. Dataset size alone does not determine the number of useful epochs, and one learning-rate recipe does not transfer unchanged across every model, adapter, and objective.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Record effective batch size, token masking, sequence packing, loss normalization, optimizer settings, and checkpoint selection. These details can change results substantially even when a method name is unchanged. Use a reproducible baseline and a bounded search over justified configurations. The architectural question is which update process provides the required behavior at acceptable cost and regression risk, not which training acronym is currently most popular.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Evaluate the task contract, not just a proxy score</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Perplexity, numerical reconstruction error, benchmark accuracy, and human preference measure different properties. A model can preserve average language-model loss while regressing on exact identifiers, rare languages, long-range reasoning, or structured extraction. Select metrics that establish the actual capability being promised rather than assuming one aggregate proxy captures every important effect.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Build representative cases with ordinary requests, difficult constraints, ambiguous inputs, missing evidence, and appropriate no-answer behavior. Use objective checks where available, and calibrate model-based or human review against explicit criteria where exact matching is inadequate. A passing schema checks shape; a passing test checks its specified behavior; neither automatically establishes complete correctness.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare candidate and baseline on the same cases and source snapshot. Inspect per-category differences and severe failures before accepting an average improvement. Report uncertainty and repeated-run behavior when sampling is relevant. A small gain from a tiny sample can be noise, while a rare but important regression can be hidden by many easy successes.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Keep held-out assessment separate from iterative tuning. Version the model, tokenizer, prompts, decoding, data, and relevant serving settings with each result. This makes it possible to tell whether an observed change comes from the technique being tested or from another part of the stack. The useful conclusion is that a configuration meets a defined task requirement under measured conditions, not that it is universally near-lossless or best.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use controlled comparisons and meaningful ablations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Before changing a model or serving configuration, write the hypothesis and the expected measurable effect. If the proposed change is meant to reduce cache memory, measure cache memory separately from weights. If it is meant to improve evidence use, hold the evidence constant while testing the model behavior. A successful output after several simultaneous changes does not reveal which intervention mattered.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Vary one important factor at a time where practical, then evaluate interactions deliberately. Rank, scaling, learning rate, target modules, precision, and batch size can affect one another. A fair comparison may require either equal training compute, equal parameter budget, equal memory, or equal quality; state which resource is held fixed. Different choices answer different engineering questions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use a simple reference and include negative controls. For example, a mask test should fail when the future-token restriction is deliberately removed, and an evaluator should notice an intentionally unsupported claim. Such checks establish that the experiment is sensitive to the property it claims to measure. They are often more informative than increasing the benchmark size without inspecting examples.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Preserve configurations and intermediate artifacts needed to interpret results. Record failed runs and resource limits rather than reporting only the best seed. Once required checks pass, broaden experiments only to resolve a new uncertainty or justify a deployment decision. The aim is enough evidence for a reliable choice, not an endless collection of attractive but incomparable numbers.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15595\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Position interpolation</a></p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00071\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">YaRN</a></p>\n</div>"},{"q":"What is the lost-in-the-middle effect and how do you design around it?","g":["long context"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The lost-in-the-middle problem is a pattern in which a language model uses relevant information less reliably when that information appears in the middle of a long input than when it appears near the beginning or end. It is a warning about effective use of context, not merely context capacity. A model can accept a prompt without error and still fail to use a decisive passage within it. For RAG systems, that distinction affects how evidence is selected, arranged, compressed, and evaluated.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The original research demonstrated position-sensitive performance on tasks such as multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval. Those results motivate testing, but they do not establish one permanent curve for every current model. The magnitude depends on the model, task, prompt, evidence type, distractors, and overall length. A senior implementation answer therefore treats lost-in-the-middle as a measurable failure mode, rather than assuming that moving passages to a particular position always solves it.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate window size from usable evidence</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A context window is a technical limit on the material a model can process within an interaction. Effective evidence use is a behavioral property. Increasing the window can make more documents available, but it does not ensure accurate comparison, exception handling, or citation assignment across those documents. A prompt containing every possible source can still perform worse than a smaller, carefully selected one.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Imagine a policy question requiring a general rule and one exception. The prompt includes twenty related passages. The rule appears first, the exception is buried after several long background sections, and a final FAQ repeats the general rule without qualifications. The model answers from the prominent repeated statement. The exception technically fits in context, but its inclusion has not produced effective grounding. This is the product failure that a token-limit dashboard would miss.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Confirm the failure before applying a remedy</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Start by checking that the decisive text is actually present in the final prompt and accurately extracted. A missing paragraph is not a position-use failure. Neither is an unsupported expected answer that does not follow from the supplied source. Verify the question, evidence, source status, and required reasoning before designing a position experiment.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Then hold the evidence and instructions constant while changing placement. Put the same passage near the beginning, middle, and end among the same distractors. Keep total length approximately constant and repeat across several questions. If correctness changes systematically with placement, position sensitivity is a credible explanation. If every arrangement fails, investigate missing context, model capability, confusing instructions, or an incorrect reference answer instead.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Reduce irrelevant context, not required coverage</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The first useful intervention is often to remove material that contributes no evidence toward the question. Reranking, deduplication, source filtering, and query-aware selection can reduce distraction and token cost simultaneously. However, sending only three passages does not eliminate position effects or guarantee completeness. A short context can still contain misleading ordering, and a multi-hop question may need more than three sources.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Selection should optimize a sufficient evidence set. For a refund question, that may include the rule, the applicable exception, and the effective-date amendment. A general product history page can be omitted even if it is semantically similar. Track evidence-group coverage after pruning, because an aggressive reduction can make the answer look cleaner while removing the only clause that changes the conclusion.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use source structure to make scope visible</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A passage is easier to interpret when its title, section, version, and subject remain visible. Clearly distinguish the current policy from an archived FAQ and an organization-specific amendment. These labels help the model understand relationships without inferring them from scattered prose. Structure is useful even when positional sensitivity is not the main cause.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For example, label one passage as the general policy and another as an amendment overriding a named section. Preserve the language establishing precedence. Merely placing the amendment last is weaker than explicitly showing why it governs. If the model must discover authority solely from position, the prompt has made an important business relationship implicit. Good context assembly supplies that relationship as evidence rather than relying on a layout trick.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Reorder evidence as an experiment</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">One strategy places highly useful passages near the beginning and end, leaving weaker background in the middle. Another keeps related evidence together so the model can compare a rule and exception locally. Neither is universally best. Evaluate them on your actual questions and models, especially when document order itself has meaning, such as chronological amendments or procedural steps.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Do not reorder table rows, numbered instructions, or quoted legal clauses in ways that change their interpretation. Reordering independent source blocks is different from rearranging content inside a source. Preserve provenance and original sequence metadata so citations remain inspectable. When two documents conflict, use an explicit authority rule rather than assuming the last document should win because it is placed near the question.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Compress carefully and preserve qualifications</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Extractive compression selects answer-relevant sentences or source spans while retaining their original wording. This can reduce the distance between useful pieces of evidence and remove distractors. It is often easier to audit than a fully abstractive summary because the retained text can be traced directly to the source. Still, extraction can omit context needed to interpret a sentence.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The words unless, except, before, after, and only can be decisive. A compressor that retains a refund window but drops its exception creates a new information-loss failure. Evaluate compression against required facts and source relationships, not just compression ratio. Preserve headings, units, dates, row labels, and links between footnotes and the text they qualify. A short but misleading context is not an improvement.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Distinguish summarization from evidence preservation</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Abstractive compression can be useful when sources are verbose, but it creates another generation stage that may introduce errors or merge conflicting claims. If the final answer is wrong, you must inspect both the compressed evidence and the answer generator. A faithful final answer to a flawed summary remains wrong for the user.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For sensitive facts, retain original excerpts alongside summaries or require a source-span mapping for every compressed claim. The final generator can then consult the exact wording when needed. Summaries may help navigation, while original passages establish the claim. This layered design costs some additional tokens but makes it easier to detect when a neat summary has erased an essential distinction.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Place the task clearly without duplicating instructions blindly</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Restating a concise question after the evidence can make the information need salient. It can also help distinguish source material from the action the assistant should perform. However, the effect depends on the model and prompt design. Do not treat repeating the question as an assured accuracy improvement or as a substitute for adequate evidence selection.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Avoid conflicting versions of the task at different prompt locations. If an early instruction asks for a broad summary and a final instruction asks for a precise eligibility decision, the inconsistency may look like a context-use failure. Keep trusted application instructions distinct from untrusted source content. Repeating user text should not promote instructions embedded in a retrieved document into higher-authority control.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use hierarchical processing for broad synthesis</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">When the task genuinely requires many documents, one large prompt may be a poor execution plan. A hierarchical approach processes bounded groups, extracts relevant facts with provenance, then combines those intermediate results. A map-reduce approach can summarize independent sources before a synthesis step, while iterative retrieval can gather additional evidence only when a gap is identified.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">These techniques move the challenge rather than removing it. Intermediate summaries can lose minority findings, contradictory evidence, or rare exceptions. Define what must survive each stage and verify it. For a corpus-wide theme question, track source coverage and contrary examples. For a comparison, retain structured attributes and evidence identifiers rather than relying entirely on prose summaries that are difficult to reconcile.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Support multi-evidence reasoning explicitly</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A question may require joining two facts that appear far apart. Instead of only changing document order, assemble a small evidence bundle identifying the relevant relationship: product version, applicable rule, exception, and effective date. The model should not have to scan a long collection to infer which pieces belong together.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">This is particularly useful for amendments and regional policies. A bundle can state that passage S1 provides the baseline and passage S2 modifies it for the user's region, while still supplying both original excerpts. The annotation itself must be derived reliably and checked against sources. If the assembler invents the relationship, it has simply moved hallucination upstream. Treat relationship construction as another testable boundary.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Evaluate position robustness systematically</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Create a controlled set with several prompt lengths and evidence positions. Include single-fact questions, rule-plus-exception cases, table interpretation, comparisons, and multi-document synthesis. Measure answer correctness, required-fact coverage, citation support, and abstention. A retrieval-only metric will not expose whether the generator can use evidence once it is present.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare the same model and configuration across reordered prompts, then compare alternative models if needed. Use repeated runs when sampling variation is material. Report per-category effects rather than only one average. A model might be robust on exact key lookup yet fail when the middle passage contains a subtle exception. The operational mitigation should target the category that actually fails.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Avoid misleading success criteria</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A system that always answers from the first source may look strong when the benchmark always places the answer first. Randomize or deliberately vary source positions during evaluation. Likewise, synthetic questions copied from a source can make matching too easy. Include distractors that share terminology but differ in product, date, or eligibility conditions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Check that a model has not merely memorized the answer or inferred it from prior knowledge. One controlled test changes an otherwise plausible source fact and asks whether the response follows the supplied evidence. Such tests need careful construction so the altered fact remains internally coherent. The goal is to assess evidence use, not reward a model for ignoring documents that happen to contradict its training.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Consider the cost-quality trade-off</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Reducing context can improve latency and cost, but extra reranking and compression also consume resources. Measure complete request latency rather than assuming fewer prompt tokens always means a faster application. A two-stage compression pipeline may save generation cost while adding enough upstream delay to violate the user experience requirement.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Set operational budgets and compare approaches on supported answer success per unit cost. For a small stable corpus, direct long-context prompting may remain appropriate. For a large dynamic corpus, retrieval and selective expansion may be better. The lost-in-the-middle concern does not dictate one architecture; it explains why fitting more material into the prompt is not, by itself, a sufficient design argument.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">What the mitigation should accomplish</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A good mitigation makes the decisive evidence easier to identify and use without hiding required context or altering source meaning. That can involve better selection, explicit source relationships, tested ordering, cautious compression, or hierarchical processing. The correct choice follows from a controlled diagnosis and regression evaluation, not from an unconditional top-three rule.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">In an interview, I would say that lost-in-the-middle is position-sensitive evidence use in long contexts. I verify it by holding evidence constant and changing placement, then reduce irrelevant material, preserve exceptions, structure related evidence, and test ordering or hierarchical processing. I monitor final-answer correctness and evidence retention, because a smaller prompt is useful only if it still supports the complete answer.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">A controlled mitigation example</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Suppose ten policy questions are answered correctly when the decisive exception is first, but only six are correct when the same exception is placed in the middle of an otherwise unchanged context. Before declaring a general model weakness, verify that the reordering did not break source labels, separate a table from its note, or alter the question. Then repeat with more representative questions and another context length. The initial result supports a hypothesis, not a reliable population estimate.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Test three interventions independently. First remove passages that have no bearing on eligibility while preserving every required evidence group. Second keep the original passages but place the rule and exception next to each other with their relationship labeled. Third apply an extractive compressor that retains both clauses and their source references. Measure whether each intervention improves correctness without increasing unsupported claims or losing citations. A compression method that answers nine questions correctly but silently drops a critical condition on the tenth may require different handling for that category.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The resulting engineering decision might be to use compact evidence bundles for policy questions and hierarchical summaries for broad research questions. That is more defensible than applying one reordering rule to every prompt. Preserve the failed arrangement as a regression case, and run it again when changing the model, prompt template, or context assembler. Position sensitivity is a property of the complete interaction, so a later upgrade can change both the problem and the effectiveness of the mitigation.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Lost in the Middle research</a></p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://github.com/nelson-liu/lost-in-the-middle\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Research code and evaluation materials</a></p>\n</div>"},{"q":"Compare chain-of-thought, self-consistency, tree-of-thoughts and ReAct as reasoning techniques.","g":["reasoning models"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Chain-of-thought, self-consistency, Tree of Thoughts, and ReAct change how a system approaches a problem, but they operate at different levels. Chain-of-thought introduces intermediate reasoning, self-consistency aggregates sampled solutions, Tree of Thoughts searches over partial states, and ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions and observations. They can be combined, and none establishes correctness merely by producing a more elaborate process.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Chain-of-thought as intermediate computation</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The basic idea is to generate intermediate steps rather than jump directly to a final answer. This can help some multi-step tasks because later output conditions on earlier work. It can also propagate an incorrect assumption or generate a plausible explanation after a wrong conclusion. The visible reasoning text is not guaranteed to be a faithful account of internal computation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Chain-of-thought is not inherently greedy: the intermediate sequence can be sampled or produced under other decoding rules. Its cost depends on length and the model. For reasoning-capable models, requesting detailed private reasoning may be unnecessary or unsupported. Ask for concise explanations, calculations, or evidence where useful, while using available model controls appropriately.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Self-consistency aggregates candidate answers</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Self-consistency samples several reasoning paths and aggregates their final answers, commonly through majority or consistency after normalization. This can improve reliability when diverse paths arrive at the same valid result. It requires a meaningful way to decide which outputs agree and a sample set containing useful alternatives.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Errors are not independent merely because sampling randomness differs. Several outputs can share the same misconception, missing fact, or source error. Majority agreement is therefore not proof. For open-ended tasks, exact voting is harder, but semantic clustering, ranking, or verifiers can extend the idea; it is too strong to say aggregation cannot work at all outside discrete answers.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Tree of Thoughts adds explicit search</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Tree of Thoughts represents partial progress as states, generates possible next thoughts or actions, evaluates them, and searches with a chosen strategy such as breadth-first or depth-first exploration. Backtracking can help tasks where an early choice leads to a dead end and an alternative branch is worth exploring.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The difficult parts are state representation, branch generation, evaluation, and budget. A weak evaluator can prune the correct path or favor fluent but invalid progress. Cost depends on branching and depth, not a guaranteed fixed multiplier. Search is useful when the problem admits meaningful partial states and the evaluation signal guides exploration better than a simple continuation.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">ReAct brings in external observations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">ReAct alternates decisions with tool actions and returned evidence. A troubleshooting agent can read logs, check a configuration, and revise its next step. This addresses missing or incorrect assumptions about an external environment, which extra internal deliberation alone cannot reliably repair.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">The model can still choose the wrong tool, misread the result, or report success prematurely. Tools need authorization, clear results, and verification. ReAct is not universally the most important technique for every application; a fixed retrieval workflow or direct computation can be better for a well-defined task.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Choose by the bottleneck</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">If the problem is a missed calculation, a calculator may beat several sampled explanations. If it is an uncertain plan with recoverable branches, structured search can help. If it is missing live evidence, tool interaction is necessary. Compare approaches at a stated resource budget and evaluate accepted outcomes, not reasoning length. Modern reasoning models change the cost-benefit of explicit prompting, but do not eliminate the value of external evidence, bounded search, or verification.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Allocate additional inference work according to measured value</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Test-time computation can include longer internal reasoning, several candidate solutions, search over intermediate states, tool use, verification, or iterative revision. These mechanisms are not interchangeable. More generated tokens do not necessarily correspond to more useful reasoning, and spending additional compute does not guarantee monotonic accuracy gains on every task.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use a task-specific acceptance signal when possible. A calculator can check arithmetic, a test can check specified code behavior, and source evidence can support factual claims. Majority agreement among samples is weaker when mistakes are correlated or the correct answer is absent from all candidates. Search quality depends on both candidate generation and the evaluator used to keep or prune branches.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Control total latency, cost, and output behavior. A reasoning-capable model may be valuable for a difficult extraction or summary, while a routine task may not benefit enough to justify it. Avoid rigid categories that declare one model type always unnecessary. Compare actual successful outcomes against a simpler baseline at an equal resource budget where appropriate.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Do not require private internal reasoning as an audit log or training artifact. Concise explanations, verified calculations, plans, tool observations, and final evidence can support inspection without claiming to reveal the model's exact computation. Provider reasoning controls and billing differ. The useful design is an explicit allocation policy backed by evaluation, not an assumption that longer hidden deliberation is inherently more trustworthy.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate sequence likelihood, task utility, and output constraints</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Decoding selects an output sequence from a model's conditional distribution. The highest-probability next token, the highest-probability complete sequence, and the most useful answer are different objectives. A decoding method can optimize one while failing another. Explain the objective before labeling a strategy better or worse.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Greedy selection follows one locally maximal path. Beam methods retain several partial paths under a scoring rule, often with length handling and stopping rules. Sampling introduces controlled variation through a distribution and optional filtering. Implementation details matter: penalties, constraints, temperature, and truncation order can change the resulting distribution and behavior.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A parser-facing task needs an explicit format contract and validation rather than relying on low randomness alone. Schema-constrained generation can enforce supported structural rules while semantic checks establish whether the values are correct. A valid JSON object can still contain the wrong ID, missing work, or an unsupported claim.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Evaluate generation under the intended use: accuracy and completeness for factual tasks, useful diversity for ideation, valid constraints for structured data, and latency for serving. Do not assume every translation has one correct wording or every open-ended task needs sampling. Deterministic mathematical selection also does not imply identical service output across model or runtime changes. Choose decoding according to measured utility and constraints, not a universal preference for maximum probability or maximum variety.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use the strongest available check for each requirement</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Verification should match the property being claimed. Arithmetic can be checked with calculation, code behavior with relevant tests, schema shape with a validator, and source support with evidence review. A model-generated explanation of why it is correct is not an independent guarantee. Equally, a narrow objective check does not establish every aspect of a broad task.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For reasoning tasks, distinguish a correct final answer from a valid method and from a robust process. Several sampled solutions can agree on the same wrong assumption. A verifier may catch some errors, but can itself be incomplete, exploitable, or dependent on an incorrect reference. Test verifier failure modes rather than assuming that an executable signal makes training or inference automatically safe.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For numerical and performance methods, verify the claimed resource saving separately from task quality. Smaller tensors do not establish faster serving, and close output logits do not establish unchanged user outcomes. Check the full configuration under the conditions where the claim will be used.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">When no adequate deterministic check exists, use explicit rubrics, calibrated model judgment, or human review. Preserve uncertainty instead of inventing a false binary certainty. Associate verification with the exact artifact or model version evaluated. A later revision, merge, precision conversion, or decoding change may need reassessment. Verification is useful when it limits what can legitimately be concluded, not when it becomes a ceremonial pass label.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Evaluate representations against the information need</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A representation is useful when it supports the comparison or retrieval task it was trained for. Two passages can be topically similar while differing on product version, jurisdiction, identifier, or exception. Nearest-vector scores are ranking signals, not calibrated probabilities that a result answers the user's question.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use labeled query-evidence pairs or evidence groups appropriate to the application. Recall measures coverage, ranking metrics measure order, and precision measures the useful share under a specified definition. Approximate-neighbor recall against exhaustive vector search is a different quantity from human-judged relevance. Measure both when tuning an approximate index so embedding limitations are not confused with search approximation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Keep query and document encoders in a compatible learned space, including required prefixes or input modes. Changing an embedding configuration can require rebuilding the index and recalibrating thresholds. Matching dimensionality alone is not enough. Check normalization, distance semantics, sequence truncation, and language coverage.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For applications, preserve source identity, versions, and authorization through retrieval and final context assembly. A good initial ranking is insufficient if compression removes a decisive condition later. Compare the entire evidence path and the supported answer, not only a public embedding score. This turns representation selection into a workload decision and reveals when lexical search, structured filters, or a live-data tool should complement semantic similarity.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Preserve the evidence needed for the next decision</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Context length is a capacity limit, not a guarantee that every supplied fact will be used correctly. Select information according to the task, maintain important constraints and source relationships, and remove redundant material deliberately. A smaller prompt can still be incomplete or misleading, while a larger prompt can sometimes be justified for broad synthesis.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Distinguish absence from ineffective use. If a passage was never included, the issue is selection or assembly. If complete evidence is present but the answer ignores it, investigate position, interference, instructions, and model capability with controlled comparisons. Moving the same evidence while holding other factors fixed can reveal position sensitivity without assuming every model has the same pattern.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compression and summarization create additional transformation boundaries. Preserve exceptions, units, dates, negations, and provenance. A summary that erases a condition may make the final generator appear faithful while the complete system remains wrong. Hierarchical processing can help large inputs, but intermediate representations must retain the facts required for the final task.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Evaluate single facts, multiple required facts, comparisons, and conflicting sources across relevant lengths and positions. Simple needle retrieval is useful but limited. The operational target is correct, supported completion at an acceptable cost, not merely accepting the largest advertised input. This distinction applies equally to long-context models, retrieval systems, and cached prefixes.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Evaluate the task contract, not just a proxy score</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Perplexity, numerical reconstruction error, benchmark accuracy, and human preference measure different properties. A model can preserve average language-model loss while regressing on exact identifiers, rare languages, long-range reasoning, or structured extraction. Select metrics that establish the actual capability being promised rather than assuming one aggregate proxy captures every important effect.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Build representative cases with ordinary requests, difficult constraints, ambiguous inputs, missing evidence, and appropriate no-answer behavior. Use objective checks where available, and calibrate model-based or human review against explicit criteria where exact matching is inadequate. A passing schema checks shape; a passing test checks its specified behavior; neither automatically establishes complete correctness.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare candidate and baseline on the same cases and source snapshot. Inspect per-category differences and severe failures before accepting an average improvement. Report uncertainty and repeated-run behavior when sampling is relevant. A small gain from a tiny sample can be noise, while a rare but important regression can be hidden by many easy successes.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Keep held-out assessment separate from iterative tuning. Version the model, tokenizer, prompts, decoding, data, and relevant serving settings with each result. This makes it possible to tell whether an observed change comes from the technique being tested or from another part of the stack. The useful conclusion is that a configuration meets a defined task requirement under measured conditions, not that it is universally near-lossless or best.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use controlled comparisons and meaningful ablations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Before changing a model or serving configuration, write the hypothesis and the expected measurable effect. If the proposed change is meant to reduce cache memory, measure cache memory separately from weights. If it is meant to improve evidence use, hold the evidence constant while testing the model behavior. A successful output after several simultaneous changes does not reveal which intervention mattered.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Vary one important factor at a time where practical, then evaluate interactions deliberately. Rank, scaling, learning rate, target modules, precision, and batch size can affect one another. A fair comparison may require either equal training compute, equal parameter budget, equal memory, or equal quality; state which resource is held fixed. Different choices answer different engineering questions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use a simple reference and include negative controls. For example, a mask test should fail when the future-token restriction is deliberately removed, and an evaluator should notice an intentionally unsupported claim. Such checks establish that the experiment is sensitive to the property it claims to measure. They are often more informative than increasing the benchmark size without inspecting examples.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Preserve configurations and intermediate artifacts needed to interpret results. Record failed runs and resource limits rather than reporting only the best seed. Once required checks pass, broaden experiments only to resolve a new uncertainty or justify a deployment decision. The aim is enough evidence for a reliable choice, not an endless collection of attractive but incomparable numbers.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Record enough information to reconstruct the experiment</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Model behavior depends on more than a checkpoint name. Preserve the tokenizer, prompt template, data version, preprocessing, numeric settings, decoding configuration, seeds where meaningful, and hardware-software environment. A moving model alias or a library upgrade can change results without any apparent change to application code.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Deterministic mathematics does not guarantee identical operational output. Floating-point reductions, parallel scheduling, kernel choices, and provider changes can introduce differences. Low sampling randomness may reduce one source of variation but cannot make an incorrect method correct or establish perfect repeatability across every platform.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use small reference cases to localize divergence, then test representative workloads. Compare intermediate tensors for numerical changes and task outcomes for behavioral changes. Record failures and unsupported configurations rather than silently excluding them. A successful run under one environment does not prove compatibility under another.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For applications with external evidence, preserve the relevant source snapshot or governed artifact references. A rerun against updated documents is not a clean reproduction of the original result. Hashes can verify identity, but they cannot recover missing inputs. Decide what must remain accessible under the retention policy. The goal is a result that another qualified engineer can interpret and test, even when exact bitwise replay is not feasible.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Self-consistency</a></p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10601\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Tree of Thoughts</a></p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">ReAct</a></p>\n</div>"},{"q":"What are reasoning models and test-time compute? When are they worth it?","g":["reasoning models"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Reasoning models are models designed or post-trained to perform more useful intermediate computation before producing a final response. Test-time compute is the broader resource spent during inference to improve an answer, including internal deliberation, candidate sampling, search, tools, and verification. Increasing that resource provides another possible quality axis besides larger models and more training, but improvements depend on task and allocation strategy.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Describe the behavior without assuming one training recipe</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Some reasoning models use reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, while other training and architectural choices can also support reasoning behavior. They may learn to revise, check, or pursue longer solution paths. Not every model exposes a direct thinking-budget control, and not every longer response reflects useful reasoning.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A reasoning summary, when provided, is not necessarily a complete or faithful log of internal computation. Do not use it as a substitute for tool traces, evidence, calculations, or authoritative outcomes. An application can require a concise explanation of a result without demanding private internal reasoning.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Identify tasks where additional work can matter</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Difficult planning, code investigation, mathematical reasoning, and reconciliation of conflicting evidence can benefit. The key is whether extra computation addresses the limiting uncertainty. If the necessary policy or current account fact is absent, more internal reasoning cannot manufacture reliable evidence. Retrieval or a structured tool remains necessary.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">It is too categorical to say reasoning models never help extraction, classification, or summarization. A complex legal-condition extraction or a summary requiring contradiction handling may be difficult. Conversely, many routine cases do not justify the additional latency or cost. Evaluate complexity and observed failure, not only the task label.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Allocate effort adaptively and safely</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A router can use a cheaper path for straightforward requests and escalate ambiguous or difficult cases. The router itself needs evaluation, including false confidence and missed escalation. A model's self-reported certainty is not a reliable sole signal for how much compute is needed.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A hypothetical code assistant might use direct parsing for a known configuration, a standard model for a small edit, and a more capable reasoning path for an intermittent failure involving several components. External tests and resource limits remain in place for every path. More capability does not grant broader permission or remove verification requirements.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Include hidden and downstream costs</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Internal computation can increase billed usage and time to answer, but accounting and exposed controls vary by provider. Use actual usage records and service terms rather than assuming all hidden tokens are billed identically. Measure time to first useful information, complete latency, throughput, and cost per successful task.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Longer computation can also produce unnecessary branches or overcomplicate a simple request. Compare a shorter effort setting and a simpler model at the same acceptance criteria. More compute is useful only when its marginal benefit exceeds its resource and complexity cost for the workload.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Evaluate the full decision process</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use held-out difficult and ordinary cases, repeated runs where relevant, and objective checks or calibrated review. Test no-answer behavior and false premises so additional reasoning does not become more persuasive fabrication. Prompting advice is model-specific: examples can help or hurt, and a generic instruction to think step by step is not a universal improvement. The practical answer is measured allocation of inference work with evidence and verification, not buying a reasoning label and assuming every response becomes more trustworthy.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Allocate additional inference work according to measured value</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Test-time computation can include longer internal reasoning, several candidate solutions, search over intermediate states, tool use, verification, or iterative revision. These mechanisms are not interchangeable. More generated tokens do not necessarily correspond to more useful reasoning, and spending additional compute does not guarantee monotonic accuracy gains on every task.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use a task-specific acceptance signal when possible. A calculator can check arithmetic, a test can check specified code behavior, and source evidence can support factual claims. Majority agreement among samples is weaker when mistakes are correlated or the correct answer is absent from all candidates. Search quality depends on both candidate generation and the evaluator used to keep or prune branches.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Control total latency, cost, and output behavior. A reasoning-capable model may be valuable for a difficult extraction or summary, while a routine task may not benefit enough to justify it. Avoid rigid categories that declare one model type always unnecessary. Compare actual successful outcomes against a simpler baseline at an equal resource budget where appropriate.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Do not require private internal reasoning as an audit log or training artifact. Concise explanations, verified calculations, plans, tool observations, and final evidence can support inspection without claiming to reveal the model's exact computation. Provider reasoning controls and billing differ. The useful design is an explicit allocation policy backed by evaluation, not an assumption that longer hidden deliberation is inherently more trustworthy.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate prefill, decoding, and training behavior</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A decoder-based language model has different execution regimes. Training commonly processes known sequences in parallel while computing gradients. Prefill processes the available prompt and establishes state for generation. Autoregressive decoding then produces successive tokens conditioned on previous ones. These regimes share model components but differ in shapes, parallelism, and resource pressure.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">An optimization that helps prefill may do little for long-output decoding. Reusing a prompt prefix can reduce repeated prompt processing while each new output token still attends to a growing context. A faster attention kernel may have a different benefit at one query position than at thousands. User-visible responsiveness and completed-task cost can favor different configurations.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Training measurements need their own accounting: examples or tokens processed, optimizer steps, activation strategy, gradient accumulation, and communication. A technique that reduces trainable parameters may still require backpropagation through much of the network. A speedup measured in one operator is not automatically the same speedup for the whole request.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Distributed execution adds communication and scheduling effects. Tensor parallelism, expert routing, sharding, and offloading can move the bottleneck away from arithmetic. Network topology and interconnect bandwidth matter, as do uneven work distribution and synchronization waits. A theoretically sparse computation may become communication-heavy in the actual deployment.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use profiling to identify whether the limiting resource is compute, bandwidth, memory capacity, I/O, or coordination. Then choose an optimization that addresses that limit. Avoid universal claims that modern kernels are always memory-bound or that a certain numeric format always makes decoding faster. Performance conclusions should name the model, workload, hardware, and software conditions under which they were observed.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use the strongest available check for each requirement</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Verification should match the property being claimed. Arithmetic can be checked with calculation, code behavior with relevant tests, schema shape with a validator, and source support with evidence review. A model-generated explanation of why it is correct is not an independent guarantee. Equally, a narrow objective check does not establish every aspect of a broad task.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For reasoning tasks, distinguish a correct final answer from a valid method and from a robust process. Several sampled solutions can agree on the same wrong assumption. A verifier may catch some errors, but can itself be incomplete, exploitable, or dependent on an incorrect reference. Test verifier failure modes rather than assuming that an executable signal makes training or inference automatically safe.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For numerical and performance methods, verify the claimed resource saving separately from task quality. Smaller tensors do not establish faster serving, and close output logits do not establish unchanged user outcomes. Check the full configuration under the conditions where the claim will be used.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">When no adequate deterministic check exists, use explicit rubrics, calibrated model judgment, or human review. Public benchmarks can help shortlist models and understand broad capabilities. Task-specific held-out evaluation supports a shipping decision. Human review and calibrated judges assess qualities that lack exact checks. Production metrics reveal whether real users receive successful, timely, and authorized results. None of these layers replaces the others.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Understand the benchmark construct</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A multiple-choice knowledge benchmark, a difficult domain question set, a function-level code test, and a repository-level issue benchmark measure different things. Their score units and harnesses are not interchangeable. A model strong on one can fail a product requiring fresh evidence, long conversations, private terminology, or reliable tool actions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Avoid reducing every benchmark to memorized recall. Many tasks involve reasoning and application of knowledge, but they still represent a selected distribution. The question is whether that distribution and scoring contract match the deployment. Public results are useful evidence when interpreted with their actual scope.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Investigate contamination and comparability</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Evaluation material can appear in training, synthetic data, public solutions, or tuning feedback. This can inflate apparent generalization, but the degree must be investigated rather than asserted for every model. Source dates, exposure records, contamination analysis, and carefully designed fresh tasks can help, with limitations.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare prompting, tools, sampling, test-time budgets, and scoring rules. A multi-attempt score should not be compared casually with a single-attempt score. Some evaluations permit tools or execution environments that others do not. An impressive leaderboard difference can partly reflect harness and resource choices rather than a general capability gap.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Avoid saturation and average-score traps</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Some benchmarks become less discriminating as scores approach their ceiling; others remain difficult. Small differences may be within noise or evaluator variation. Averages can also hide weak languages, rare constraints, safety behavior, and failure categories important to the business.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Report slices and inspect examples. A model that improves common FAQ responses while mishandling version-specific exceptions may be inappropriate for a policy assistant. The highest overall public score is not automatically the best choice for that application.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Build an application evaluation contract</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Collect representative queries and expected behaviors, including ambiguous, unanswerable, adversarial, and access-restricted cases. Report the metric matching the real retry policy, inspect paired changes, and preserve severe invariant checks separately from average quality. Include latency, throughput, memory, cost per successful task, and human correction effort.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">After deployment, monitor user outcomes and incidents without treating positive feedback as complete ground truth. Convert verified failures into regression cases while retaining representative coverage. The architectural framing is that public benchmarks inform what to try, and a well-designed application evaluation informs what can be shipped under the actual requirements. Neither a leaderboard nor one attractive demo is enough.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Evaluate the task contract, not just a proxy score</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Perplexity, numerical reconstruction error, benchmark accuracy, and human preference measure different properties. A model can preserve average language-model loss while regressing on exact identifiers, rare languages, long-range reasoning, or structured extraction. Select metrics that establish the actual capability being promised rather than assuming one aggregate proxy captures every important effect.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Build representative cases with ordinary requests, difficult constraints, ambiguous inputs, missing evidence, and appropriate no-answer behavior. High-quality examples should match the intended task and include the constraints that change answers. A polished synthetic explanation can still be wrong, and a large corpus can underrepresent important languages, edge cases, or user groups.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Track provenance, source permissions, transformation steps, and applicable use restrictions. Separate examples used for tuning from held-out assessment, and group near duplicates or related task families appropriately when splitting. Otherwise, the evaluation can reward memorization or template recognition rather than the capability the product needs.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Balance filtering with coverage. Removing obvious corruption and duplicates can help, but a narrow quality classifier can discard dialects, technical formats, or rare but legitimate material. Inspect what is rejected and evaluate category-level effects. Repeated text can be boilerplate, meaningful code, or deliberate emphasis; deduplication needs a unit and policy appropriate to the dataset rather than indiscriminate deletion.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use human review and objective checks where they are valuable, while acknowledging their limits. A passing test may not cover all requirements, and a preference label can reflect style rather than factual quality. Preserve disagreement and uncertainty when the evidence does not support one definitive label. Data curation is a measurable information-management process, not a claim that smaller or larger datasets always win.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use the strongest available check for each requirement</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Verification should match the property being claimed. Arithmetic can be checked with calculation, code behavior with relevant tests, schema shape with a validator, and source support with evidence review. A model-generated explanation of why it is correct is not an independent guarantee. Equally, a narrow objective check does not establish every aspect of a broad task.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For reasoning tasks, distinguish a correct final answer from a valid method and from a robust process. Several sampled solutions can agree on the same wrong assumption. A verifier may catch some errors, but can itself be incomplete, exploitable, or dependent on an incorrect reference. Test verifier failure modes rather than assuming that an executable signal makes training or inference automatically safe.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For numerical and performance methods, verify the claimed resource saving separately from task quality. Smaller tensors do not establish faster serving, and close output logits do not establish unchanged user outcomes. Check the full configuration under the conditions where the claim will be used.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">When no adequate deterministic check exists, use explicit rubrics, calibrated model judgment, or human review. Preserve uncertainty instead of inventing a false binary certainty. Associate verification with the exact artifact or model version evaluated. A later revision, merge, precision conversion, or decoding change may need reassessment. Verification is useful when it limits what can legitimately be concluded, not when it becomes a ceremonial pass label.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Record enough information to reconstruct the experiment</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Model behavior depends on more than a checkpoint name. Preserve the tokenizer, prompt template, data version, preprocessing, numeric settings, decoding configuration, seeds where meaningful, and hardware-software environment. A moving model alias or a library upgrade can change results without any apparent change to application code.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Deterministic mathematics does not guarantee identical operational output. Floating-point reductions, parallel scheduling, kernel choices, and provider changes can introduce differences. Low sampling randomness may reduce one source of variation but cannot make an incorrect method correct or establish perfect repeatability across every platform.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use small reference cases to localize divergence, then test representative workloads. Compare intermediate tensors for numerical changes and task outcomes for behavioral changes. Record failures and unsupported configurations rather than silently excluding them. A successful run under one environment does not prove compatibility under another.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For applications with external evidence, preserve the relevant source snapshot or governed artifact references. A rerun against updated documents is not a clean reproduction of the original result. Hashes can verify identity, but they cannot recover missing inputs. Decide what must remain accessible under the retention policy. The goal is a result that another qualified engineer can interpret and test, even when exact bitwise replay is not feasible.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use controlled comparisons and meaningful ablations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Before changing a model or serving configuration, write the hypothesis and the expected measurable effect. If the proposed change is meant to reduce cache memory, measure cache memory separately from weights. If it is meant to improve evidence use, hold the evidence constant while testing the model behavior. A successful output after several simultaneous changes does not reveal which intervention mattered.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Vary one important factor at a time where practical, then evaluate interactions deliberately. Rank, scaling, learning rate, target modules, precision, and batch size can affect one another. A fair comparison may require either equal training compute, equal parameter budget, equal memory, or equal quality; state which resource is held fixed. Different choices answer different engineering questions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use a simple reference and include negative controls. For example, a mask test should fail when the future-token restriction is deliberately removed, and an evaluator should notice an intentionally unsupported claim. Such checks establish that the experiment is sensitive to the property it claims to measure. They are often more informative than increasing the benchmark size without inspecting examples.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Preserve configurations and intermediate artifacts needed to interpret results. Record failed runs and resource limits rather than reporting only the best seed. Once required checks pass, broaden experiments only to resolve a new uncertainty or justify a deployment decision. The aim is enough evidence for a reliable choice, not an endless collection of attractive but incomparable numbers.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Control data use and exposure across the lifecycle</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Training, inference, evaluation, caching, and logging can all expose information. Define the allowed data sources, purposes, access scopes, and retention rules for the actual application. Synthetic data is not automatically private, compressed weights are not automatically safe from memorization, and a separate adapter does not by itself establish tenant isolation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Minimize sensitive content where the task permits, and preserve necessary context through controlled references or tokenization rather than indiscriminate removal. A preprocessing rule can damage meaning or make a task impossible if it strips the identifier or qualification needed to answer. Evaluate both privacy controls and task fidelity.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Keep credentials out of ordinary prompts, generated rationales, shared caches, and unrestricted logs. Protect model artifacts and derived datasets according to their contents and use. When information is deleted or access is revoked, consider dependent indexes, summaries, cached outputs, and retained evaluation records rather than only one source row.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use provenance and permission metadata to support review, but do not confuse metadata with a complete legal or security determination. Requirements depend on the data and deployment context. The engineering responsibility is to make sources, transformations, access decisions, and lifecycle behavior inspectable and enforceable. A quality or speed improvement is not an adequate reason to bypass those boundaries.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate sequence likelihood, task utility, and output constraints</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Decoding selects an output sequence from a model's conditional distribution. The highest-probability next token, the highest-probability complete sequence, and the most useful answer are different objectives. A decoding method can optimize one while failing another. Explain the objective before labeling a strategy better or worse.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Greedy selection follows one locally maximal path. Beam methods retain several partial paths under a scoring rule, often with length handling and stopping rules. Sampling introduces controlled variation through a distribution and optional filtering. Implementation details matter: penalties, constraints, temperature, and truncation order can change the resulting distribution and behavior.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A parser-facing task needs an explicit format contract and validation rather than relying on low randomness alone. Schema-constrained generation can enforce supported structural rules while semantic checks establish whether the values are correct. A valid JSON object can still contain the wrong ID, missing work, or an unsupported claim.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Evaluate generation under the intended use: accuracy and completeness for factual tasks, useful diversity for ideation, valid constraints for structured data, and latency for serving. Do not assume every translation has one correct wording or every open-ended task needs sampling. Deterministic mathematical selection also does not imply identical service output across model or runtime changes. Choose decoding according to measured utility and constraints, not a universal preference for maximum probability or maximum variety.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Include artifact compatibility and lifecycle in the design</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A model is deployed with a tokenizer, configuration, numeric representations, runtime kernels, and often adapters or auxiliary models. These components must agree. A weight file that loads successfully can still be interpreted with the wrong token IDs, positional settings, chat template, or quantization metadata. Validate the effective deployed configuration rather than only the training checkpoint.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Version the complete artifact set and keep dependencies explicit. An adapter usually depends on a particular base checkpoint; a prefix cache depends on compatible model computation; a compressed representation depends on its scales and format. Changes to one component can invalidate another. Plan conversion and merging steps with enough temporary memory and quality checks instead of assuming deployment is a file copy.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Measure startup, steady-state behavior, concurrency, failure recovery, and rollback. A configuration that fits after warm-up may exceed memory during loading or produce poor latency after cache eviction. A model update can affect long-running sessions and stored outputs. Decide how active work migrates or remains on an earlier version, and how permissions and source freshness continue to apply.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Avoid attaching guarantees to brand names or broad formats. Supported kernels, licences, APIs, and hardware paths change over time. Use the current documented capabilities for the chosen versions and verify the behavior that matters to your workload. Deployment quality includes maintainability and recoverability as well as the best latency achieved in a notebook.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07316\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">MTEB as a task-specific benchmark example</a></p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">LLM-as-a-judge evaluation research</a></p>\n</div>"},{"q":"How are embedding models trained, and how do you evaluate one?","g":["llm evaluation"],"a":"<div style=\"font-size:15px; line-height:1.9; max-width:100%; min-width:0; overflow-wrap:anywhere\"><p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Embedding models learn representations intended to make useful comparisons efficient.
