Greedy chooses the highest-scoring next token at each step. Beam search keeps several partial sequences under a sequence-scoring rule. Sampling draws from a distribution, possibly modified by temperature or candidate filtering. None is universally best because sequence likelihood, usefulness, correctness, diversity, and structural validity are different objectives.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Greedy decoding is locally optimal</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Greedy selection follows one path, making it simple and often efficient. It does not generally maximize the probability of the complete sequence. For a fixed two-position example, suppose first-token probabilities are 0.6 for A and 0.4 for B. The best second-token probability after A is 0.51, while after B it is 0.99. The best paths then have probabilities 0.306 and 0.396 respectively, so the locally preferred A path is not the best complete candidate.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Mathematical argmax is deterministic for fixed scores and tie handling, but production outputs can still vary with model versions, numerics, and serving. Greedy decoding also does not establish factual correctness or valid JSON by itself.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Beam search retains alternatives</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A beam of width B expands and prunes partial sequences according to a score, often a sum of log probabilities with length or stopping adjustments. It can avoid some early greedy mistakes, but finite-width pruning can still remove the best eventual path. It is an approximate search procedure, not a guarantee of global maximum likelihood.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Additional branches require state and work, including cache handling. The runtime cost need not be exactly B times one greedy run because batching and shared prefixes matter, but it can be substantial. Streaming is harder when branches disagree, though systems can use shared prefixes or policies rather than waiting for every beam to converge completely.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Why open-ended chat often uses other approaches</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Maximum-likelihood sequence search can favor generic, repetitive, or unusually short outputs under some model and scoring conditions. The text-degeneration literature illustrates that higher sequence likelihood is not the same as more natural or useful text. Modern instruction training changes behavior, so those observations should not be treated as proof that every beam output is bland.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Open-ended tasks also admit many valid continuations, making diversity useful. Sampling can explore alternatives without maintaining a full beam. Temperature changes concentration, top-k limits candidate count, and top-p limits a cumulative-probability set. These controls can improve a workload, but they can also increase error or remove useful rare tokens.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Preserve the task constraints</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Translation and summarization do not have only one correct wording. Code and extraction can also admit several valid outputs. Choose decoding according to the acceptance criterion and evaluate the real task. Beam search can be useful for some constrained or sequence-transduction settings; sampling or greedy methods can be useful for others.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For structured output, supported grammar or schema constraints and semantic validation matter more than a blanket recommendation for temperature zero. Repetition penalties can damage required repeated identifiers or code syntax, so apply them only when measured. A perfectly probable or syntactically valid sequence can still be wrong.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Compare under equal resources and requirements</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Measure correctness, completeness, diversity where needed, latency, throughput, and failure behavior. Include length and stopping policies because they affect both quality and cost. The senior answer is that beam search is less common in many open-ended assistant paths because its extra search does not necessarily optimize user utility, while sampling and constrained methods offer other trade-offs. The best choice follows the model and task contract rather than a universal decoding recipe.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate sequence likelihood, task utility, and output constraints</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Decoding selects an output sequence from a model's conditional distribution. The highest-probability next token, the highest-probability complete sequence, and the most useful answer are different objectives. A decoding method can optimize one while failing another. Explain the objective before labeling a strategy better or worse.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Greedy selection follows one locally maximal path. Beam methods retain several partial paths under a scoring rule, often with length handling and stopping rules. Sampling introduces controlled variation through a distribution and optional filtering. Implementation details matter: penalties, constraints, temperature, and truncation order can change the resulting distribution and behavior.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A parser-facing task needs an explicit format contract and validation rather than relying on low randomness alone. Schema-constrained generation can enforce supported structural rules while semantic checks establish whether the values are correct. A valid JSON object can still contain the wrong ID, missing work, or an unsupported claim.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Evaluate generation under the intended use: accuracy and completeness for factual tasks, useful diversity for ideation, valid constraints for structured data, and latency for serving. Do not assume every translation has one correct wording or every open-ended task needs sampling. Deterministic mathematical selection also does not imply identical service output across model or runtime changes. Choose decoding according to measured utility and constraints, not a universal preference for maximum probability or maximum variety.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate mathematical equivalence from floating-point behavior</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Equations describe ideal arithmetic, while implementations use finite representations, approximations, reduction orders, and hardware-specific kernels. Two implementations can compute the same mathematical operation without producing bit-identical results. Small differences are often harmless, but they can matter near a decision boundary or grow across a long generated sequence. State which equivalence claim is being made.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use stable normalization and inspect the quantities that can overflow or underflow. Softmax is commonly evaluated after subtracting the row maximum, which preserves its mathematical value while reducing numerical risk. This does not solve every issue: fully masked rows, invalid inputs, extreme scales, or low-precision accumulation still need defined behavior. Scaling and normalization should follow the model and kernel contract rather than an improvised rule.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Precision choices affect weights, activations, gradients, optimizer state, and caches differently. A model described as four-bit may keep several of these in higher precision. Quantization scales and metadata also consume memory. Report the actual representations instead of assuming one advertised bit width describes the entire training or serving system.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare against a suitable higher-precision reference with explicit tolerances and task checks. A tiny tensor error does not automatically establish a negligible application effect, and a changed generated token does not automatically establish a meaningful quality regression. Inspect both numerical behavior and downstream requirements. This distinction prevents claims such as exact attention means identical bits or lower precision always preserves quality.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Separate prefill, decoding, and training behavior</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">A decoder-based language model has different execution regimes. Training commonly processes known sequences in parallel while computing gradients. Prefill processes the available prompt and establishes state for generation. Autoregressive decoding then produces successive tokens conditioned on previous ones. These regimes share model components but differ in shapes, parallelism, and resource pressure.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">An optimization that helps prefill may do little for long-output decoding. Reusing a prompt prefix can reduce repeated prompt processing while each new output token still attends to a growing context. A faster attention kernel may have a different benefit at one query position than at thousands. Conversely, an approach that improves low-batch decoding can reduce throughput when the device is already well utilized.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Record time to first token, output-token latency, total completion time, throughput, and tail latency under realistic concurrency. Include input and output length distributions. A benchmark using a tiny prompt and huge answer is not interchangeable with document analysis using a long prompt and a short answer. User-visible responsiveness and completed-task cost can favor different configurations.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Training measurements need their own accounting: examples or tokens processed, optimizer steps, activation strategy, gradient accumulation, and communication. A technique that reduces trainable parameters may still require backpropagation through much of the network. Keep these distinctions explicit so an inference optimization is not mistakenly presented as a universal training acceleration, or a storage saving as a complete reduction in computation.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Account for the complete memory footprint</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Model capacity planning requires more than multiplying parameter count by an advertised storage precision. Weights may need scales, zero points, alignment, and selected higher-precision tensors. Training adds gradients, optimizer states, activations, and temporary buffers. Serving adds cache blocks, request metadata, workspaces, and memory needed for batching or speculative branches.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Write a component budget in bytes and distinguish decimal gigabytes from binary gibibytes. For float32, one parameter value occupies four bytes; for packed low-bit values, metadata and incomplete packing alter the effective average. A nominal reduction in one component is not the same ratio for the entire process. If weights are compressed while caches dominate, total concurrency may improve much less than expected.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Peak memory can decide feasibility. Loading, adapter merging, checkpoint saving, attention computation, and optimizer steps can create temporary allocations beyond the steady state. Distributed sharding and offloading change where memory resides, but introduce communication and transfer costs. Do not call a configuration impossible or guaranteed to fit without stating the hardware and execution assumptions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Measure allocated and reserved memory with the actual framework, representative lengths, batch sizes, and active features. Include worst-important cases, not only a short warm-up prompt. Leave operational headroom for concurrent requests and maintenance. This makes memory estimates useful for choosing a design while avoiding false precision from a formula that omits half the serving stack.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Benchmark the hardware-software combination actually deployed</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Accelerator specifications do not guarantee that a model uses their fastest path. Datatype support, matrix shapes, kernel availability, memory layout, compiler behavior, and library versions determine realized performance. A compressed checkpoint can occupy less storage yet run slowly if the backend repeatedly converts it or lacks an efficient kernel for that representation.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare the same workload at the same quality target. Warm-up, synchronization, batch size, concurrency, device placement, and cache state must be controlled or reported. Include end-to-end service overhead where it affects users, while preserving separate kernel measurements for diagnosis. A speedup measured in one operator is not automatically the same speedup for the whole request.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Distributed execution adds communication and scheduling effects. Tensor parallelism, expert routing, sharding, and offloading can move the bottleneck away from arithmetic. Network topology and interconnect bandwidth matter, as do uneven work distribution and synchronization waits. A theoretically sparse computation may become communication-heavy in the actual deployment.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use profiling to identify whether the limiting resource is compute, bandwidth, memory capacity, I/O, or coordination. Then choose an optimization that addresses that limit. Avoid universal claims that modern kernels are always memory-bound or that a certain numeric format always makes decoding faster. Performance conclusions should name the model, workload, hardware, and software conditions under which they were observed.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use the strongest available check for each requirement</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Verification should match the property being claimed. Arithmetic can be checked with calculation, code behavior with relevant tests, schema shape with a validator, and source support with evidence review. A model-generated explanation of why it is correct is not an independent guarantee. Equally, a narrow objective check does not establish every aspect of a broad task.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For reasoning tasks, distinguish a correct final answer from a valid method and from a robust process. Several sampled solutions can agree on the same wrong assumption. A verifier may catch some errors, but can itself be incomplete, exploitable, or dependent on an incorrect reference. Test verifier failure modes rather than assuming that an executable signal makes training or inference automatically safe.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">For numerical and performance methods, verify the claimed resource saving separately from task quality. Smaller tensors do not establish faster serving, and close output logits do not establish unchanged user outcomes. Check the full configuration under the conditions where the claim will be used.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">When no adequate deterministic check exists, use explicit rubrics, calibrated model judgment, or human review. Preserve uncertainty instead of inventing a false binary certainty. Associate verification with the exact artifact or model version evaluated. A later revision, merge, precision conversion, or decoding change may need reassessment. Verification is useful when it limits what can legitimately be concluded, not when it becomes a ceremonial pass label.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Evaluate the task contract, not just a proxy score</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Perplexity, numerical reconstruction error, benchmark accuracy, and human preference measure different properties. A model can preserve average language-model loss while regressing on exact identifiers, rare languages, long-range reasoning, or structured extraction. Select metrics that establish the actual capability being promised rather than assuming one aggregate proxy captures every important effect.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Build representative cases with ordinary requests, difficult constraints, ambiguous inputs, missing evidence, and appropriate no-answer behavior. Use objective checks where available, and calibrate model-based or human review against explicit criteria where exact matching is inadequate. A passing schema checks shape; a passing test checks its specified behavior; neither automatically establishes complete correctness.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Compare candidate and baseline on the same cases and source snapshot. Inspect per-category differences and severe failures before accepting an average improvement. Report uncertainty and repeated-run behavior when sampling is relevant. A small gain from a tiny sample can be noise, while a rare but important regression can be hidden by many easy successes.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Keep held-out assessment separate from iterative tuning. Version the model, tokenizer, prompts, decoding, data, and relevant serving settings with each result. This makes it possible to tell whether an observed change comes from the technique being tested or from another part of the stack. The useful conclusion is that a configuration meets a defined task requirement under measured conditions, not that it is universally near-lossless or best.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Use controlled comparisons and meaningful ablations</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Before changing a model or serving configuration, write the hypothesis and the expected measurable effect. If the proposed change is meant to reduce cache memory, measure cache memory separately from weights. If it is meant to improve evidence use, hold the evidence constant while testing the model behavior. A successful output after several simultaneous changes does not reveal which intervention mattered.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Vary one important factor at a time where practical, then evaluate interactions deliberately. Rank, scaling, learning rate, target modules, precision, and batch size can affect one another. A fair comparison may require either equal training compute, equal parameter budget, equal memory, or equal quality; state which resource is held fixed. Different choices answer different engineering questions.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Use a simple reference and include negative controls. For example, a mask test should fail when the future-token restriction is deliberately removed, and an evaluator should notice an intentionally unsupported claim. Such checks establish that the experiment is sensitive to the property it claims to measure. They are often more informative than increasing the benchmark size without inspecting examples.</p>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\">Preserve configurations and intermediate artifacts needed to interpret results. Record failed runs and resource limits rather than reporting only the best seed. Once required checks pass, broaden experiments only to resolve a new uncertainty or justify a deployment decision. The aim is enough evidence for a reliable choice, not an endless collection of attractive but incomparable numbers.</p>\n<h3 style=\"margin:28px 0 12px; font-size:17px; font-weight:600; line-height:1.5\">Further reading</h3>\n<p style=\"margin:0 0 16px\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09751\" style=\"text-decoration:underline; text-underline-offset:3px\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\">Neural text degeneration and nucleus sampling</a></p>\n</div>"}]
